entry.title: Milne’s rationality conjecture and geometry after reduction
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 001 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A geometric object defined by polynomial equations can be studied over the complex numbers or reduced modulo a prime. These two settings have different tools. Complex geometry uses topology and differential forms; geometry in characteristic ppp uses arithmetic substitutes that retain information invisible to ordinary point counting.

Suppose both descriptions produce an intersection number. Must they produce the same rational number? For actual algebraic subvarieties, the geometry supplies a common answer. The difficulty is that topology predicts classes which are not already known to come from algebraic subvarieties, while reduction can create additional divisors that did not exist upstairs.

Family 001 concerns this gap for abelian varieties. Its manuscript, M1, claims Milne’s rationality conjecture: a rational Hodge class, after good reduction, has the same rational pairing with every complementary product of divisors in all the specified cohomology theories. A stronger consequence supplies an actual algebraic cycle on the reduction, using a separate theorem about complex multiplication. Keeping these two assertions distinct is essential to understanding the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

Abelian varieties and reduction

An abelian variety is a smooth projective algebraic variety with a commutative algebraic group law. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example. Over the complex numbers, an abelian variety of dimension ddd looks analytically like Cd/Λ\mathbb C^d/\LambdaCd/Λ, where Λ\LambdaΛ is a lattice of rank 2d2d2d, with an additional condition ensuring projectivity.

The coefficients of the variety here belong to Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​, the field of algebraic numbers. They can be placed in a number field. Choosing a prime above a rational prime ppp then permits reduction of an integral model. Good reduction means that the resulting special fiber is again a smooth abelian variety. Write the original variety as AAA and its reduction, over an algebraic closure of the field with ppp elements, as A0A_0A0​.

Good reduction preserves much structure, but it need not preserve the collection of available algebraic subvarieties. In particular, A0A_0A0​ may have divisors that do not lift to AAA. The question is therefore not settled simply by reducing intersections already performed in characteristic zero.

Cycles, Hodge classes, and realizations

An algebraic cycle of codimension rrr is a finite formal combination of subvarieties of dimension d−rd-rd−r. Rational coefficients are allowed throughout this digest. A divisor has codimension one. Intersecting a codimension-rrr cycle with d−rd-rd−r divisors gives a zero-dimensional cycle, whose degree is a rational number.

Cohomology assigns a linear-algebraic class to a cycle. Over C\mathbb CC, the relevant group is H2r(A(C),Q)H^{2r}(A(\mathbb C),\mathbb Q)H2r(A(C),Q). Complex differential forms split cohomology into types (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), according to the numbers of holomorphic and antiholomorphic directions. A rational Hodge class in degree 2r2r2r is a rational cohomology class of type (r,r)(r,r)(r,r). Algebraic cycles give such classes. The rational Hodge conjecture asks for the converse.

A realization is one of the compatible cohomological descriptions used in different arithmetic settings. For each prime ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p, étale cohomology uses the field Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​ of ℓ\ellℓ-adic numbers. At ppp, crystalline cohomology plays the corresponding role. A ppp-adic completion of Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​, denoted Cw\mathbb C_wCw​, is used for the comparison in M1.

The notation Q(r)\mathbb Q(r)Q(r), and its arithmetic analogues, denotes a Tate twist. Here its role is normalization: it makes cycle classes and the trace on top-degree cohomology agree with geometric degree. Understanding the claim does not require constructing the twist explicitly.

For a divisor DDD, write c1(D)c_1(D)c1​(D) for its cohomology class. Multiplication of classes is the cup product, the cohomological counterpart of intersection. The trace Tr⁡\operatorname{Tr}Tr turns a top-degree class into its numerical intersection value. A Lefschetz class is a rational linear combination of products of divisor classes.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The broad background is the relationship between Hodge classes in characteristic zero and Tate classes in positive characteristic. A Tate class is, roughly, an appropriately normalized arithmetic cohomology class fixed by a power of Frobenius, the symmetry induced by raising coordinates to the field characteristic. These classes are candidates for algebraic cycle classes, just as Hodge classes are over the complex numbers.

Deligne’s theorem that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are absolute Hodge supplies strong compatibility between their realizations. Blasius’s work establishes the needed ppp-adic comparison. These results make it possible to transport the classes between theories, but compatibility alone does not say that pairing with a newly appearing divisor is rational. M1 reviews this distinction in its introduction; the original comparison result is Blasius’s A p-adic property of Hodge classes on abelian varieties.

Milne developed rationality formulations while studying reductions of Shimura varieties and the Langlands–Rapoport conjecture. His Rational Tate classes explains why one would like a common rational algebra inside the different Tate-class spaces. Such an algebra would support rational cohomological correspondences even before algebraic representatives were available.

One earlier positive case involves a CM abelian variety with simple ordinary reduction, together with its powers. In that setting the divisor classes on the reduction lift, removing the central obstruction. The general case must handle divisors that exist only after reduction.

A CM abelian variety has especially many commuting algebraic symmetries: for dimension ddd, its rational endomorphism algebra contains a commutative semisimple algebra of dimension 2d2d2d. “CM” abbreviates complex multiplication. Earlier work of André reduces Hodge-class questions to special determinant-type classes associated with such symmetries. Milne’s 2025 account develops the lifting strategy and explains conditional criteria along this route.

M1 claims to complete the rationality argument through carefully controlled auxiliary lifts and a common rational normalization. The stronger algebraicity consequence uses the separately stated CM Hodge theorem. Neither the historical comparison theorems nor rationality by itself should be conflated with that additional input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

One rational number in every realization

Fix a prime ppp and a place www above it. Let A/Q‾A/\overline{\mathbb Q}A/Q​ have dimension ddd and good reduction A0A_0A0​, and let

γ∈H2r(A(C),Q(r)),0≤r≤d,\gamma\in H^{2r}(A(\mathbb C),\mathbb Q(r)),\qquad 0\leq r\leq d,γ∈H2r(A(C),Q(r)),0≤r≤d,

be a rational Hodge class. Write γ0,ℓ\gamma_{0,\ell}γ0,ℓ​ and γ0,p\gamma_{0,p}γ0,p​ for its specialized realizations. Given any Cartier divisors D1,…,Dd−rD_1,\ldots,D_{d-r}D1​,…,Dd−r​ on A0A_0A0​, M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that one number q∈Qq\in\mathbb Qq∈Q satisfies

Tr⁡ℓ ⁣(γ0,ℓ∏j=1d−rc1,ℓ(Dj))=q(ℓ≠p),\operatorname{Tr}_{\ell}\!\left(\gamma_{0,\ell}\prod_{j=1}^{d-r}c_{1,\ell}(D_j)\right)=q\qquad(\ell\ne p),Trℓ​(γ0,ℓ​j=1∏d−r​c1,ℓ​(Dj​))=q(ℓ=p),

and

Tr⁡p ⁣(γ0,p∏j=1d−rc1,cris(Dj))=q.\operatorname{Tr}_{p}\!\left(\gamma_{0,p}\prod_{j=1}^{d-r}c_{1,\mathrm{cris}}(D_j)\right)=q.Trp​(γ0,p​j=1∏d−r​c1,cris​(Dj​))=q.

The first equalities take place in Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​; the crystalline equality is interpreted after extending coefficients to Cw\mathbb C_wCw​. They identify the images of the same rational number in these different fields. When r=dr=dr=d, the empty divisor product means one.

The theorem includes p=2p=2p=2, arbitrary dimension, and divisors acquired only on reduction. It compares realizations at the fixed reduction place. It does not say that reductions at different places produce the same number.

A common class, then an algebraic representative

Using Milne’s equivalence between CM rationality and a good theory of rational Tate classes, M1’s Corollary 6.3 places every specialized Hodge class in one fixed such rational theory. The cohomological class is unique within that theory and has all the required realizations.

Corollary 6.4 adds the CM Hodge theorem from family 032. With this input, it claims one rational algebraic cycle zγz_\gammazγ​ on A0A_0A0​ whose cycle class equals γ0,ℓ\gamma_{0,\ell}γ0,ℓ​ for every ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p, and equals γ0,p\gamma_{0,p}γ0,p​ in the crystalline comparison. Pairing with any complementary algebraic cycle then gives its rational intersection number.

The paper explicitly separates this consequence from Theorem 1.1: its rationality proof does not use the CM Hodge theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The result addresses a structural obstacle in moving between complex geometry and arithmetic geometry. It would supply a common rational meaning to pairings computed in coefficient fields that otherwise look unrelated, while accommodating geometric classes that appear only after reduction.

For a simple analogy, several measurement systems may each report a compatible value without demonstrating that the value comes from a single rational geometric quantity. Rationality identifies that shared quantity. The algebraicity consequence goes further by supplying a geometric representative whose intersection degree explains it.

The distinction has consequences for motives, which organize cohomological information and correspondences in a common framework. Rational Tate classes provide cohomological correspondences; actual algebraic cycles provide stronger geometric information. The rating reflects the breadth of this connection and the arbitrary-dimensional scope, while recognizing that the strongest cycle statement uses a separate major theorem.

6. The main idea

Transport to a more symmetric setting

The first step moves the specialized class to an auxiliary CM abelian variety. An isogeny is a surjective group homomorphism with finite kernel; a quasi-isogeny allows rational inverses to such maps. Working up to isogeny permits the paper to use rational homomorphisms between special fibers and powers of varieties.

The transport must carry the original rational class in every realization. A collection of locally proportional classes would not suffice, since the proportionality factors might differ between coefficient fields. M1 normalizes these factors by ratios of rational divisor intersections, claiming one common rational scalar.

The maps at this stage concern reductions. The construction does not require an isogeny between the original characteristic-zero variety and its CM auxiliary.

Reduce to determinant-type classes

The CM symmetries decompose the relevant linear spaces into eigenspaces. Special Weil classes are built from their top alternating forms, analogous to determinant forms. A balanced signature means that conjugate eigenspaces occur with matching Hodge multiplicities. M1 reduces the general class to rational combinations of pullbacks of these balanced classes.

For such a class, the key claim is a dichotomy. Either all its complementary pairings with divisor products vanish, or the specialized class itself is one rational polynomial in divisor classes across all realizations. The first case supplies the rational answer zero. The second reduces the desired numerical comparison to ordinary intersections of divisors.

Lift the extra divisor with the right structure

In the second case, a suitable endomorphism produces a divisor with a nondegenerate pairing on the relevant eigenspaces. The construction chooses a filtration, a nested sequence of linear subspaces recording Hodge-type information, compatible with the divisor, the symmetry action, and the polarization.

Arithmetic deformation results are then used to realize this prescribed filtration on a second auxiliary abelian variety over a local field. This second auxiliary need not have complex multiplication and serves a different purpose from the first. Keeping its divisor and selected algebraic maps liftable is the point of the construction.

After passing to a complex realization of this lift, coefficient extraction in polynomial identities expresses the determinant-type class as a rational combination of divisor products. That rational identity specializes in every cohomology theory, and pullback returns it to the original reduction.

For the additional algebraicity statement, the CM Hodge theorem supplies an algebraic representative upstairs on the CM auxiliary. Specialization and rational pullback then give one representative on A0A_0A0​. This explains precisely where the extra theorem enters.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns abelian varieties over algebraic numbers with good reduction at a fixed place. It does not cover arbitrary varieties or bad reduction. Rational coefficients are essential; an integral cycle statement with controlled denominators is stronger than what is asserted here.

The rationality conclusion tests complementary products of divisors. Pairing with arbitrary complementary algebraic cycles is part of the stronger algebraicity consequence and uses its additional CM input.

The resulting cycle lies on the special fiber. M1 does not claim that it lifts to a cycle on the original variety, or that it proves the Hodge conjecture for arbitrary abelian varieties in characteristic zero. Nor is the representing algebraic cycle asserted to be unique modulo rational equivalence: uniqueness of its class in a fixed rational cohomological theory is a different assertion.

These boundaries leave natural further questions about integral refinements, behavior under bad reduction, and lifting algebraic representatives back to characteristic zero. They also indicate why a common intersection value, a common cohomology class, and a common algebraic cycle are three distinct levels of information.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the rationality statement; Corollaries 6.3 and 6.4 distinguish rational Tate classes from algebraic specialization. Its introduction describes the history and the two different auxiliary lifts.

Milne’s Rational Tate classes and Abelian motives and Shimura varieties in nonzero characteristic supply the motivating framework. His notes on abelian varieties offer background on the geometric objects, divisors, and isogenies used here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Milne’s rationality conjecture for abelian varieties (October 7, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A fixed zero-free region for zeta and Dirichlet L-functions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 003 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Prime numbers become less frequent as numbers grow, but their local distribution is irregular. One way to study that irregularity is to replace the primes by a complex function whose zeros encode fluctuations in prime counts. The Riemann hypothesis predicts an extraordinarily precise location for those zeros. A weaker question has also resisted solution: can they at least be kept a fixed positive distance away from the vertical line with real part one?

Family 003 claims an affirmative answer. Its strongest manuscript, M1, states that the Riemann zeta function and every Dirichlet L-function have no zeros in

Re⁡s>78.\operatorname{Re}s>\frac78.Res>87​.

The same assertion covers finite-order Hecke L-functions over one particular quadratic number field. M2 supplies a separate presentation of a weaker fixed boundary, 11/1211/1211/12, and several arithmetic consequences. M3 addresses the exceptional real zeros called Landau–Siegel zeros through a different, algebraic argument.

The distinction between these claims and the Riemann hypothesis is substantial. Moving the forbidden boundary from one to seven-eighths would be a major advance, but the conjectured boundary is one-half. This digest reports the manuscripts’ claims; it does not establish their correctness.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a complex number s=σ+its=\sigma+its=σ+it, the number σ\sigmaσ is its real part and ttt its height. Initially, for σ>1\sigma>1σ>1, the zeta function is defined by

ζ(s)=∑n=1∞1ns=∏p prime(1−p−s)−1.\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^s} =\prod_{p\text{ prime}}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}.ζ(s)=n=1∑∞​ns1​=p prime∏​(1−p−s)−1.

The product explains why this analytic function knows about primes. Analytic continuation extends it beyond the region where this series converges, with a pole at s=1s=1s=1. A pole is a singularity, not a zero. Its nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip 0<σ<10<\sigma<10<σ<1; the Riemann hypothesis places them on σ=1/2\sigma=1/2σ=1/2.

A Dirichlet character χ\chiχ modulo a positive integer qqq is a periodic, multiplicative function of integers. It is zero on integers sharing a factor with qqq, and takes root-of-unity values on the others. Characters separate residue classes in sums, allowing one to count primes such as those congruent to one or three modulo four. Their functions are

L(s,χ)=∑n=1∞χ(n)ns=∏p(1−χ(p)p−s)−1(σ>1).L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\chi(n)}{n^s} =\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1} \qquad(\sigma>1).L(s,χ)=n=1∑∞​nsχ(n)​=p∏​(1−χ(p)p−s)−1(σ>1).

The conductor is the smallest modulus from which the character is induced. A character is primitive if its displayed modulus is that conductor. Real nonprincipal characters take values 0,1,−10,1,-10,1,−1; a real zero very close to one is the potential exceptional phenomenon in classical zero-free theorems.

Hecke characters generalize this language from integers to ideals of a number field. Here the field is

K=Q(−3),OK=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3}),\qquad\mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z[\omega],\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}.K=Q(−3​),OK​=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.

An ideal is an additive subgroup of this ring closed under multiplication by every ring element. Its norm NaN\mathfrak aNa is the number of elements in the finite quotient OK/a\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak aOK​/a. A finite-order Hecke character η\etaη assigns roots of unity to ideals, subject to multiplicativity and congruence conditions, and is extended by zero at ideals not coprime to its conductor. Its L-series replaces nnn by NaN\mathfrak aNa.

“Fixed zero-free half-plane” means a single boundary works for every height and every character under consideration. Constants in intermediate estimates may depend on a character without changing that common boundary.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Riemann’s 1859 memoir connected prime counting with the zeros of ζ\zetaζ. In 1896, Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved that no zero lies on σ=1\sigma=1σ=1, leading to the prime number theorem: the number of primes up to xxx is asymptotic to x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx. Hadamard’s original paper makes that connection explicit.

Later work pushed the zero-free region slightly left of one. A classical Dirichlet L-function theorem has a boundary of the approximate shape

σ>1−clog⁡(q(∣t∣+3)),\sigma>1-\frac{c}{\log(q(|t|+3))},σ>1−log(q(∣t∣+3))c​,

with an absolute positive constant ccc, apart from a possible simple real zero for a real character. The permitted width shrinks as conductor or height grows. Vinogradov–Korobov estimates improve the height dependence for zeta; Ford’s account and explicit estimates develop that direction. Their boundary still approaches one at large height. A fixed strip is a qualitatively different conclusion.

The possible real exception has its own history. Siegel’s 1935 theorem gives a strong lower bound for L(1,χ)L(1,\chi)L(1,χ), but its constant is ineffective: the argument does not provide a computable value. Page’s theorem severely limits how many exceptional characters can occur in a conductor range. Deuring–Heilbronn repulsion says that an exceptional zero pushes other zeros away. These results constrain the obstruction without uniformly eliminating it. M3 situates its claim in this development.

The analytic manuscripts draw on another line: Kubota’s automorphic functions, Patterson’s cubic theta series, and large-sieve inequalities controlling averages of character sums. Dunn and Radziwiłł’s work on cubic Gauss sums supplies unconditional theta-expansion formulas used in this framework. Their conditional prime asymptotic is not an input to M1. The separate unconditional Patterson claim in family 023 is also not an input to M1.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Three different statements

M1, Theorem 1.1, asserts that every finite-order Hecke L-function over K=Q(−3)K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})K=Q(−3​), and every Dirichlet L-function, is zero-free for σ>7/8\sigma>7/8σ>7/8. Principal characters may have a pole at one. The boundary line itself is excluded from the assertion.

M2, Theorem 1.1, states the same families are zero-free for σ>11/12\sigma>11/12σ>11/12. Since 7/8<11/127/8<11/127/8<11/12, M1 gives the stronger exclusion. M2 isolates a shorter argument and spells out consequences; these are companion treatments within one family, not three equivalent formulations of RH.

M3 states that there is an absolute c>0c>0c>0 such that every real zero β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1)β∈(0,1) of a primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet character of conductor q≥3q\ge3q≥3 satisfies

(1−β)log⁡q≥c.(1-\beta)\log q\ge c.(1−β)logq≥c.

This is a uniform logarithmic gap for real zeros. It addresses the exceptional-zero problem but does not itself supply a fixed half-plane for all complex zeros. The stronger conclusions of M1 and M2 overlap its real-zero consequence.

Consequences stated in M2

Let π(x;q,a)\pi(x;q,a)π(x;q,a) count primes at most xxx congruent to aaa modulo qqq, and let φ(q)\varphi(q)φ(q) count the residue classes coprime to qqq. M2 gives

sup⁡1≤q≤x(a,q)=1∣π(x;q,a)−1φ(q)∫2xdtlog⁡t∣≪x11/12log⁡x.\sup_{\substack{1\le q\le x\\(a,q)=1}}\left|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac1{\varphi(q)}\int_2^x\frac{dt}{\log t}\right|\ll x^{11/12}\log x.1≤q≤x(a,q)=1​sup​​π(x;q,a)−φ(q)1​∫2x​logtdt​​≪x11/12logx.

Here ≪\ll≪ means bounded by an absolute constant times the expression on the right; M2 states that constant is effective. For very large qqq, the error can exceed the main term. Uniformity alone does not make this a useful relative approximation in every progression.

M2 also claims a fixed-power-of-log⁡p\log plogp bound for the least quadratic nonresidue modulo an odd prime ppp: the smallest positive integer that is not a nonzero square modulo ppp. Through the Tonelli–Shanks procedure, this gives deterministic square-root extraction in time polynomial in the number of digits of ppp. Its consequence for Miller’s primality test supplies another deterministic implementation; polynomial-time primality testing itself was already known through AKS.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. A uniform fixed zero-free region would change the available unconditional tools across analytic number theory. It addresses a central longstanding obstruction and yields consequences for prime distributions, quadratic fields, and algorithms.

The gain is stronger than a better numerical constant in the classical shrinking region. For example, knowing that no zero lies farther right than seven-eighths controls contributions from zeros by a fixed power of the scale. Classical regions often give savings that diminish with height. That difference propagates into applications.

M3 is important for a complementary reason: it claims to eliminate an obstruction whose possible existence has forced many results to carry an exception or an ineffective constant. The score reflects these mathematical consequences if the claims hold, not an assessment of proof reliability.

6. The main idea

Turn a zero question into a cancellation question

The integer Möbius function μ(n)\mu(n)μ(n) is zero if a square of a prime divides nnn, and otherwise equals (−1)k(-1)^k(−1)k when nnn has kkk distinct prime factors. In the absolutely convergent region,

1ζ(s)=∑n=1∞μ(n)ns.\frac1{\zeta(s)}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(n)}{n^s}.ζ(s)1​=n=1∑∞​nsμ(n)​.

Strong cancellation in sums of these signs can continue the reciprocal farther left. A zero of zeta would be a pole of that reciprocal, so analytic continuation with suitable bounds excludes zeros. The same principle works for character twists and the ideal Möbius function.

M2 studies smoothed sums

A1(D)=∑aμ(a)η(a)W(Na/D),A_1(D)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}\mu(\mathfrak a)\eta(\mathfrak a)W(N\mathfrak a/D),A1​(D)=a∑​μ(a)η(a)W(Na/D),

with the manuscript’s coprimality restrictions. The smooth function WWW selects ideals whose norms are comparable to DDD. A trivial estimate is roughly DDD; the target is D11/12+εD^{11/12+\varepsilon}D11/12+ε for every positive ε\varepsilonε.

Instead of estimating this one sum directly, M2 inserts sixth-power residue characters and studies a family Au(D)A_u(D)Au​(D). A mean-square bound says that these sums are small on average. Many indices uuu that are sixth powers reproduce the original sum up to controlled omissions. Consequently, an oversized original sum would force too many large members of the family.

Poisson summation, a form of Fourier duality, transforms the average. Finite Fourier transforms of residue characters produce Gauss sums. Arithmetic identities combine these with Möbius signs to produce cubic theta coefficients. Transformation laws of the theta function and recursive mean-square estimates then provide the asserted cancellation. Retaining full cube-divisor contributions is part of that argument, not a removable cosmetic detail.

How the stronger boundary is approached

M1 also compares two descriptions of completed cubic-theta sums: a reflected expression controlled by mean-square estimates, and a Poisson expression containing a reciprocal L-function. The first stage reaches 11/1211/1211/12. A second stage changes the weighting at selected primes and uses unequal averaging scales.

A hypothetical zero produces two large finite sums with the same character and height: one has Möbius coefficients, the other does not. Separate moment estimates bound how often both can be large. The manuscript combines these bounds, while treating principal terms and residues separately, to move the common boundary to 7/87/87/8. The simultaneous treatment of Hecke characters matters even for zeta, because transformations introduce additional twists.

The algebraic route in M3

M3 translates a hypothetical exceptional zero into an imbalance between primes on which a real character takes signs +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. It then constructs a nonzero interpolation determinant from algebraic numbers in a biquadratic field, a degree-four extension obtained by adjoining two square roots.

At primes of the plentiful sign, taking a ppp-th power modulo ppp acts like a particular field conjugation. Row operations therefore force high powers of many primes to divide the determinant’s norm, which is a nonzero integer. A carefully weighted selection of polynomial rows keeps its ordinary size small. The claimed contradiction is between excessive arithmetic divisibility and this size bound. This mechanism differs from the theta-function comparisons in M1 and M2.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The Riemann hypothesis and generalized Riemann hypotheses remain open in these manuscripts: neither boundary reaches one-half. No conclusion is asserted on the line σ=7/8\sigma=7/8σ=7/8 itself. The Hecke theorem is stated for finite-order characters of the specified imaginary quadratic field, not arbitrary automorphic L-functions over all number fields.

The three source statements should retain their different strengths. M3’s logarithmic real-zero exclusion is not a substitute for M1’s full fixed half-plane. M2’s algorithmic applications also do not make every algorithm previously conditional on GRH unconditional; each reduction has its own hypotheses.

Further questions include whether the analytic estimates can reach a smaller fixed boundary, whether related methods extend to other fields and higher-degree L-functions, and which applications can make efficient use of the explicit savings. These are directions suggested by the statements, not additional conclusions of this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction and proof overview explain the two-stage 11/1211/1211/12-to-7/87/87/8 strategy. M2’s Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2, and Section 2 provide the shorter claim, applications, and Möbius-sum outline. M3’s introduction describes the real-zero theorem and determinant mechanism.

The historical links in Section 3 lead to primary papers. For a systematic background reference, Iwaniec and Kowalski’s Analytic Number Theory develops characters, explicit formulas, and large sieves. The Möbius function is a useful optional entry point to the cancellation viewpoint.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane Re(s)>7/8 (30 September 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros (October 1, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Catalan’s constant: a determinant approach to irrationality
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 005 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Consider the alternating sum

G=1−132+152−172+⋯=∑j=0∞(−1)j(2j+1)2.G=1-\frac1{3^2}+\frac1{5^2}-\frac1{7^2}+\cdots =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^j}{(2j+1)^2}.G=1−321​+521​−721​+⋯=j=0∑∞​(2j+1)2(−1)j​.

This is Catalan’s constant, approximately 0.9160.9160.916. Its definition is elementary, and it can be calculated to very high precision. Yet computing digits does not answer a basic arithmetic question: is it a ratio of two integers?

Family 005 consists of one manuscript claiming that Catalan’s constant is irrational. Its strategy compares two kinds of size estimates for a sequence of determinants. If GGG were rational, prime-factor information would prevent these determinants from becoming too small. An integral representation is then used to show that they become smaller than that arithmetic bound permits.

The difficult part is arranging both estimates for the same nonzero quantities. This is a useful example of a general lesson in irrationality proofs: accurate approximation alone is not enough; one must also control the arithmetic cost of that accuracy.

2. Background and essential definitions

A real number is rational if it equals a/ba/ba/b for integers a,ba,ba,b with b≠0b\ne0b=0. Otherwise it is irrational. Transcendence is stronger: a transcendental number is not a root of any nonzero integer-coefficient polynomial. The manuscript claims irrationality, not transcendence.

Catalan’s constant is the value at two of the Dirichlet beta function,

β(s)=∑j=0∞(−1)j(2j+1)s.\beta(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^j}{(2j+1)^s}.β(s)=j=0∑∞​(2j+1)s(−1)j​.

At positive odd integers, beta values are known rational multiples of powers of π\piπ, for example β(1)=π/4\beta(1)=\pi/4β(1)=π/4 and β(3)=π3/32\beta(3)=\pi^3/32β(3)=π3/32. Even arguments present a different arithmetic problem. The alternating sign pattern comes from the character modulo four that is one on integers congruent to one, minus one on those congruent to three, and zero on even integers.

One classical irrationality criterion seeks integers Am,BmA_m,B_mAm​,Bm​ such that

0<∣AmG−Bm∣⟶0.0<|A_mG-B_m|\longrightarrow0.0<∣Am​G−Bm​∣⟶0.

If G=a/bG=a/bG=a/b, then b(AmG−Bm)b(A_mG-B_m)b(Am​G−Bm​) would be a nonzero integer tending to zero, which is impossible. The nonzero condition is essential.

This criterion is stronger than Bm/Am→GB_m/A_m\to GBm​/Am​→G. For instance, an approximation error of order Am−0.6A_m^{-0.6}Am−0.6​ tends to zero, but multiplication by AmA_mAm​ gives a quantity of order Am0.4A_m^{0.4}Am0.4​, which need not be small. Fast numerical convergence and useful integer linear forms are different achievements.

A determinant combines entries of a square matrix into a number that vanishes exactly when its rows are linearly dependent. The manuscript replaces individual linear forms by determinants of growing size. A moment here means an integral of a polynomial against a fixed kernel; assembling many moments creates a matrix whose determinant has both an arithmetic description and an analytic one.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of ζ(3)\zeta(3)ζ(3), followed by Beukers’s integral proofs for ζ(2)\zeta(2)ζ(2) and ζ(3)\zeta(3)ζ(3), demonstrated how recurrence relations and multiple integrals can yield small integer linear forms. Their success encouraged analogous constructions for other special values.

For beta values, Rivoal and Zudilin proved that infinitely many even values are irrational and that at least one among β(2),β(4),…,β(14)\beta(2),\beta(4),\ldots,\beta(14)β(2),β(4),…,β(14) is irrational. Later work reduced the finite list, ultimately to the five values through β(10)\beta(10)β(10), as recorded by Lai and Zhou. Such statements do not identify which member of the list is irrational.

For Catalan’s constant specifically, Zudilin constructed an Apéry-like recurrence and continued fraction. The rational approximations converge rapidly, but the resulting integer linear forms fail to decay after denominators are cleared. Rivoal and then Krattenthaler–Rivoal established important cancellations in those denominators. They sharpened the arithmetic estimates without overcoming the entire obstruction.

A later determinantal approach of Zudilin compared denominator growth with integral estimates on a quadratic scale in matrix size. For positive moment matrices, positivity provides nonvanishing. The Catalan construction considered there still suffered from excessive denominator growth. The present manuscript uses a different, signed mixture of moments, requiring a separate nonvanishing argument.

Nearby successes also need careful separation. Calegari, Dimitrov, and Tang established linear independence involving a character of conductor three, whereas Catalan’s constant uses conductor four. Irrationality of a 2-adic analogue likewise concerns a different number system and does not settle the real constant. Finally, M1 notes an earlier 2026 preprint by Zhi-Wei Sun announcing the same qualitative conclusion; it states that it does not use that preprint. The digest therefore does not assign priority to this manuscript.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states simply

G∉Q.G\notin\mathbb Q.G∈/Q.

There are no conditional hypotheses in that theorem. The manuscript describes a qualitative irrationality argument, without claiming a bound on how well GGG can be approximated by arbitrary rational numbers.

Its central objects are determinants ΔN\Delta_NΔN​ of size 48N48N48N, for positive integers NNN. Define the normalized logarithm

LN=log⁡∣ΔN∣(48N)2−12log⁡2.L_N=\frac{\log|\Delta_N|}{(48N)^2}-\frac12\log2.LN​=(48N)2log∣ΔN​∣​−21​log2.

Under the temporary hypothesis that GGG is rational, M1 claims two arithmetic facts: the determinants are rational, and Δp≠0\Delta_p\ne0Δp​=0 for every sufficiently large prime ppp. On any sequence of nonzero determinants its denominator estimates give

lim inf⁡N→∞LN>−2.29084.\liminf_{N\to\infty}L_N>-2.29084.N→∞liminf​LN​>−2.29084.

An independent real-variable estimate gives

lim sup⁡N→∞LN≤−2.290939875.\limsup_{N\to\infty}L_N\le-2.290939875.N→∞limsup​LN​≤−2.290939875.

Applying both bounds along the prime sequence produces the stated contradiction. The numerical separation is small but strict: the proposed upper bound is below the proposed lower bound.

M1 also draws a geometric corollary. With sectional curvature normalized to −1-1−1, Agol’s theorem identifies 4G4G4G as the minimum volume of an orientable, complete, finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold with exactly two cusps. A cusp is an end extending to infinity while contributing finite volume. Irrationality of GGG therefore makes this minimum irrational. The manuscript additionally obtains irrationality for arithmetic hyperbolic three-orbifold volumes defined over Q(i)\mathbb Q(i)Q(i), because their known volume formulas are positive rational multiples of GGG.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Catalan’s constant is a prominent elementary special value whose arithmetic has resisted methods successful for related constants. Identifying this individual number as irrational would resolve a longstanding question rather than merely guarantee an unspecified irrational member of a family.

The proposed method is also significant. It combines carefully engineered cancellation of unwanted constants, prime-by-prime denominator bounds, algebraic nonvanishing, and real analytic estimates. A successful construction of this kind could inform attempts on other special values, although no general extension is established here.

The geometric consequences illustrate how a question about a short alternating series can affect the arithmetic nature of volumes. The rating reflects this combination of centrality within irrationality theory and broader connections, conditional on the stated result.

6. The main idea

First remove the unwanted constant

The manuscript starts from two elementary integration kernels. Their moments are rational linear combinations of three quantities:

1,G,ζ(2)=π26.1,\qquad G,\qquad \zeta(2)=\frac{\pi^2}{6}.1,G,ζ(2)=6π2​.

Assuming GGG rational would not make such moments rational if a ζ(2)\zeta(2)ζ(2) term remained. The polynomial rows are therefore designed so that two expressions have many equal initial Taylor coefficients. This high-order agreement makes the unwanted ζ(2)\zeta(2)ζ(2) coefficients cancel in the mixed entries.

The rows are built from Chebyshev polynomials, characterized by Td(cos⁡θ)=cos⁡(dθ)T_d(\cos\theta)=\cos(d\theta)Td​(cosθ)=cos(dθ). Their integral coefficients and recurrence relations give simultaneous control over Taylor behavior and arithmetic divisibility. They serve more than an approximation role: their arithmetic structure is used later in the denominator estimates.

After cancellation, each matrix entry lies in Q+QG\mathbb Q+\mathbb QGQ+QG. Thus the hypothesis G∈QG\in\mathbb QG∈Q makes the whole determinant rational. It need not be a linear form in GGG; rationality of its entries is what the argument needs.

Denominators set a lower limit on size

If a nonzero rational number has denominator dividing a positive integer DDD, its absolute value is at least 1/D1/D1/D. More generally, for nonzero rational rrr, write vp(r)v_p(r)vp​(r) for the exponent of ppp in its prime factorization, allowing negative exponents. Then

log⁡∣r∣=∑pvp(r)log⁡p.\log|r|=\sum_p v_p(r)\log p.log∣r∣=p∑​vp​(r)logp.

Only finitely many terms are nonzero. This relation lets the manuscript convert information at finite primes into an ordinary real lower bound for ∣ΔN∣|\Delta_N|∣ΔN​∣.

At the large odd primes contributing to the leading estimate, the construction has denominator layers involving both p2p^2p2 and ppp. M1 tracks both; controlling only the first would not yield its final inequality. The prime two receives a separate estimate. The only prime-distribution input stated for this stage is the ordinary prime number theorem, not the new zero-free claims in family 003.

Make sure the determinant does not vanish

Because the moments are mixed with signs, positivity cannot simply certify a nonzero determinant. M1 instead specializes the scale to a large prime N=pN=pN=p.

Modulo ppp, taking a ppp-th power simplifies polynomial expressions through the identity (x+y)p=xp+yp(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p(x+y)p=xp+yp. Together with changes of polynomial bases, this reduces the growing nonvanishing problem to three fixed rational matrices. The manuscript supplies exact finite certificates for those matrices and uses them to claim nonvanishing for all sufficiently large prime scales. This is an arithmetic nonvanishing argument, not a claim that every determinant is positive.

The integral description makes it too small

An integration identity rewrites the determinant as a multiple integral involving products of differences between nodes. Such products are Vandermonde factors, familiar from polynomial interpolation. Their logarithms are sums of terms such as log⁡∣xi−xj∣\log|x_i-x_j|log∣xi​−xj​∣, which can be treated as interactions among points.

The construction’s rational parametrization has two branches. M1 retains both, using bounded holomorphic interpolation in one range of configurations and a determinant norm bound in the other. The interpolation estimate is formulated to remain uniform when nodes approach each other; dividing by a small Vandermonde determinant would otherwise lose control.

The remaining optimization is expressed through Chebyshev expansions of logarithmic kernels and explicit rational trial data. M1 reports certificates enclosing stationary points and controlling complete intervals around them. These data supply the stated strict upper bound, rather than merely plotting a likely maximum. The digest describes that role without independently checking the certificates.

All three ingredients are needed together: rationality under the hypothesis, nonvanishing on an unbounded sequence, and incompatible size estimates on that same sequence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The conclusion is qualitative irrationality. It does not establish transcendence of GGG, algebraic independence from π\piπ, or an irrationality measure controlling every sufficiently accurate rational approximation. The manuscript explicitly says that the latter would require additional information.

The prime-scale nonvanishing assertion is made under the rationality hypothesis used for contradiction. One should not silently replace it by unconditional positivity for all NNN. Likewise, the precision of the displayed constants is part of the source’s claimed estimates; their appearance here is not an independent numerical verification.

Questions remain about the other individual even beta values, the extent to which similar determinant constructions can isolate them, and whether a quantitative approximation theorem can accompany this qualitative result. The hyperbolic-volume corollary concerns the stated geometric classes and normalization, not arbitrary hyperbolic volumes.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction states the approximation obstruction and determinant strategy. Sections 2–4 address cancellation, denominator control, and nonvanishing; Sections 5–7 develop the analytic bound; Section 8 gives the final comparison and geometric consequences.

The historical papers in Section 3 provide the successive approximation and denominator results. Agol’s two-cusped volume theorem supplies the geometric identification used in the corollary. For optional background, see Catalan’s constant and Chebyshev polynomials.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Catalan’s constant is irrational (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals: a claimed limit of algorithms
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 004 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Suppose a computer receives a polynomial with integer coefficients, such as

f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.f(X,Y)=X^2+Y^2-3.f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.

Can one algorithm always decide whether the equation f=0f=0f=0 has a solution whose coordinates are rational numbers? The algorithm may take a long time, but it must eventually return the correct yes or no for every input. Both the polynomial and its number of variables are allowed to vary.

This is Hilbert’s tenth problem over Q\mathbb QQ. Family 004’s main manuscript, M1, claims that no such algorithm exists. It further places the problem at the same level of Turing unsolvability as the halting problem and retains that conclusion for polynomials of degree at most four.

A companion, M2, supplies an elliptic-curve theorem used in the construction. The connection is unexpected: information about rational points and L-functions becomes part of an argument about the limits of computation. The route does not produce a single polynomial definition of the integers inside the rationals, a distinction essential to understanding the claim.

2. Background and essential definitions

A polynomial is a finite sum of monomials with specified coefficients. A rational zero of f∈Z[X1,…,Xn]f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_n]f∈Z[X1​,…,Xn​] is a tuple (a1,…,an)∈Qn(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb Q^n(a1​,…,an​)∈Qn for which f(a1,…,an)=0f(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=0f(a1​,…,an​)=0. Rational and integer solvability differ: 2X−1=02X-1=02X−1=0 has a rational solution but no integer solution. Allowing fractions does not preserve an integer-solvability problem unchanged.

A decision algorithm must halt on both yes and no instances. Rational solvability is already computably enumerable: enumerate all rational tuples and test them exactly. If a solution exists, this search eventually finds it. If none exists, enumeration continues forever. The missing ingredient is a procedure that also settles every negative instance.

The halting problem asks whether a given program eventually stops on a given input. A Turing reduction to another problem is an algorithm allowed to ask an oracle for answers to that other problem, possibly several times and adaptively. Two problems have the same Turing degree if each can be solved with an oracle for the other. The degree of the halting problem is denoted 0′0'0′.

An existential polynomial condition asks whether additional rational witnesses exist satisfying specified polynomial equations. Saying that Z\mathbb ZZ is Diophantine in Q\mathbb QQ would mean that there is one fixed polynomial PPP such that

x∈Z⟺∃y1,…,ym∈Q:P(x,y1,…,ym)=0.x\in\mathbb Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb Q:P(x,y_1,\ldots,y_m)=0.x∈Z⟺∃y1​,…,ym​∈Q:P(x,y1​,…,ym​)=0.

That would provide a direct translation of integer problems. A Turing reduction need not have this form.

The arithmetic ingredients include elliptic curves: smooth cubic curves with a distinguished identity point and an addition law on their rational points. If an infinite-order point PPP generates a rank-one subgroup, its multiples nPnPnP can encode integers nnn. The challenge is to recover multiplication of those indices using rational polynomial conditions; the curve’s addition law directly provides only addition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hilbert’s original 1900 problem concerned integer solutions. Davis, Putnam, and Robinson connected equations to computably enumerable sets, and Matiyasevich’s 1970 work completed the polynomial representation theorem. Every computably enumerable relation on positive integers can be encoded by polynomial solvability. As a consequence, integer solvability cannot be decided by an algorithm. The 1961 Davis–Putnam–Robinson paper is a principal milestone in that development.

Transferring this conclusion to rational solutions has been much harder. Julia Robinson’s 1949 work defined integers within rational arithmetic using both existential and universal quantifiers. Later refinements culminated in Koenigsmann’s universal definition. Universal quantifiers mean “for every rational number”; polynomial solvability permits only existential witnesses. The quantifier difference prevents the immediate transfer one might expect.

Another approach enlarges the integers by allowing denominators from a chosen set of primes SSS. The resulting ring is Z[S−1]\mathbb Z[S^{-1}]Z[S−1]. Poonen’s 2003 construction proves undecidability for certain such rings even when the permitted primes have density one. These remain proper subrings of Q\mathbb QQ: a sparse excluded set can still carry crucial information.

More recently, Koymans and Pagano proved undecidability for every infinite ring finitely generated over Z\mathbb ZZ. Their work uses elliptic curves and additive combinatorics. The rational field is not finitely generated as a Z\mathbb ZZ-algebra: finitely many generators cannot introduce denominators involving every prime. Thus this major result does not itself settle the rational problem.

Geometry also cautions against identifying undecidability with an existential definition of the integers. Mazur’s conjecture about closures of rational points would obstruct such a definition and even certain Diophantine models of integer arithmetic. M1 pursues a finite-test oracle reduction instead. Its conclusion is designed to address the decision problem without asserting one of these stronger definability statements.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Rational solvability and its degree

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that no algorithm decides, for an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial in an arbitrary finite number of variables, whether it has a rational zero.

Corollary 7.1 strengthens the computational description: the set of solvable inputs has Turing degree 0′0'0′. The same degree is asserted for each of these restricted input forms:

  • a polynomial of total degree at most four;
  • a supplied finite nonempty list of polynomials q1,…,qsq_1,\ldots,q_sq1​,…,qs​, each of degree at most two, asking whether ∑i=1sqi2\sum_{i=1}^s q_i^2∑i=1s​qi2​ has a rational zero.

There is no bound on the number of variables, the number of summands, or the sizes of the integer coefficients. The list is part of the second problem’s input; one need not recognize whether an arbitrary polynomial admits such a presentation.

The reduction from integer solvability is a Turing reduction, not a claimed single-instance many-one reduction. M1 explicitly does not establish many-one completeness or a single existential definition of Z\mathbb ZZ in Q\mathbb QQ.

The companion elliptic-curve statement

For an elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, let E(Q)[2]E(\mathbb Q)[2]E(Q)[2] be the subgroup of rational points killed by doubling. Let

s2(E)=corank⁡Z2Sel⁡2∞(E/Q).s_2(E)=\operatorname{corank}_{\mathbb Z_2}\operatorname{Sel}_{2^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q).s2​(E)=corankZ2​​Sel2∞​(E/Q).

The full 2-power Selmer group collects compatible arithmetic information from doubling and from all completions of Q\mathbb QQ. Its corank counts its unbounded 2-divisible directions. It includes the rational-point rank and potentially a contribution from the Shafarevich–Tate group Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q), which measures certain failures to pass from local solutions to global ones.

M2, Theorem 1.1, assumes

E(Q)[2]≠0,s2(E)∈{0,1}.E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0,\qquad s_2(E)\in\{0,1\}.E(Q)[2]=0,s2​(E)∈{0,1}.

It concludes that the order of vanishing of L(E,s)L(E,s)L(E,s) at s=1s=1s=1, the rational-point rank, and s2(E)s_2(E)s2​(E) are equal, and that the whole group Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q) is finite. No restriction on reduction at the prime two is imposed. A rank bound alone is not its hypothesis, and the theorem does not assert the complete BSD leading-coefficient formula.

M1 uses M2 together with the prime-two Fontaine–Mazur modularity claim discussed in family 010. M2 presents its own treatment of rational two-torsion, without using the broader converse as an input.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The rational version of Hilbert’s tenth problem is a central question connecting arithmetic geometry and logic. A negative answer would identify a fundamental limit on rational-point algorithms, not merely show that some existing method is too slow.

The quartic consequence is especially instructive. Bounded polynomial degree does not make the problem decidable when the number of unknowns is unrestricted. Complicated computation can be distributed across many simple equations and then assembled into one equation.

The distinction between a decision theorem and a definability theorem also matters conceptually. It would show that rational arithmetic can support maximal computably enumerable Turing complexity even through a reduction weaker than a direct existential encoding of all integer arithmetic. This rating is conditional on the manuscripts’ mathematical claims.

6. The main idea

Replace one translation by a sequence of tests

For an integer polynomial fff, M1 constructs an effectively generated sequence of finite tests, each answerable by finitely many rational-solvability queries. Its key equivalence is

f has an integer zero⟺every finite test succeeds.f\text{ has an integer zero}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{every finite test succeeds}.f has an integer zero⟺every finite test succeeds.

Assume temporarily that a rational-solvability algorithm exists. Run two searches together. One enumerates integer tuples looking for a zero. The other examines the tests looking for a failure. If the equivalence holds, exactly one search eventually certifies the correct answer. That would decide integer solvability, contradicting the classical theorem.

All the difficulty is therefore concentrated in showing that an integer-unsolvable equation eventually fails a test. A finite failure is the stopping certificate; no advance bound on which test will fail is required.

Force modeled indices to become ordinary integers

Suppose every test succeeds. The compactness theorem of logic says that a collection of first-order conditions has a model if every finite subcollection does. M1 uses this to obtain an ambient extension containing modeled root coordinates and elliptic points attached to ring elements.

These points have indices in an enlarged integer structure that may include numbers larger than every ordinary integer. The construction initially makes the index assignment additive and injective. It does not automatically preserve multiplication, so substituting these indices into fff need not yet give zero.

The manuscript compares the ring values and their elliptic indices prime by prime. For a rational number, the valuation vpv_pvp​ records the exponent of ppp in its numerator minus that in its denominator. Local elliptic logarithms turn the curve’s addition law into addition near its identity. Two conjugate local tests are used to recover index congruences while controlling denominators.

A global height estimate then joins these local comparisons. For coprime integers u,vu,vu,v, the logarithmic height of (u:v)(u:v)(u:v) is

h(u:v)=log⁡max⁡{∣u∣,∣v∣}.h(u:v)=\log\max\{|u|,|v|\}.h(u:v)=logmax{∣u∣,∣v∣}.

M1 selects five points on the projective line and looks at primes where a rational point meets one of them with odd valuation, outside a fixed exceptional set. If M(s)M(s)M(s) is the product of those distinct primes, the claimed estimate has the form

h(s)≤C M(s)ch(s)\le C\,M(s)^ch(s)≤CM(s)c

for fixed positive constants C,cC,cC,c. This is an estimate for the logarithmic height; replacing it by a bound for eh(s)e^{h(s)}eh(s) would change the assertion.

Write δ\deltaδ for fff evaluated at the modeled integer indices. If δ≠0\delta\ne0δ=0, the local tests force the relevant contact primes to divide this same integer to high precision. The height estimate then bounds heights throughout the modeled ring in terms of the largest root index BBB. But the height of an elliptic multiple grows quadratically in its index. The resulting comparison has the shape B2≤CfBB^2\le C_f BB2≤Cf​B, forcing the indices into an ordinary finite interval. They then identify the modeled roots with genuine integers, giving the desired contradiction.

Why the elliptic companion is needed

M2 supplies pointwise rational-point information for individual curves used in existential conditions controlling denominator parity. An average result about almost all twists would not settle those particular curves.

Its strategy arranges finite families of quadratic twists at the vertices of a binary cube. The target curve occupies one vertex. Auxiliary primes make central L-values or derivatives nonzero at the other vertices, with uniformly controlled powers of two. Integral interpolation recovers the missing target value. The construction must preserve bounds as the cube grows and, in rank one, make two related tests succeed simultaneously. This is the role of the arithmetic prime networks described in M2.

Finally, M1 obtains degree four by expressing a polynomial computation as addition and multiplication gates. Each gate gives an equation of degree at most two. Over Q\mathbb QQ, a sum of their squares vanishes exactly when every gate equation vanishes, producing the quartic normal form.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Undecidability concerns a single algorithm for all inputs. It does not say that every individual equation is inaccessible, or that useful algorithms for special classes cease to exist. Nor does it establish the same theorem with a fixed number of variables or bounded coefficient sizes.

The argument’s arithmetic dependencies are substantial and are claims in the same collection. They should not be concealed behind the short logical parallel-search argument. The rational-two-torsion companion is narrower than the general BSD statements in family 002, but has a specific role here.

The manuscript leaves existential definability of the integers and many-one completeness outside its conclusions. Determining the sharp restrictions on degree, dimension, and geometric type under which rational solvability becomes decidable remains a separate collection of questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Sections 1–2 give the finite-test reduction and its arithmetic architecture; Section 4 states and develops the height estimate; Section 7 explains the Turing degree and degree-four conversion. M2’s introduction and Theorem 1.1 state the pointwise 2-converse and describe its interpolation method.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 distinguish the established integer theorem, definability results, and proper-subring results. Poonen’s paper also explains why large subrings and the entire rational field can behave differently. For optional terminology, see Hilbert’s tenth problem and Turing reduction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rational numbers (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A pointwise 2-converse for elliptic curves with rational two-torsion (October 7, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Goldfeld’s conjecture: half the twists have rank zero, half rank one
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 006 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An elliptic curve can have finitely many rational points or infinitely many generated from a finite collection. Its rank measures the number of independent generators of infinite order. If one varies a curve in a natural one-parameter family, how often should extra generators appear?

Goldfeld’s prediction is strikingly simple: in a quadratic-twist family, half the curves should have rank zero, half rank one, and larger ranks should be exceptional. The analytic version concerns the order of vanishing of an L-function. A further prediction says that the average analytic rank should tend to one-half.

Family 006 contains two manuscripts addressing these assertions. M1 claims the half-and-half analytic distribution for every elliptic curve over Q\mathbb QQ, using a new pointwise implication from Selmer groups to L-functions. M2 claims the mean is also one-half by separately controlling rare twists of large analytic rank. That second step is necessary: knowing what happens almost everywhere need not determine an average.

2. Background and essential definitions

An elliptic curve over Q\mathbb QQ can be represented by a nonsingular cubic

E:y2=x3+Ax+B,E:\quad y^2=x^3+Ax+B,E:y2=x3+Ax+B,

with rational coefficients, together with a point at infinity serving as the identity for its group law. Its rational points form a finitely generated abelian group,

E(Q)≅Zr(E)⊕T,E(\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Z^{r(E)}\oplus T,E(Q)≅Zr(E)⊕T,

where TTT is finite. The nonnegative integer r(E)r(E)r(E) is the algebraic, or Mordell–Weil, rank.

For a nonzero squarefree integer ddd, the quadratic twist can be written as

E(d):dy2=x3+Ax+B.E^{(d)}:\quad dy^2=x^3+Ax+B.E(d):dy2=x3+Ax+B.

Over the field obtained by adjoining d\sqrt dd​, a change of variable identifies it with EEE. Over Q\mathbb QQ, its rational points can behave differently. Squarefree means that no prime square divides ddd; using these parameters avoids repeating the same squareclass.

The L-function L(E,s)L(E,s)L(E,s) packages counts of points modulo primes. Modularity supplies its analytic continuation and functional equation. Its analytic rank is

a(E)=ord⁡s=1L(E,s),a(E)=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s),a(E)=ords=1​L(E,s),

the multiplicity of its central zero; a nonzero value gives rank zero. The functional equation has a sign, called the root number. A positive sign permits even analytic rank, while a negative sign forces odd analytic rank. Ranks zero and one are the smallest possibilities in the two cases. The BSD conjecture predicts a(E)=r(E)a(E)=r(E)a(E)=r(E).

The full 2-power Selmer group is an arithmetic enlargement of the rational-point information obtained from repeated doubling and local solvability. Its corank satisfies

c2(E)=r(E)+corank⁡Z2Sha⁡(E/Q)[2∞].c_2(E)=r(E)+\operatorname{corank}_{\mathbb Z_2}\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty].c2​(E)=r(E)+corankZ2​​Sha(E/Q)[2∞].

Here Sha⁡\operatorname{Sha}Sha is the Shafarevich–Tate group, measuring certain obstructions to passing from local to global solutions, and [2∞][2^\infty][2∞] denotes its subgroup killed by powers of two. Thus low rational-point rank alone does not ensure low Selmer corank.

Both manuscripts count the same set:

D(X)={d∈Z:0<∣d∣≤X, d squarefree}.\mathcal D(X)=\{d\in\mathbb Z:0<|d|\le X,\ d\text{ squarefree}\}.D(X)={d∈Z:0<∣d∣≤X, d squarefree}.

Positive and negative parameters are included together and ordered by absolute value. Density is a limiting proportion within this set.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Goldfeld’s 1979 paper proposed an average analytic-rank prediction using quadratic-field discriminants. The present manuscripts formulate their conclusions in the signed squarefree convention above. Different orderings and restrictions need to be kept explicit when comparing theorems.

Analytic work established many twists with nonzero central values or nonzero first derivatives. Results of Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein, Murty–Murty, Iwaniec, and Perelli–Pomykała developed this approach. Positive proportions were obtained in special families, including Vatsal’s work on a particular modular curve and Kriz–Li’s results for curves admitting a rational 3-isogeny. These advances did not yield the exact two half-densities for every curve.

The arithmetic side developed through Selmer statistics. Alexander Smith’s unrestricted theorem establishes that full 2-power Selmer coranks zero and one each occur half the time for every rational elliptic curve’s quadratic twists. Its analytic consequence assumes BSD. M1 uses this Selmer distribution as an input and claims to supply the missing pointwise analytic implication.

The direction of that implication matters. Gross–Zagier and Kolyvagin established that analytic rank zero or one gives the corresponding algebraic rank and finiteness of Sha⁡\operatorname{Sha}Sha. A converse starts from Selmer information and must produce analytic nonvanishing. Earlier converse results covered substantial ranges at odd primes, with reduction or residual-representation conditions, and important complex-multiplication cases at two. M1 claims to remove these restrictions at the prime two.

For means, conditional results already illustrated the extra difficulty. Heath-Brown bounded analytic-rank averages under Riemann-hypothesis assumptions for twists. Fiorilli obtained an exact conditional mean, using both a Riemann-hypothesis assumption and an additional averaged cancellation hypothesis. M2 claims an unconditional analytic tail estimate instead. Its separate algebraic-moment consequence uses exponential rank bounds of Koymans and Smith.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Pointwise converse and half-densities

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q,

c2(E)∈{0,1}⟹a(E)=r(E)=c2(E),Sha⁡(E/Q) is finite.c_2(E)\in\{0,1\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(E)=r(E)=c_2(E),\qquad \operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\text{ is finite}.c2​(E)∈{0,1}⟹a(E)=r(E)=c2​(E),Sha(E/Q) is finite.

There are no restrictions on reduction type, complex multiplication, rational torsion, or rational isogenies. It concerns the full 2-power Selmer corank, not the dimension of a single finite Selmer group.

Combining this with Smith’s statistics, M1, Theorem 1.2, claims that for j=0,1j=0,1j=0,1,

lim⁡X→∞#{d∈D(X):a(E(d))=j}#D(X)=12.\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{\#\{d\in\mathcal D(X):a(E^{(d)})=j\}} {\#\mathcal D(X)}=\frac12.X→∞lim​#D(X)#{d∈D(X):a(E(d))=j}​=21​.

Consequently, analytic rank at least two has density zero. On a density-one set, analytic and algebraic ranks agree and the whole Shafarevich–Tate group is finite.

M1 also gives a finite-descent criterion. Put

d2(E)=dim⁡F2Sel⁡2(E/Q)−dim⁡F2E(Q)[2],d_2(E)=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{Sel}_2(E/\mathbb Q) -\dim_{\mathbb F_2}E(\mathbb Q)[2],d2​(E)=dimF2​​Sel2​(E/Q)−dimF2​​E(Q)[2],

where E(Q)[2]E(\mathbb Q)[2]E(Q)[2] consists of rational points killed by doubling. If d2(E)d_2(E)d2​(E) is zero or one, Corollary 1.3 concludes that all three ranks equal d2(E)d_2(E)d2​(E), Sha⁡\operatorname{Sha}Sha is finite, and its entire 2-primary subgroup is trivial.

Mean and tail control

M2, Theorem 1.1, claims

lim⁡X→∞1#D(X)∑d∈D(X)a(E(d))=12.\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1{\#\mathcal D(X)}\sum_{d\in\mathcal D(X)}a(E^{(d)})=\frac12.X→∞lim​#D(X)1​d∈D(X)∑​a(E(d))=21​.

The additional input is its Theorem 1.2: for constants CE>0C_E>0CE​>0 and an integer threshold RER_ERE​, every integer R≥RER\ge R_ER≥RE​ satisfies

lim sup⁡X→∞1X∑d∈D(X)a(E(d))>Ra(E(d))≤CER.\limsup_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\sum_{\substack{d\in\mathcal D(X)\\a(E^{(d)})>R}} a(E^{(d)})\le\frac{C_E}{R}.X→∞limsup​X1​d∈D(X)a(E(d))>R​∑​a(E(d))≤RCE​​.

The height limit comes first; the rank threshold is then allowed to grow. This is a bound on total rank contribution, not merely on how many exceptional twists occur.

M2 also gives algebraic-rank moment limits. For fixed real ttt and fixed positive integer mmm,

lim⁡X→∞1#D(X)∑d∈D(X)etr(E(d))=1+et2,lim⁡X→∞1#D(X)∑d∈D(X)r(E(d))m=12.\begin{aligned}\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1{\#\mathcal D(X)}\sum_{d\in\mathcal D(X)} e^{t r(E^{(d)})}&=\frac{1+e^t}{2},\\\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1{\#\mathcal D(X)}\sum_{d\in\mathcal D(X)} r(E^{(d)})^m&=\frac12.\end{aligned}X→∞lim​#D(X)1​d∈D(X)∑​etr(E(d))X→∞lim​#D(X)1​d∈D(X)∑​r(E(d))m​=21+et​,=21​.​

These stronger moment statements concern algebraic ranks. They are not higher analytic-rank moment theorems.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Goldfeld’s conjecture is a central prediction about the distribution of rational points in families. Resolving both its analytic density and mean formulations for every fixed rational elliptic curve would connect detailed arithmetic statistics to analytic behavior with exceptional generality.

The pointwise converse also matters independently. Statistical statements allow exceptions; a pointwise theorem applies to a prescribed curve once its Selmer hypothesis is known. That makes the result useful beyond the distribution problem and explains its role in the BSD claims of family 002.

The two manuscripts also clarify a general probabilistic issue. Among NNN objects, one exceptional object of value NNN has proportion 1/N1/N1/N, tending to zero, but contributes one to the average. Density-zero high ranks therefore cannot simply be ignored. M2’s tail estimate is the part that rules out this obstruction for analytic rank.

6. The main idea

Recover one curve from many auxiliary twists

M1 fixes the target curve and constructs finite families of twists indexed by binary vectors

x∈F2b.x\in\mathbb F_2^b.x∈F2b​.

The zero vector represents the original curve. Auxiliary primes enter each twist according to linear functions of xxx, while prescribed local behavior at the original bad primes is preserved.

The other vertices are arranged to have nonzero central values or simple central zeros, as appropriate, with uniformly bounded normalized powers of two. An integral interpolation argument then recovers nonvanishing at the missing zero vertex. The uniformity is crucial: the family can grow, but the bound needed for interpolation must not deteriorate with its dimension.

For corank zero, the arithmetic object being interpolated is related to Kato’s classes and detects L(E,1)L(E,1)L(E,1). For corank one, it comes from Heegner points, special points constructed using an imaginary quadratic field. Their heights relate to a central derivative. A fixed companion twist with nonzero central value turns the relevant product formula into a detector for the target derivative.

The finite construction has two branches. With rational two-torsion, graphs encode prescribed quadratic residue signs between auxiliary primes and enforce simultaneous nonvanishing of coefficient tests. Without rational two-torsion, matrices over F2\mathbb F_2F2​ encode local Selmer constraints. Their kernel dimensions interact with identities among coefficient tests to construct the required families. The manuscript does not identify those tests with matrix determinants merely because they satisfy related identities.

Once the unrestricted pointwise converse is obtained, Smith’s half-densities for Selmer coranks transfer to analytic ranks. The arithmetic statistics and the analytic implication have distinct roles.

Control the rank carried by rare exceptions

M2 starts from a basic fact: if an analytic function has a zero of order greater than kkk, its kkk-th derivative vanishes there. Applied to the completed L-function, this produces an exact identity for a weighted series.

The manuscript designs smooth weights and short mollifiers, finite approximations to reciprocal Euler products. Their purpose is to make the first portion of the series close to a positive main contribution while keeping later portions smaller on most twists. Mean-square estimates control the exceptional parameters. Consecutive derivative orders handle both functional-equation signs.

The asserted counting estimate is of order X/k2X/k^2X/k2 for ranks exceeding kkk, uniformly up to

k=(log⁡X)3/5.k=(\log X)^{3/5}.k=(logX)3/5.

A separate pointwise bound of order log⁡X\log XlogX controls ranks beyond that range. Combining the count at the largest admissible kkk with the pointwise bound makes the far tail negligible. Summing the remaining tail counts yields the displayed rank-weighted estimate.

Finally, split the average into ranks zero and one, ranks two through a fixed RRR, and ranks greater than RRR. M1 supplies the contribution one-half from rank one and makes the middle part vanish. M2 controls the last part by a quantity tending to zero as RRR grows. This is the passage from densities to the mean.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Every theorem fixes an elliptic curve before the twist parameter tends to infinity. The conclusions do not state uniform rates across all curves. The half-and-half assertion uses both signs of squarefree parameters together; an arbitrary residue class can fix the functional-equation sign and need not have that distribution.

Density zero does not mean finitely many higher-rank twists. The manuscripts do not settle all questions about the existence, frequency, or maximal size of high ranks. M2’s higher moment formulas are algebraic only, with moment order fixed before the limit; no corresponding assertion is made for growing moment orders or thin polynomial subfamilies.

Rank equality and finiteness of Sha⁡\operatorname{Sha}Sha are distinct from the exact BSD leading-coefficient formula. That formula requires the additional manuscripts discussed in family 002. Neither a general BSD theorem for every rank nor a rule deciding every curve’s rank follows from the statements here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 state the pointwise converse, densities, and finite-descent criterion. Its introduction explains the finite-twist interpolation strategy. M2’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 separate the mean from the tail estimate; Corollary 1.3 gives the algebraic moments.

Goldfeld’s original paper and Smith’s Selmer-distribution theorem are linked in Section 3. Silverman’s The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves supplies a systematic background treatment. For optional definitions, see quadratic twists and the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Goldfeld’s analytic density conjecture and the 2-converse for elliptic curves (October 7, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The mean analytic rank of quadratic twists of elliptic curves (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two-point Chowla: do neighboring integers forget prime-factor parity?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 007 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Count the prime factors of a positive integer, including repetitions, and record whether that count is even or odd. For example, 12=22⋅312=2^2\cdot312=22⋅3 has three prime factors and 10=2⋅510=2\cdot510=2⋅5 has two. Does the parity for nnn give any persistent information about the parity for n+1n+1n+1?

The two-point Chowla conjecture predicts that the two parities become uncorrelated when averaged over longer and longer initial intervals. The same question can be asked about nnn and n+hn+hn+h for any fixed positive shift hhh, or about two nonproportional linear expressions in nnn.

Family 007’s manuscript claims ordinary two-point cancellation at every sufficiently large scale, with a power-of-logarithm saving for the Liouville function. It also claims a broader qualitative theorem for bounded multiplicative functions that do not imitate a periodic character times a smooth multiplicative oscillation.

The word “ordinary” carries much of the significance. Each integer receives equal weight. Earlier theorems established logarithmically weighted cancellation, averages over shifts, or conclusions outside exceptional sets of scales. Those are major partial results, but they do not by themselves give the asserted every-cutoff conclusion.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let Ω(n)\Omega(n)Ω(n) count prime factors with multiplicity, and define the Liouville function by

λ(n)=(−1)Ω(n).\lambda(n)=(-1)^{\Omega(n)}.λ(n)=(−1)Ω(n).

Thus λ(12)=−1\lambda(12)=-1λ(12)=−1, λ(10)=1\lambda(10)=1λ(10)=1, and λ(1)=1\lambda(1)=1λ(1)=1. It is completely multiplicative:

λ(mn)=λ(m)λ(n)\lambda(mn)=\lambda(m)\lambda(n)λ(mn)=λ(m)λ(n)

for all positive integers m,nm,nm,n, even when they share factors.

The correlation

1X∑1≤n≤Xλ(n)λ(n+h)\frac1X\sum_{1\le n\le X}\lambda(n)\lambda(n+h)X1​1≤n≤X∑​λ(n)λ(n+h)

is the difference between the proportions of equal and unequal parities, up to the harmless use of XXX rather than ⌊X⌋\lfloor X\rfloor⌊X⌋. Tending to zero means these two possibilities balance asymptotically. It does not make the deterministic sequence literally random.

Compare ordinary and logarithmic averages of a bounded sequence u(n)u(n)u(n):

1X∑n≤Xu(n),1log⁡X∑n≤Xu(n)n.\frac1X\sum_{n\le X}u(n),\qquad\frac1{\log X}\sum_{n\le X}\frac{u(n)}n.X1​n≤X∑​u(n),logX1​n≤X∑​nu(n)​.

The logarithmic average gives comparable total weight to intervals whose endpoints differ by the same multiplicative factor. An ordinary average is much more sensitive to what happens near its final scale. Cancellation in the ordinary sense implies logarithmic cancellation by summation, but the reverse implication is unavailable in general.

A function fff is multiplicative if f(mn)=f(m)f(n)f(mn)=f(m)f(n)f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever m,nm,nm,n are coprime. This weaker condition permits independent choices at prime powers. The manuscript allows complex values with ∣f(n)∣≤1|f(n)|\le1∣f(n)∣≤1, including zero.

Some such functions have obvious structure. A Dirichlet character χ\chiχ is multiplicative and periodic, with root-of-unity values away from its modulus. The function nit=eitlog⁡nn^{it}=e^{it\log n}nit=eitlogn, for real ttt, is also multiplicative. Their products are natural obstructions to blanket cancellation theorems.

To measure imitation, define the nonnegative distance

D(f,χnit;X)2=∑p≤X1−Re⁡(f(p)χ(p)‾p−it)p,\mathbb D(f,\chi n^{it};X)^2=\sum_{p\le X}\frac{1-\operatorname{Re}\bigl(f(p)\overline{\chi(p)}p^{-it}\bigr)}p,D(f,χnit;X)2=p≤X∑​p1−Re(f(p)χ(p)​p−it)​,

where the sum is over primes. Uniform nonpretentiousness means that for every fixed character χ\chiχ,

inf⁡∣t∣≤ND(f,χnit;N)⟶∞.\inf_{|t|\le N}\mathbb D(f,\chi n^{it};N)\longrightarrow\infty.∣t∣≤Ninf​D(f,χnit;N)⟶∞.

The possible twist ttt varies with the scale. Excluding only each fixed ttt separately would be a weaker hypothesis.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Chowla proposed a general vanishing principle for products of Liouville values at distinct fixed shifts. The binary case is already difficult because multiplicativity controls products of arguments, while the question compares additive shifts.

Elliott extended the problem to correlations of bounded multiplicative functions. Work of Matomäki, Radziwiłł, and Tao identified a necessary correction for complex functions: a function can resemble different twists at successive scales without resembling one fixed twist globally. Their averaged form of Chowla’s conjecture explains the corrected condition and proves cancellation averaged over ranges of shifts.

Matomäki and Radziwiłł’s short-interval theorem showed that most short averages of a bounded real multiplicative function approximate its long average. They also obtained a strict improvement over the trivial fixed-shift correlation bound, without showing the normalized correlation tends to zero at every cutoff.

Tao’s logarithmically averaged theorem established the binary corrected Elliott conclusion with logarithmic weights, including nonproportional affine forms. Helfgott and Radziwiłł then developed divisibility graphs and quantitative expansion estimates. Pilatte’s work improved the saving for the logarithmically weighted two-point Liouville correlation to a power of a logarithm.

For ordinary averages, Tao and Teräväinen obtained binary cancellation outside a set of scales of logarithmic density zero. Later work of Klurman, Mangerel, and Teräväinen allowed a weaker nonpretentiousness assumption along a suitable set of scales. M1 claims to remove exceptional cutoffs under the uniform condition stated above, and to give a quantitative Liouville bound for fixed affine forms.
