It then filters expressions by the number of appearances of BBB. A filtration groups terms by a measure of complexity; passing to its associated graded object retains the leading pieces while discarding lower-order interactions.

M1 claims that the leading pentagon relation transfers to a simpler algebra associated with a cyclotomic hyperplane arrangement, an arrangement of linear hyperplanes that records certain roots-of-unity symmetries. The proof compares ordering procedures on the two sides and keeps their common count-preserving terms. The purpose is to constrain possible leading pieces without presuming the desired independence in the target algebra.

Detect the leading pieces

Deletion operators remove letters from words in controlled ways, acting as algebraic analogues of differentiation for iterated integrals. The manuscript proves the necessary identities integrally and uses them after reduction.

These operators are used to show that setting A=0A=0A=0 does not lose a relevant leading solution. A shift symmetry in BBB, combined with polynomial interpolation, confines the image to the ordinary free Lie algebra generated by

ad⁡Ck(B),k≥1,\operatorname{ad}_C^k(B),\qquad k\ge1,adCk​(B),k≥1,

where ad⁡C(z)=[C,z]\operatorname{ad}_C(z)=[C,z]adC​(z)=[C,z]. Since CCC has weight two and BBB weight one, these generators have weights 2k+12k+12k+1. This is the predicted sequence 3,5,7,…3,5,7,\ldots3,5,7,…, now emerging from the simplified pentagon.

Injectivity of the leading projection gives the dimension upper bound. Merely producing expressions of the right weights would not suffice; one must also prevent extra solutions from disappearing under the projection.

Fill every available dimension

For the lower bound, M1 compares two versions of braid holonomy, the formal transport obtained by integrating a connection along paths. One version is changed by conjugating paths and negating chord generators. The logarithm of their comparison produces the required odd-weight solutions.

A convergent integral gives a nonzero depth-one coefficient. The manuscript does not need a statement that a collection of real zeta values is arithmetically independent; nonvanishing of this one component serves a different purpose.

The final induction chooses integral generators weight by weight. Standard bracket words in previously chosen generators are shown independent through their leading reductions. At each odd weight there is room for one new depth-one element; at even weights the earlier bracket words already fill the predicted dimension. Matching the upper and lower bounds forces both generation and freeness. The completed theorem follows by taking the product of the finite-dimensional weightwise identifications.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the rational Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra and its completion by weight. It does not identify every profinite arithmetic symmetry group, nor compute all cohomology of the graph complex.

Freeness of this formal symmetry algebra should not be read as algebraic independence of numerical multiple zeta values. Passing from motivic or formal structures to numerical periods involves additional arithmetic questions. M1 explicitly avoids such an independence assumption in its construction of odd-weight values.

The characteristic-two stage also retains ordinary Lie algebras, where [u,u]=0[u,u]=0[u,u]=0. In characteristic two, the collection of primitive elements in an associative enveloping algebra can be larger than the ordinary Lie algebra; the manuscript does not identify those two objects. Its theorem likewise does not assert that every solution modulo two lifts to a rational solution.

Explicit choices of generators, more refined depth information, and other graph-cohomological degrees remain distinct questions beyond the headline description.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the graded and completed statements. Sections 3–5 develop the all-weight upper bound, Sections 6–7 construct odd-weight values, and Section 8 combines the two sides.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 distinguish existence, freeness, and exhaustion. For introductory algebra, see Lie algebras and free Lie algebras. Reutenauer’s Free Lie Algebras develops the bases and integral constructions underlying the dimension arguments.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Deligne-Drinfeld conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Inverse Goldbach: why the primes cannot split into a sumset
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 013 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The familiar Goldbach problem asks whether even integers can be expressed as sums of two primes. Ostmann’s inverse Goldbach problem reverses the structural question: can the primes themselves be obtained by adding elements from two simpler sets?

For sets A,BA,BA,B of nonnegative integers, their sumset is

A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.

The requirement is demanding. Every sufficiently large prime must occur, and every sufficiently large sum must be prime. It is not enough to represent many primes while also producing many composites.

Family 013 claims that such a decomposition is impossible when both summands contain at least two elements, even if one changes finitely many members of the prime set. This is Ostmann’s conjecture on the additive indecomposability of the primes.

The apparent simplicity hides a tension between local and global information. Avoiding composites forces restrictions modulo every prime. Covering all large primes forces the summands to be sufficiently large and sufficiently well coordinated. The manuscript aims to show that these demands cannot coexist.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let P\mathcal PP be the positive primes and N0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}N0​={0,1,2,…}. The symmetric difference

S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)S\mathbin{\triangle}T=(S\setminus T)\cup(T\setminus S)S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)

consists of elements belonging to exactly one of the sets. Saying that (A+B)△P(A+B)\triangle\mathcal P(A+B)△P is finite means that the two sets agree beyond some threshold. This is eventual equality, not equality of densities or an approximation in proportion.

The condition on summand size removes trivial decompositions. For example, {0}+P=P\{0\}+\mathcal P=\mathcal P{0}+P=P, but one summand has only one element. Both finite and infinite sets are initially allowed as long as each has at least two elements.

Define the counting functions

A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).A(x)=\#(A\cap[0,x]),\qquad B(x)=\#(B\cap[0,x]).A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).

If every large prime at most xxx must be a sum, then there must be enough pairs, so roughly

A(x)B(x)≳xlog⁡x.A(x)B(x)\gtrsim\frac{x}{\log x}.A(x)B(x)≳logxx​.

Several pairs can represent the same prime, so this is only a necessary lower bound. An upper bound of order xxx would still leave room between the two estimates.

For a prime qqq, the residue set A mod qA\bmod qAmodq records which remainders occur. If sufficiently large a∈Aa\in Aa∈A and b∈Bb\in Bb∈B satisfy a≡−b(modq)a\equiv-b\pmod qa≡−b(modq), then a+ba+ba+b is divisible by qqq. Once the sum exceeds qqq, it is composite. Therefore the tails of AAA and −B-B−B must occupy disjoint residue sets modulo every qqq.

A sieve combines such local restrictions across many primes to bound the size of an integer set. An inverse sieve asks what structure a set must have if it nearly attains those bounds. Squares provide a model example: modulo an odd prime, they occupy about half the residue classes, yet there are about x\sqrt xx​ squares below xxx.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ostmann formulated the conjecture in his 1956 treatise on additive number theory. Laffer and Mann later showed that a hypothetical nontrivial eventual decomposition must have two infinite summands. This already rules out representing the primes as finitely many fixed translates of another set.

Work of Hornfeck, Pomerance–Sárközy–Stewart, Hofmann–Wolke, and Elsholtz progressively restricted possible decompositions. Elsholtz combined large and larger sieves to force both summands to have approximately square-root size, up to logarithmic factors, and ruled out three nontrivial summands. A ternary impossibility is not the binary result: adding a third set creates additional constraints.

Elsholtz and Harper sharpened the binary size restrictions. In their positive-integer formulation, a hypothetical decomposition forces each counting function between quantities of the approximate forms

xlog⁡xlog⁡log⁡xandxlog⁡log⁡x,\frac{\sqrt x}{\log x\log\log x}\quad\text{and}\quad\sqrt x\log\log x,logxloglogxx​​andx​loglogx,

up to constants. Such bounds sharply narrow the possibilities without contradicting prime coverage.

Green and Harper’s inverse-sieve work proposed a structural route. Sets near the square-root bound and occupying about half the classes modulo primes should resemble quadratic images. A sufficiently strong classification would imply Ostmann’s conjecture. Their work established important partial results, not the required full inverse theorem.

Hanson proved that suitable sets have additive correlation and a substantial intersection with a quadratic image. More recent quadratic inverse-sieve work strengthened the intersection conclusions, as described in M1’s introduction. Large intersections still fall short of near-containment in one quadratic structure, especially when the quadratic may vary with the scale.

The manuscript claims a different final route: use the simultaneous residue restrictions together with coverage of every sufficiently large prime, without proving the general inverse-sieve classification. Its stated advance is a contradiction for the prime sumset problem itself.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every pair A,B⊆N0A,B\subseteq\mathbb N_0A,B⊆N0​ with ∣A∣,∣B∣≥2|A|,|B|\ge2∣A∣,∣B∣≥2,

(A+B)△Pis infinite.(A+B)\mathbin{\triangle}\mathcal P\quad\text{is infinite}.(A+B)△Pis infinite.

Equivalently, no finite modification of the set of primes can be written as a sumset of two nontrivial sets of nonnegative integers.

The conclusion contains two possible ways a candidate decomposition can fail: it can omit infinitely many primes, or contain infinitely many nonprimes, or both. In particular, if it contains every sufficiently large prime, then it must contain infinitely many composite numbers. The only nonprime nonnegative integers that are not composite are zero and one, so finite initial irregularities cannot account for that infinite failure.

No density or regularity assumptions on the summands are imposed. They need not be arithmetic progressions, polynomial images, computable sets, or sets with a known asymptotic counting formula.

The theorem does not say that two nontrivial sets cannot produce some primes, or even infinitely many primes. It says their full sumset cannot agree eventually with the full prime set. The exact coverage and exclusion conditions are both used in the manuscript.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Ostmann’s conjecture is a longstanding structural question about how an arithmetically defined set can arise from addition. Resolving it would show that the entire prime set has a rigidity invisible from its density alone.

The challenge is stronger than a simple parity obstruction. Choosing one summand even and the other odd can ensure odd sums, but oddness leaves many composites. One must simultaneously avoid divisibility by every prime while still reaching every large prime. Existing size bounds demonstrated the narrowness of that possibility; the claimed theorem rules it out completely.

The method would also connect local residue information, multiplicative character estimates, and global additive coverage. Its significance includes overcoming the need for a general structural classification that earlier conditional approaches sought. The score measures that mathematical importance if the claim is correct.

6. The main idea

Reduce to two infinite summands

Assume eventual equality. If AAA were finite, two distinct elements of AAA would require two fixed translates of the tail of BBB to consist of primes. A standard upper-bound sieve limits such a set to order x/(log⁡x)2x/(\log x)^2x/(logx)2. Finitely many translates of it cannot cover the order x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx primes below xxx. M1 includes this short reduction before tackling infinite summands.

For the remaining case, set D=−BD=-BD=−B. At each prime qqq, sufficiently long tails of AAA and DDD occupy disjoint subsets of Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, the field of residues modulo qqq. Complete those subsets to a partition Sq,SqcS_q,S_q^cSq​,Sqc​. Collision estimates, which count how often two elements share a residue, show that on suitable averages these parts must be approximately balanced and the summands approximately uniform within them.

This creates many local partitions. The problem is to exploit their compatibility across primes without assuming they all have a simple algebraic form.

Eliminate persistent character patterns

A multiplicative character on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​ assigns roots of unity to nonzero residues and is multiplicative, with value zero at zero. The quadratic character distinguishes nonzero squares from nonsquares. Translating its argument produces a test centered at a chosen residue.

M1 first studies persistent correlations with translated quadratic characters. Moment estimates and Poisson summation are used to force independently chosen local centers into a common rational pattern. A quadratic large-sieve argument would then confine positive portions of the summands to a small family of quadratic structures, contradicting the required collision behavior.

Higher-order characters require further repeated Cauchy–Schwarz steps. Auxiliary anchor variables separate copied terms and control diagonal coincidences. The output is a mixed-character decorrelation estimate. This is a statement about the specific residue patterns forced by a hypothetical decomposition, not a general classification of all large sets with restricted residues.

Use prime coverage as an additional input

Avoiding composite sums supplied the residue partitions. Coverage of all large primes now supplies something different: their additive Fourier transforms cannot be too small on too much of the relevant prime average.

For a function fff on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, its additive Fourier transform is

f^(a)=1q∑x∈Fqf(x)e−2πiax/q.\widehat f(a)=\frac1q\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_q} f(x)e^{-2\pi i ax/q}.f​(a)=q1​x∈Fq​∑​f(x)e−2πiax/q.

It measures correlation with additive oscillations. M1 compares a nonnegative sumset statistic with an average over primes, deriving a lower bound that retains more coverage information than the preliminary estimate for A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x).

This lower bound is central. A contradiction based only on sets avoiding certain residue classes would face the legitimate square-like examples that motivate the inverse-sieve problem. The full decomposition assumption contributes an extra positive statistic.

Force incompatible upper and lower bounds

Repeated transfers arrange terms in binary-tree patterns. A finite-field comparison uses the mixed-character decorrelation to control their correlations. Its hypotheses allow nonuniform pointwise values, which is necessary for the actual Fourier transforms of the residue indicators.

The arithmetic comparison then keeps track of repeated prime labels, coprimality restrictions, and the possible exceptional real character in prime-distribution estimates. In the final step, M1 averages over permutations of many bulk variables. Most pairs of arrangements overlap in too few components to maintain a large correlation. The remaining exceptional pairs and diagonal terms are bounded separately.

The resulting upper bound is claimed to contradict the positive lower bound inherited from prime coverage. The transfer depth is chosen large but fixed before the main scale grows. This is how the argument seeks to exclude every hypothetical eventual decomposition rather than merely improve its counting bounds.

M1 cites the zero-free theorem from family 003 only for an optional refinement in Remark 5.4. It explicitly states that the relevant proof uses its classical prime-distribution estimate and exceptional-character treatment instead. The indecomposability theorem is therefore not presented as depending on that new zero-free claim.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The summands lie in the nonnegative integers, and each must contain at least two elements. The theorem concerns eventual equality after finitely many changes. It does not give a quantitative lower bound on how many composite sums a covering pair must produce.

A sumset can contain an interesting thin set of primes without being an eventual decomposition of all primes. Results and questions about such thin sumsets remain distinct. The theorem also does not resolve the ordinary binary Goldbach conjecture, whose target is the even integers and whose summands are primes.

The argument does not establish Green–Harper’s general inverse-sieve conjecture. A broad classification of sets near sieve bounds remains a separate structural problem. Other multiplicatively defined sets, restricted summand classes, and quantitative measures of failure require their own conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the eventual indecomposability result. Section 2 handles finite summands and residue restrictions; Sections 3–5 develop character decorrelation and the separate use of prime coverage; Sections 6–9 complete the tree comparison and contradiction.

The Elsholtz–Harper and Green–Harper papers linked in Section 3 explain the square-root barrier and the inverse-sieve approach. Optional background on sumsets and sieve theory may help place the problem within additive and analytic number theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The additive indecomposability of the primes (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Arthur parameters and geometric Langlands over finite fields
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 014 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Many problems in number theory ask how large an arithmetic eigenvalue can be. An eigenvalue measures how a function changes under an averaging operation; unusually large values signal extra structure. The Ramanujan conjectures predict sharp bounds for important classes of these functions. Arthur’s framework goes further: when the simplest bound fails, it predicts an organized algebraic reason for that failure.

Family 014 studies this picture over function fields, such as the field of rational functions over a finite field. Its eight manuscripts connect numerical eigenvalue bounds with a geometric correspondence between two kinds of objects: bundles on a curve and representations describing transport around that curve.

There are several questions here. Can the same algebraic pattern explain eigenvalues at every place? Can those local patterns be assembled into one global Arthur parameter? Does the geometric correspondence reach every allowed parameter? Can it produce well-behaved eigensheaves with specified ramification? The manuscripts address these questions in different, explicitly delimited settings.

2. Background and essential definitions

From a curve to arithmetic eigenvalues

Let XXX be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over the finite field Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, and let F=Fq(X)F=\mathbb F_q(X)F=Fq​(X) be its field of rational functions. A closed point xxx plays the role of a prime; its residue field has size qx=qdxq_x=q^{d_x}qx​=qdx​, where dxd_xdx​ is its degree.

A group GGG, such as SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, specifies the symmetries under consideration. A principal bundle is a family locally modeled on this group, with compatible transition functions. Automorphic functions can be described as functions on isomorphism classes of bundles. A Hecke operator averages over prescribed modifications of a bundle at a point. Simultaneous eigenfunctions of these operators are the arithmetic counterpart of modes in Fourier analysis.

A cuspidal function has vanishing constant terms along every proper parabolic subgroup. Parabolic subgroups generalize block upper-triangular matrices; their constant terms detect contributions induced from smaller groups. Cuspidality removes these induced constant terms.

A level divisor DDD records extra data at finitely many points. Full level means a trivialization on the entire finite subscheme DDD, including its multiplicities. A representation is unramified at a point when it has vectors fixed by the usual integral maximal compact subgroup there. At such a point, its Hecke eigenvalues are encoded by a Satake parameter, a semisimple conjugacy class in the Langlands dual group G^\widehat GG. This dual group exchanges the root and coroot data of GGG.

Temperedness and the extra SL2

For a unitary local representation, temperedness means weak containment in the regular representation: its matrix coefficients have the decay expected from ordinary harmonic analysis. At an unramified point, the normalized Satake parameter is then conjugate into a compact subgroup of G^(C)\widehat G(\mathbb C)G(C).

Arthur’s extra ingredient is an algebraic homomorphism

ϕ:SL2⟶G^.\phi:\mathrm{SL}_2\longrightarrow\widehat G.ϕ:SL2​⟶G.

Its standard nilpotent matrix maps to a nilpotent element of the dual Lie algebra. A matrix is nilpotent when some power is zero; a nilpotent orbit groups such elements under conjugation. The homomorphism contributes a controlled size factor

ϕ ⁣(qx1/200qx−1/2).\phi\!\begin{pmatrix}q_x^{1/2}&0\\0&q_x^{-1/2}\end{pmatrix}.ϕ(qx1/2​0​0qx−1/2​​).

Thus an unramified parameter can have a compact part multiplied by an explicitly structured noncompact part. The zero nilpotent orbit corresponds to a trivial extra factor and hence to temperedness.

From functions to sheaves

A local system assigns vector spaces with consistent transport along paths, interpreted algebraically through the étale fundamental group. A dual-group local system assigns such a system to every representation of G^\widehat GG, compatibly with tensor products. A sheaf on the space of bundles retains geometric information that a numerical function forgets. Over a finite field, taking traces of Frobenius on a suitable sheaf recovers a function.

A Hecke eigensheaf M\mathcal MM with eigenvalue ρ\rhoρ satisfies, schematically,

HV(M)≃M⊠Vρ.\mathsf H_V(\mathcal M)\simeq\mathcal M\boxtimes V_\rho.HV​(M)≃M⊠Vρ​.

Here VVV is a dual-group representation, VρV_\rhoVρ​ its local system, and ⊠\boxtimes⊠ means exterior product. The identity says that modifying bundles has a prescribed effect determined by transport on the curve. With several moving modification points, these identities must remain compatible when points collide; this is fusion compatibility.

A perverse sheaf is a complex satisfying dimension-adjusted support and dual-support conditions. Local constructibility means finite-dimensional, stratified behavior on every finite-type chart. Neither phrase simply means “an arbitrary sheaf.” Singular support records cotangent directions where a sheaf fails to vary smoothly; a nilpotent singular-support condition restricts those directions through nilpotent Higgs fields, which are bundle-valued differential forms.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Drinfeld’s work for GL2\mathrm{GL}_2GL2​, and Laurent Lafforgue’s work for GLn\mathrm{GL}_nGLn​, established the function-field Langlands correspondence in those settings and the purity underlying Ramanujan bounds. Vincent Lafforgue later constructed global parameters for cuspidal representations of general reductive groups using excursion operators, which compare several fundamental-group elements simultaneously. These results are the starting point of M1, M3 and M4, rather than consequences first introduced here.

Arthur’s framework explains why non-tempered discrete automorphic representations should involve an additional SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​. Earlier function-field progress outside general linear groups required extra local assumptions. Ciubotaru and Harris, for example, obtained unramified temperedness from hypotheses including a tempered component and a generic unramified component. Their work also relates the possible spectral behavior to nilpotent classes. See their primary paper.

The geometric route developed through Drinfeld, Laumon, Frenkel–Gaitsgory–Vilonen and Gaitsgory’s constructions of eigensheaves, followed by categorical formulations for general groups. The characteristic-zero geometric Langlands theorem is an established input here. Gaitsgory and Raskin subsequently obtained a positive-characteristic restricted equivalence onto a union of spectral components; whether every component occurred remained a separate question. Their positive-characteristic paper explains this distinction.

Gaitsgory–Lafforgue–Raskin also formulated rational and ℓ\ellℓ-adic Arthur decompositions of automorphic functions. Raskin’s ICM account describes related unramified progress, including global enhancement under its hypotheses. Accordingly, this family’s contribution should be understood through the particular extensions it states—full finite level, rational support, ramified temperedness and prescribed tame eigensheaves—not as the beginning of these subjects.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M3 and M1: one orbit, then one global parameter

For split connected semisimple GGG, M3 claims a decomposition at every full finite level:

CD,Q=⨁OCD,O,Q.C_{D,\mathbb Q}=\bigoplus_{\mathcal O}C_{D,\mathcal O,\mathbb Q}.CD,Q​=O⨁​CD,O,Q​.

Here CD,QC_{D,\mathbb Q}CD,Q​ is the finite-dimensional rational cusp space, and the sum runs over dual nilpotent orbits. The corresponding decomposition holds after extending coefficients to Q‾ℓ\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ellQ​ℓ​, for ℓ≠char⁡Fq\ell\ne\operatorname{char}\mathbb F_qℓ=charFq​. Every eigenvalue in a summand has the same orbit factor at every unramified point, and its residual compactness holds under every complex embedding. Divisor multiplicities are unrestricted.

For split connected adjoint absolutely simple groups, M3 further claims that genericity at one unramified place implies temperedness at all unramified places. Genericity means having a nonzero Whittaker functional, a nondegenerate Fourier coefficient along a maximal unipotent subgroup. Global genericity supplies this local condition.

M1 takes the finite-level decomposition as an explicit input. For each occurring excursion parameter σ\sigmaσ, it claims a global homomorphism ϕ\phiϕ and a commuting Weil-group representation τ\tauτ such that, after one simultaneous conjugation,

σ(w)=τ(w)ϕ ⁣(adeg⁡w00a−deg⁡w),a=q1/2.\sigma(w)=\tau(w)\phi\!\begin{pmatrix}a^{\deg w}&0\\0&a^{-\deg w}\end{pmatrix},\qquad a=q^{1/2}.σ(w)=τ(w)ϕ(adegw0​0a−degw​),a=q1/2.

The square root is interpreted in the chosen ℓ\ellℓ-adic coefficient field. The Weil group consists of fundamental-group elements with integral Frobenius degree. The formula holds for all its elements, including inertia. The representation τ\tauτ lands in the full centralizer of ϕ(SL2)\phi(\mathrm{SL}_2)ϕ(SL2​), which can be disconnected, and its good Frobenius eigenvalues have weight zero: all complex absolute values equal one. This is stronger than choosing unrelated local factorizations.

M4: the ramified exceptional places

M4 claims that every local component of a globally generic cuspidal representation is tempered for split connected adjoint groups of types

G2, F4, E6, E7, E8.G_2,\ F_4,\ E_6,\ E_7,\ E_8.G2​, F4​, E6​, E7​, E8​.

Its statement imposes no characteristic or ramification-depth restriction. It uses M3 for the unramified places and supplies a separate argument for the ramified ones, where monodromy information is essential.

M2 and M5: rationality and full spectral support

Several geometric statements share four characteristic hypotheses. In Lie-algebra language these require: a nondegenerate invariant symmetric form remaining nondegenerate on the center of every Levi Lie algebra; Chevalley restriction for every Levi; semisimple centralizers that are Levi subgroups; and, over every field extension, containment of each nilpotent element in the Lie algebra of a parabolic’s unipotent radical. A Levi is the block-diagonal-type reductive part of a parabolic. Chevalley restriction says that invariant polynomial functions are detected on a maximal torus. These conditions are part of the results, not optional conveniences.

Under these hypotheses, M2 claims rationality of every canonical unramified Arthur-filtration step on all finitely supported automorphic functions, including noncuspidal ones. If AEA_EAE​ is this function space with E=Q‾ℓE=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ellE=Q​ℓ​, and FYF_YFY​ is the step associated with a closed invariant union YYY of nilpotent orbits, then

FYAE=E⊗Q(AQ∩FYAE).F_YA_E=E\otimes_{\mathbb Q}(A_{\mathbb Q}\cap F_YA_E).FY​AE​=E⊗Q​(AQ​∩FY​AE​).

The filtration therefore comes from rational functions and is independent of the coefficient prime in the stated sense. No Hecke-finiteness or rational-point assumption is imposed. On cusp spaces it agrees with the appropriate orbit sums from M3 in their common scope.

M5 claims that the restricted geometric Langlands equivalence reaches every spectral component. It treats connected reductive groups under the four hypotheses over an algebraic closure of a finite field. For an arbitrary algebraically closed base, it additionally assumes that the characteristic is very good for the group and does not divide its Weyl-group order. “Very good” is a root-system restriction; for example, type ArA_rAr​ excludes primes dividing r+1r+1r+1, while type E8E_8E8​ excludes 2,3,52,3,52,3,5.

The resulting general eigenobjects are in an ind-constructible category; bounded constructibility and perversity do not follow automatically. M5 also has a rational-coefficient support statement for a specified rational spectral action. Its rational arithmetic trace consequence remains conditional on the corresponding primed trace comparison supplied as input.

M6–M8: actual tame perverse eigensheaves

These three papers impose genus at least two and dense parameters. Zariski density means the image is contained in no proper algebraic subgroup. Tame unipotent monodromy kills wild inertia and has the form exp⁡(tℓN)\exp(t_\ell N)exp(tℓ​N), where NNN is nilpotent and tℓt_\elltℓ​ is the tame ℓ\ellℓ-adic inertia coordinate. Borel level specifies a flag at each marked point.

PaperGroup and marked pointsParameter and conclusion
M6Simple simply connected group; one point; four characteristic hypothesesGeometric dense dual local system with regular-unipotent monodromy; nonzero locally constructible perverse eigensheaf.
M7SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, characteristic p>np>np>n; at least two pointsGeometric dense PGLn\mathrm{PGL}_nPGLn​ local system; any unipotent Jordan types, including zero; the same kind of eigensheaf.
M8SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, p>np>np>n; one pointArithmetic, geometrically dense PGLn\mathrm{PGL}_nPGLn​ parameter with regular-unipotent monodromy; a perverse Weil eigensheaf after a finite extension of constants.

Regular means that the nilpotent centralizer has the smallest possible dimension, equal to the group’s rank. All three constructions include parabolic nilpotent singular support and the full tensor, permutation and fusion compatibilities. M8 additionally preserves Frobenius on the entire eigenstructure, not merely on its underlying sheaf.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Taken as stated, this is an exceptional collection of advances linking central spectral predictions to geometric realization. The common-orbit decomposition controls the possible departure from temperedness; global enhancement turns that control into one arithmetic object. The exceptional-group theorem reaches ramified components, where unramified eigenvalue information alone is insufficient.

On the geometric side, full support removes the possibility of allowed parameters having no corresponding automorphic category. The tame papers then produce more concrete sheaves with specified finiteness, perversity and compatibility properties. These are substantial improvements over existence of an unrestricted categorical object. The rating reflects this combined reach within function-field Langlands, not a claim to solve every Langlands conjecture.

6. The main idea

Spectral sizes become geometric degree bounds

M3 interprets an offending eigenvalue through cohomology of shtukas, geometric objects combining bundles, modifications and Frobenius. Two arguments bound the same cohomological degree. One bound grows with the eigenvalue’s size; the other is controlled by compatible nilpotent orbits. Scaling the modification forces a contradiction unless the size comes from an allowed SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​ factor. Purity then makes the orbit consistent across places.

M1 retains whole excursion tuples and a nilpotent operator in one global geometric support. Locally, the useful configurations form an open orbit. If every test missed it, products of suitable boundary tests would annihilate the global support. A cuspidal Hecke quotient simultaneously forces the same object to survive. The resulting contradiction produces a global enhancement, including simultaneous conjugacy.

M2 detects filtration membership through bilinear pairings of functions and measures on compact parameter sets. These are finite complex measures, not necessarily positive probability measures. Preventing cancellation from lower orbit boundaries is crucial. Once the detector uses only rational operations, coefficient descent gives the rational filtration.

Ramification and specialization require additional information

At a ramified place, a Weil–Deligne parameter includes a nilpotent monodromy operator. M4 compares two possible completions of the same semisimple parameter: one arising from global purity and one from local representation theory. Adjoint regularity places both monodromies in the same open orbit. Purity then contradicts the positive exponent that a non-tempered representation would require.

M5 supposes a spectral component is missing and transports a nonzero characteristic-zero sheaf toward positive characteristic. Two Hecke modifications and transverse slices detect a nonzero nearby-cycle contribution, contradicting the disappearance required by a missing component.

M6 and M7 use two specializations. A nodal degeneration first creates flag level in characteristic zero; mixed-characteristic specialization then reaches the desired finite-field curve. Separate nonvanishing arguments, perverse truncation and descent from enhanced flags preserve the required eigenstructure. M8 makes this construction Frobenius compatible, including the gluing at the node. A finite constant-field extension enters when an auxiliary point must be fixed by a power of Frobenius.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are function-field and geometric statements. They do not establish number-field Ramanujan or a complete Arthur packet classification. M1 does not provide an ellipticity assertion or multiplicity formula, and explicitly depends on the decomposition input. M3 alone concerns temperedness at unramified places; M4’s stated all-place theorem has the exceptional adjoint scope above.

The characteristic restrictions of M2, M5 and M6 must not be silently transferred away by M3’s unrestricted statement. Similarly, M7’s arbitrary unipotent types at several points do not turn M8 into an arithmetic theorem for arbitrary tame data. M8 permits extension of constants and concerns Weil structures; it does not promise realization over the original finite field without extension.

Broader ramification, nondense parameters, relaxed characteristic assumptions and stronger finiteness properties outside the stated eigensheaf cases remain separate questions. The eight papers fit together, but their hypotheses do not merge into one universal theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

For the numerical side, begin with M3, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, then M1, Theorem 1.2, and M4, Theorem 1.1. For rationality and categorical support, read M2, Assumption 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, and M5, Hypotheses 1.1–1.3 and Theorems 1.4–1.5. M6–M8 each state their eigensheaf theorem as Theorem 1.1.

The historical papers linked in section 3 explain why parameters, spectral support and eigensheaves are different stages of the problem. M3’s introduction gives references to Drinfeld, both Lafforgues, Arthur and geometric Satake; M6–M8 explain the earlier geometric constructions and the role of gluing. Optional background on the Langlands program can help orient the terminology, but the claims here use the specific hypotheses above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global Arthur Enhancements of Cuspidal Excursion Parameters (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Rationality of the Canonical Unramified Arthur Filtration (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Ramanujan-Arthur Decompositions of Cuspidal Functions at Full Finite Level (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Temperedness at ramified places for globally generic exceptional groups (October 5, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, The Restricted Geometric Langlands Equivalence in Positive Characteristic (September 24, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Constructible tame Hecke eigensheaves in positive characteristic (October 5, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Tame Hecke Eigensheaves with Several Marked Points (October 5, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, Frobenius Structures on Tame Hecke Eigensheaves (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How well can fractions approximate pi?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 017 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The fractions 22/722/722/7 and 355/113355/113355/113 approximate π\piπ surprisingly well for their small denominators. But isolated successes do not tell us how good rational approximations can remain as the denominator grows. The real question is whether there are infinitely many exceptionally accurate fractions.

Family 017 claims the sharp answer: the irrationality exponent of π\piπ is exactly two. Roughly, errors of order the inverse square of the denominator occur infinitely often, but improving the exponent by any fixed positive amount eventually becomes impossible.

This also answers a question that initially looks unrelated. Does the positive series

∑n=1∞1n3sin⁡2n\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}n=1∑∞​n3sin2n1​

converge when angles are measured in radians? The factor n−3n^{-3}n−3 encourages convergence, but an integer very close to a multiple of π\piπ makes the sine exceptionally small. The manuscript claims that its approximation theorem controls these rare spikes well enough to prove convergence.

2. Background and essential definitions

For an irrational real number xxx, its irrationality exponent is

μ(x)=sup⁡{ν>0:0<∣x−pq∣<q−ν for infinitely many coprime p,q, q≥2}.\mu(x)=\sup\left\{\nu>0:0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<q^{-\nu}\text{ for infinitely many coprime }p,q,\ q\ge2\right\}.μ(x)=sup{ν>0:0<​x−qp​​<q−ν for infinitely many coprime p,q, q≥2}.

A larger exponent means that exceptionally accurate rational approximations occur more often in this asymptotic sense. The definition concerns infinitely many fractions, not one unusually good approximation.

Dirichlet’s approximation theorem, obtainable from the pigeonhole principle, implies μ(x)≥2\mu(x)\ge2μ(x)≥2 for every irrational xxx. Continued fractions give an explicit sequence of good approximations, the convergents pj/qjp_j/q_jpj​/qj​, satisfying

∣x−pjqj∣<1qj2.\left|x-\frac{p_j}{q_j}\right|<\frac{1}{q_j^2}.​x−qj​pj​​​<qj2​1​.

Numbers can nevertheless have much larger irrationality exponent. A Liouville number admits approximations beating every fixed power of the denominator. Irrationality by itself therefore gives no finite upper bound.

The statement μ(x)=2\mu(x)=2μ(x)=2 is best read with an epsilon:

for every ε>0,∣x−pq∣≥q−2−εfor all sufficiently large q.\text{for every }\varepsilon>0,\quad\left|x-\frac pq\right|\ge q^{-2-\varepsilon}\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }q.for every ε>0,​x−qp​​≥q−2−εfor all sufficiently large q.

The threshold can depend on ε\varepsilonε. This is weaker than a fixed inequality ∣x−p/q∣≥c/q2|x-p/q|\ge c/q^2∣x−p/q∣≥c/q2 with one positive constant ccc. That stronger property is equivalent to bounded partial quotients in the continued fraction expansion. Exponent two does not settle whether those partial quotients are bounded.

For the series application, write

∥y∥=min⁡m∈Z∣y−m∣\|y\|=\min_{m\in\mathbb Z}|y-m|∥y∥=m∈Zmin​∣y−m∣

for distance to the nearest integer. A close approximation p/qp/qp/q to π\piπ makes ∥qπ∥\|q\pi\|∥qπ∥ small. If ppp is near qπq\piqπ, then

∣sin⁡p∣=∣sin⁡(p−qπ)∣≤∣p−qπ∣.|\sin p|=|\sin(p-q\pi)|\le |p-q\pi|.∣sinp∣=∣sin(p−qπ)∣≤∣p−qπ∣.

Thus small approximation errors produce large terms of the sine-denominator series at integer numerators ppp. The arithmetic difficulty is to understand how numerous and how clustered such terms can be.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The irrationality and transcendence of π\piπ are classical, but neither supplies the predicted exponent two. Transcendence says that π\piπ satisfies no nonzero polynomial equation with integer coefficients. Rational approximation asks a different quantitative question.

Mahler’s 1953 work gave a finite irrationality measure, with exponent 42 for all denominators at least two and an eventual improvement to 30. Mignotte refined the method to 21 and eventually 20. Hata’s integral constructions reached approximately 8.016045398.016045398.01604539, and Salikhov improved this to approximately 7.6063087.6063087.606308. The manuscript’s bibliography identifies these original papers; Zudilin’s essay on irrationality measures explains the logarithmic approximation and denominator arithmetic behind this line of work.

Zeilberger and Zudilin subsequently obtained

μ(π)≤7.103205334137…\mu(\pi)\le7.103205334137\ldotsμ(π)≤7.103205334137…

through a variant of Salikhov’s integral construction, with rigorous arithmetic and asymptotic analysis. See their 2019 preprint and 2020 publication. The current manuscript also cites Bai’s September 2026 preprint, which claims a further improvement below 7.1018628323577.1018628323577.101862832357. These earlier numerical bounds provide context; the new argument does not use them as inputs.

The Flint–Hills series has its own history. Alekseyev showed that convergence requires μ(π)≤5/2\mu(\pi)\le5/2μ(π)≤5/2. Meiburg proved the sufficient strict condition μ(π)<5/2\mu(\pi)<5/2μ(π)<5/2, as explained in Bounds on Irrationality Measures and the Flint-Hills Series. Those two implications do not settle the equality boundary μ(π)=5/2\mu(\pi)=5/2μ(π)=5/2.

Against this background, the claim μ(π)=2\mu(\pi)=2μ(π)=2 is a qualitative jump to the predicted optimum, rather than another small numerical improvement. It lies comfortably inside the known sufficient range for convergence of the classical series.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript. Its Theorem 1.1 states

μ(π)=2.\boxed{\mu(\pi)=2.}μ(π)=2.​

More explicitly, for every real ν>2\nu>2ν>2, there exists an integer Q(ν)Q(\nu)Q(ν) such that

∣π−pq∣≥q−ν(p∈Z, q≥Q(ν)).\left|\pi-\frac pq\right|\ge q^{-\nu}\qquad(p\in\mathbb Z,\ q\ge Q(\nu)).​π−qp​​≥q−ν(p∈Z, q≥Q(ν)).

This inequality applies to all integer numerators and denominators, whether or not the fraction is reduced. The argument does not give an effective value of Q(ν)Q(\nu)Q(ν).

Corollary 1.2 claims convergence of the classical Flint–Hills series. Corollary 5.2 gives a broader exact criterion: for fixed real a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0,

∑n=1∞1na∣sin⁡n∣bconverges if and only ifa>max⁡{1,b}.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^a|\sin n|^b}\quad\text{converges if and only if}\quad a>\max\{1,b\}.n=1∑∞​na∣sinn∣b1​converges if and only ifa>max{1,b}.

All angles are in radians. Both boundary lines are excluded from convergence. If a≤1a\le1a≤1, the terms dominate those of the divergent series ∑n−a\sum n^{-a}∑n−a. If 1<a≤b1<a\le b1<a≤b, continued-fraction numerators give a subsequence whose summands fail to approach zero. The new approximation theorem supplies the convergence direction in the remaining region.

For instance, a=3,b=2a=3,b=2a=3,b=2 gives the classical convergent case. The case a=b=2a=b=2a=b=2 diverges, despite the familiar convergence of ∑n−2\sum n^{-2}∑n−2, because unusually small sine values keep a subsequence of terms large.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, this resolves a prominent sharp approximation problem for a fundamental transcendental constant and yields a clean boundary for an entire family of singular trigonometric series.

The optimal value two is the benchmark supplied by elementary approximation from below. Reaching it from an upper bound above seven requires controlling all hypothetical infinite sequences of exceptional approximations, not merely optimizing a familiar integral.

The method also introduces a multivariable interpolation statement whose thresholds are independent of the interpolation centers. That kind of uniformity could matter beyond this particular constant. The rating reflects the central approximation problem and methodological reach; the statement remains specifically about π\piπ, not all familiar transcendental numbers.

6. The main idea

Construct an object that cannot be too small

A standard irrationality strategy compares arithmetic discreteness with analytic smallness. A nonzero integer has absolute value at least one. More generally, a nonzero rational number with controlled denominator has a known lower bound. If analysis forces the same quantity below that bound, the assumed approximation was impossible.

Here the object is a determinant with entries in Q(i)\mathbb Q(i)Q(i), where i2=−1i^2=-1i2=−1. Clearing denominators gives an arithmetic lower bound for a nonzero minor. The challenge is to ensure nonvanishing while exploiting several exceptionally accurate approximations at once.

Assume, for contradiction, that one fixed ν>2\nu>2ν>2 admits infinitely many approximations beating q−νq^{-\nu}q−ν. The manuscript chooses finitely many with successively separated denominators. Rational multiples of these fractions approximate the exact exponential periods 2πij2\pi i j2πij, for integers jjj.

Interpolate along logarithmic curves

A jet is a finite collection of Taylor coefficients. The interpolation theorem prescribes jets of a polynomial after substitutions of the form

Y=1+t,Xi=cji+ui+log⁡(1+t).Y=1+t,\qquad X_i=c_{ji}+u_i+\log(1+t).Y=1+t,Xi​=cji​+ui​+log(1+t).

The variable ttt follows a logarithmic curve, while uiu_iui​ measures transverse displacement. The centers cjic_{ji}cji​ come from the chosen rational approximations. Weighted degree bounds keep only polynomial monomials whose weighted exponent sum fits inside a simplex.

Merely having more coefficients than conditions does not establish that arbitrary jets can be prescribed: the special positions of the centers might create hidden dependencies. The manuscript’s interpolation theorem establishes the required full rank, using multiplicity estimates, logarithmic residues and geometric positivity.

The order of choices matters. Dimension and successive coordinate weights are chosen before the center locations. The approximating denominators can then be selected to meet those already fixed thresholds. Finally the polynomial degree grows. This prevents the accuracy requirement from depending circularly on the approximations selected to satisfy it.

Two competing sources of analytic smallness

The determinant rows are translated from approximate periods to exact periods and expanded in the transverse variables. Large transverse indices contribute many powers of the tiny rational-approximation errors.

If many rows instead have small transverse indices, they fall into relatively few groups. Rows in the same group test Taylor coefficients of the same entire functions. Repeated Taylor degrees then make a determinant term vanish, so surviving terms must use sufficiently distinct degrees. This produces another strong saving.

The argument therefore covers both possibilities: many large transverse indices supply small errors, while many small indices force Taylor-degree separation. Full weighted simplices control the coefficient count and denominator cost together. Increasing the number of variables makes the combined analytic saving contradict the arithmetic lower bound for every fixed ν>2\nu>2ν>2.

Why the series needs spacing, not only individual bounds

Choose 2<ν<5/22<\nu<5/22<ν<5/2. The theorem yields a positive constant ccc with

∥qπ∥≥cq1−ν(q≥1),\|q\pi\|\ge c q^{1-\nu}\qquad(q\ge1),∥qπ∥≥cq1−ν(q≥1),

after absorbing finitely many small denominators into ccc. For K≤q<2KK\le q<2KK≤q<2K, the points qπq\piqπ modulo one are separated from zero and from each other by a distance comparable to K1−νK^{1-\nu}K1−ν. The same inequality applied to differences of denominators gives the mutual separation.

Ordering these distances on the circle bounds a whole dyadic block:

∑K≤q<2K1q3∥qπ∥2=O(K2ν−5).\sum_{K\le q<2K}\frac{1}{q^3\|q\pi\|^2}=O(K^{2\nu-5}).K≤q<2K∑​q3∥qπ∥21​=O(K2ν−5).

Because 2ν−5<02\nu-5<02ν−5<0, summing over K=1,2,4,…K=1,2,4,\ldotsK=1,2,4,… converges. Grouping integers near successive multiples of π\piπ transfers this estimate to the original sine series. This controls the frequency of spikes as well as their possible size; a crude separate estimate for every term would lose that information.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The manuscript does not claim bounded continued-fraction partial quotients of π\piπ, a uniform positive constant at exponent exactly two, or an effective denominator threshold. Those are stronger or different conclusions.

It also gives no claim about normality of the decimal expansion of π\piπ, digit frequencies or statistical independence of its digits. Rational approximation and digit randomness are distinct questions. Nor does the result automatically give exponent two for unrelated constants.

The generalized series criterion concerns fixed positive a,ba,ba,b and radian angles. It gives convergence and divergence, not an effective error bound for numerically summing the series. Exceptionally large terms can make numerical experiments misleading even when a positive series converges.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 is the main approximation claim. Theorem 2.1 states the separated-weight interpolation result; Sections 3–4 compare determinant estimates. Section 5 contains the dyadic spacing argument and Corollary 5.2’s exact generalized-series criterion.

The primary papers linked in section 3 trace the previous irrationality bounds and the Flint–Hills threshold. For optional background, continued fractions explain the convergents used above, and irrationality measure compares exponent two with stronger approximation properties.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The irrationality exponent of π is 2 (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Zilber–Pink: when too many special intersections force structure
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 016 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Two surfaces in three-dimensional space usually meet along a curve. Two curves in that space usually miss each other. Algebraic geometry packages this expectation in the formula

expected dimension=dim⁡X+dim⁡T−dim⁡S,\text{expected dimension}=\dim X+\dim T-\dim S,expected dimension=dimX+dimT−dimS,

where X,TX,TX,T lie in an ambient space SSS. An intersection larger than this prediction suggests a structural reason.

The Zilber–Pink principle asks what happens when TTT ranges over infinitely many arithmetically special subvarieties. A fixed pair might be easy to study, but infinitely many moving special targets could conceivably produce infinitely many exceptional intersections. The conjecture predicts strong finiteness once the special structure already forced by XXX is taken into account.

Family 016 contains four manuscripts. M1 claims the general abelian version over algebraic numbers. M2–M4 treat three types of special points on curves in the moduli space of principally polarized abelian surfaces, culminating in the curve case there. The two settings share a philosophy but have different meanings of “special.”

2. Background and essential definitions

The fixed abelian variety

An abelian variety is a connected projective algebraic group. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example; a product of elliptic curves gives examples in higher dimensions. A torsion point τ\tauτ satisfies mτ=0m\tau=0mτ=0 for some positive integer mmm.

Inside an abelian variety AAA, a special subvariety is a torsion coset

T=B+τ,T=B+\tau,T=B+τ,

where BBB is a connected abelian subgroup. This combines a subgroup direction with a finite-order translation. For an irreducible subvariety XXX, let S=⟨X⟩spS=\langle X\rangle_{\mathrm{sp}}S=⟨X⟩sp​ be the smallest torsion coset containing it.

An irreducible component YYY of X∩TX\cap TX∩T, with T⊆ST\subseteq ST⊆S special, is atypical if

dim⁡Y>dim⁡X+dim⁡T−dim⁡S.\dim Y>\dim X+\dim T-\dim S.dimY>dimX+dimT−dimS.

The ambient dimension is that of SSS, not automatically that of AAA. Otherwise a subvariety already lying in a smaller torsion coset would create misleading exceptional intersections.

For example, a curve in a three-dimensional abelian variety and a special curve have expected intersection dimension −1-1−1. Any intersection point is therefore atypical. A special surface has expected intersection dimension zero with the same curve, so an isolated intersection point is not atypical by this test.

“Maximal atypical” means maximal by inclusion among atypical subvarieties of XXX. Finiteness of maximal ones allows an infinite collection of exceptional points to lie inside one positive-dimensional exceptional subvariety.

The varying abelian surface

The moduli space A2\mathcal A_2A2​ parametrizes principally polarized abelian surfaces. A polarization supplies the algebraic analogue of a positive form; principal means its associated map to the dual abelian variety is an isomorphism. The space A2\mathcal A_2A2​ has dimension three, so it is often called the Siegel threefold.

Its special subvarieties are Shimura-special loci, including their Hecke translates. They encode extra endomorphisms or related Hodge-theoretic structure. A Hecke translate changes the abelian variety by a suitably compatible finite isogeny. An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism with finite kernel. A curve is Hodge generic if it lies in no proper special subvariety.

For an elliptic curve, complex multiplication, or CM, means that its geometric rational endomorphism algebra is an imaginary quadratic field instead of Q\mathbb QQ. For an abelian surface AsA_sAs​, write

End⁡0(As)=End⁡Q‾(As)⊗ZQ.\operatorname{End}^0(A_s)=\operatorname{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}(A_s)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q.End0(As​)=EndQ​​(As​)⊗Z​Q.

The full algebra matters. The matrix algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q) corresponds to a surface isogenous to the square of a non-CM elliptic curve. An indefinite quaternion division algebra is instead a four-dimensional noncommutative algebra over Q\mathbb QQ, with every nonzero element invertible, which becomes M2(R)M_2(\mathbb R)M2​(R) over R\mathbb RR. It is not the split algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Raynaud’s Manin–Mumford theorem established the torsion-point case: an irreducible subvariety with Zariski-dense torsion points must itself be a torsion coset. Zilber’s unlikely-intersection formulation and Pink’s semiabelian and Shimura formulations extend the problem to moving special subvarieties of positive dimension.

In abelian varieties, Viada and Rémond–Viada obtained early curve results in powers of CM elliptic curves. Habegger and Pila proved the curve theorem for arbitrary abelian varieties over number fields. Their 2016 paper also gives higher-dimensional results under additional quotient-dimension or height restrictions. Barroero, Kühne and Schmidt later treated curves in general semiabelian varieties. M1’s introduction distinguishes these curve theorems from unrestricted higher-dimensional maximal-atypical finiteness.

Higher-dimensional partial results included non-density when every quotient has the expected image dimension, non-density at a fixed height bound, and finiteness of certain codimension-one or codimension-two exceptional subvarieties. These are meaningful advances, but a fixed height cutoff cannot cover points of arbitrarily large height without another argument.

For A2\mathcal A_2A2​, André–Oort supplies finiteness of special points on a Hodge-generic curve. Pila and Tsimerman established this case, and Tsimerman’s later general theorem covers the broader Siegel setting. Positive-dimensional special targets require more.

Daw and Orr developed reductions from large Galois orbits to finiteness and proved important cases under degeneration assumptions. Their work on large Galois orbits under multiplicative degeneration obtains the full curve conclusion when the closure meets the zero-dimensional boundary stratum. Papas obtained further interior-period results with hypotheses involving reduction and the number of supersingular places of proximity. M2–M4 aim to remove such restrictions for the three relevant loci.

The common counting strategy comes from Pila and Zannier: arithmetic supplies many conjugates, while tame geometric counting allows few unless an unexpected algebraic structure appears. The new manuscripts place their height and period estimates within that existing framework.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: finitely many maximal atypical subvarieties

Let AAA be any abelian variety over a number field and X⊆AQ‾X\subseteq A_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}X⊆AQ​​ irreducible. M1 claims that XXX has only finitely many maximal atypical subvarieties, measured inside ⟨X⟩sp\langle X\rangle_{\mathrm{sp}}⟨X⟩sp​.

No restriction on dimension, simplicity, complex multiplication, point height or point degree is imposed. A key intermediate statement is universal non-density. If XXX lies in no proper torsion coset and d=dim⁡Xd=\dim Xd=dimX, then

X∩A[d+1]is not Zariski dense in X,X\cap A^{[d+1]}\quad\text{is not Zariski dense in }X,X∩A[d+1]is not Zariski dense in X,

where A[r]A^{[r]}A[r] is the union of all torsion cosets of codimension at least rrr. Zariski non-density means containment in a proper algebraic closed subset. For an irreducible curve, a proper closed subset is finite; in higher dimensions, non-density alone is weaker than finiteness.

M1 applies a universal reduction through optimal subvarieties to pass from this non-density theorem for all ambient varieties to the maximal-atypical conclusion. It also claims a finite-rank translated version: if Γ⊂A(Q‾)\Gamma\subset A(\overline{\mathbb Q})Γ⊂A(Q​) satisfies

dim⁡Q(Γ⊗ZQ)<∞,\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\Gamma\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q)<\infty,dimQ​(Γ⊗Z​Q)<∞,

and XXX lies in no translate of a proper algebraic subgroup, then

X(Q‾)∩(A[d+1](Q‾)+Γ)X(\overline{\mathbb Q})\cap\bigl(A^{[d+1]}(\overline{\mathbb Q})+\Gamma\bigr)X(Q​)∩(A[d+1](Q​)+Γ)

is not Zariski dense. This stronger geometric hypothesis excludes arbitrary proper translates, not just torsion translates. The group Γ\GammaΓ need not be finitely generated: division hulls and torsion groups are included.

M2–M4: three special-curve branches

Let C⊂A2C\subset\mathcal A_2C⊂A2​ be a reduced irreducible closed Hodge-generic curve over Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​. The manuscripts claim finiteness for the following sets of algebraic points:

ManuscriptCondition on the represented abelian surface
M2Isogenous to E1×E2E_1\times E_2E1​×E2​, with at least one elliptic factor having CM.
M3Full geometric rational endomorphism algebra equal to an indefinite quaternion division algebra over Q\mathbb QQ.
M4Isogenous to E2E^2E2 for a non-CM elliptic curve EEE, equivalently full endomorphism algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q).

The isogenies in the product descriptions need not preserve the given principal polarization. All degrees, CM fields, endomorphism orders, relevant quaternion algebras and polarizations are allowed. None of these statements requires the curve to meet a boundary, and complete curves are included.

M4 combines the three branches with the classification of special curves and André–Oort for special points. Its resulting theorem is

C(Q‾)∩⋃Z⊂A2 specialdim⁡Z≤1Z(Q‾)is finite.C(\overline{\mathbb Q})\cap\bigcup_{\substack{Z\subset\mathcal A_2\ \mathrm{special}\\\dim Z\le1}}Z(\overline{\mathbb Q})\quad\text{is finite}.C(Q​)∩Z⊂A2​ specialdimZ≤1​⋃​Z(Q​)is finite.

For a curve not Hodge generic in A2\mathcal A_2A2​, M4 also records the corresponding formulation inside its smallest special closure SCS_CSC​, using special targets with dim⁡Z<dim⁡SC−1\dim Z<\dim S_C-1dimZ<dimSC​−1.

A quantitative ingredient, not an effective list

For a mixed product point in M2, let N(s)N(s)N(s) be the least product-isogeny degree and DDD the absolute discriminant of the CM factor’s endomorphism order. Set c(s)=max⁡{N(s),D}c(s)=\max\{N(s),D\}c(s)=max{N(s),D}. M2 claims

#(Gal⁡(Q‾/K)⋅s)≥c c(s)1/42,\#\bigl(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/K)\cdot s\bigr)\ge c\,c(s)^{1/42},#(Gal(Q​/K)⋅s)≥cc(s)1/42,

with c>0c>0c>0 depending on the fixed curve and its field of definition KKK. The exponent is a usable positive power, not an optimized constant. The statement does not claim effectivity; its inputs include a potentially ineffective class-number estimate.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Taken as stated, M1 settles a central arbitrary-dimensional form of the abelian Zilber–Pink conjecture. M2–M4 complete another substantial case, curves in A2\mathcal A_2A2​, by treating all three special-curve branches without boundary restrictions.

The broad idea is that unexpectedly large intersections cannot occur in infinitely many unrelated ways. In the abelian setting they must be contained in finitely many maximal exceptional subvarieties. In the Hodge-generic curve setting the exceptional set itself is finite.

These conclusions strengthen the structural meaning of a dimension count. They also connect diverse methods: canonical heights, period estimates, reduction at primes, Galois orbits and geometry of definable sets. The scope merits the highest relative rating without implying that all mixed-Shimura or semiabelian versions are covered.

6. The main idea

Separate the height scales

M1 starts from a hypothetical Zariski-generic sequence of unlikely-intersection points. The canonical, or Néron–Tate, height behaves quadratically under multiplication and acts like a squared norm modulo torsion. Different projections of the points may have bounded heights or heights growing at very different rates.

The manuscript separates these scales by taking suitable quotients and normalizing each level independently. The subgroup relations then approach a limiting linear projector. Geometric positivity, built from Ax-type results and finitely many exceptional directions, constrains how this projector can annihilate the normalized points.

When every level diverges, a generalized Vojta–Rémond height inequality gives the contradiction. A bounded level needs a different argument: compare two limiting measures on a fixed low-height factor, one associated with a product map and another with consecutive differences. Their incompatible densities yield arithmetic positivity. Small sections then vanish to high order at the marked points, and a product theorem cuts out a smaller auxiliary variety, contradicting minimality.

The uniformity concerns the auxiliary varieties and their fields of definition; it does not assume that the marked intersection points have bounded degree.

Turn special structure into many controlled conjugates

M2 uses the gluing description of a mixed product surface. A product isogeny has degree n2n^2n2, while its rank-one degeneration length carries a reciprocal factor 1/n1/n1/n. This produces a height estimate growing roughly linearly in nnn, up to the CM discriminant contribution. A balanced period construction on a related abelian threefold yields a stronger n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3 contribution. Comparing them forces the required Galois-orbit growth.

M3 and M4 instead study a rank-five quadratic system arising from trace-zero endomorphisms self-adjoint for the polarization. Extra endomorphisms supply positive two-dimensional planes. Period transport compares a fixed interior exceptional point with a varying target.

At suitable finite places, traces of endomorphism products give local equations. Comparing Frobenius-conjugate equations eliminates coefficients that depend on the prime. Grouping by conjugate data controls the number of equation types even when many primes contribute.

An interpolation and product-formula argument then gives a polynomial height bound in the field degree:

h(t)≤C [K(t):K]κ.h(t)\le C\,[K(t):K]^\kappa.h(t)≤C[K(t):K]κ.

Here hhh is a fixed logarithmic height and C,κC,\kappaC,κ depend on the curve. Auxiliary level markings ensure that the equations are genuinely nonidentical; M4 uses a second marking to handle bad reduction at the chosen center.

Finally, endomorphism bounds convert height control into polynomially controlled arithmetic coordinates or large Galois orbits. Pila–Wilkie-type counting forces an algebraic family if there are too many such points. Monodromy or the established Daw–Orr implication then contradicts Hodge genericity. The elliptic-square argument is proved separately before being combined with the other branches.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 concerns torsion cosets in abelian varieties over algebraic numbers. It does not by itself prove Zilber–Pink for every semiabelian variety, every transcendental base field or every mixed Shimura variety. Its finite-rank consequence retains the stronger no-proper-translate assumption.

The A2\mathcal A_2A2​ conclusion is a theorem about curves. It does not cover arbitrary higher-dimensional subvarieties of every Ag\mathcal A_gAg​. M3 requires equality of the full endomorphism algebra with a quaternion division algebra; merely embedding such an algebra into something larger is not its stated condition.

No uniform or effective bound on the number of exceptional subvarieties is claimed. Finiteness alone does not provide a terminating procedure listing every exceptional point. Effective counts, explicit enumeration and extensions to broader moduli spaces remain additional problems.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 state the abelian and finite-rank conclusions. M2’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 give the mixed-product finiteness and Galois-orbit bound. M3’s Theorem 1.1 specifies the full quaternionic endomorphism condition. M4’s Theorems 1.1–1.3 separate the elliptic-square branch from the combined curve theorem.

The Habegger–Pila and Daw–Orr papers linked in section 3 give primary accounts of the earlier partial results and counting framework. The introductions of all four manuscripts carefully identify the height, period and monodromy inputs. Optional background on abelian varieties and complex multiplication can supplement the definitions above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The abelian Zilber-Pink conjecture (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The E×CM component of Zilber-Pink for curves in A2 (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quaternionic division points on curves in the Siegel threefold (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Elliptic squares and Zilber-Pink for curves in A2 (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The full BSD formula from a small Selmer group
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 002 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An elliptic curve can have infinitely many rational points even though its equation is very simple. The curve y2=x3+ax+by^2=x^3+ax+by2=x3+ax+b, when nonsingular and completed by its point at infinity, carries a group law. A basic arithmetic question asks how many independent rational points are needed to generate all the others, apart from a finite torsion subgroup.

The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, usually abbreviated BSD, predicts that this arithmetic information is encoded in an analytic function built from counting points modulo primes. It predicts both an order of vanishing and an exact leading coefficient. Knowing how many times a function vanishes does not determine the first nonzero coefficient, just as knowing that a polynomial has a double root does not determine its quadratic term.

Family 002 contains three manuscripts claiming the full formula when a prime-power Selmer group has corank zero or one. M2 supplies the unrestricted converse from this arithmetic condition to analytic rank and finiteness. M3 treats the exact power of two in the coefficient formula. M1 adds the odd-prime comparisons and assembles the exact equality.

The condition is on a Selmer group, not simply the number of independent rational points already found on the curve.

2. Background and essential definitions

Three measures of rank

For an elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, the Mordell–Weil theorem gives

E(Q)≅Zr⊕T,E(\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus T,E(Q)≅Zr⊕T,

where TTT is finite. The integer rrr is the Mordell–Weil rank. Rank zero means only finitely many rational points; positive rank means infinitely many.

At a prime ℓ\ellℓ of good reduction, let NℓN_\ellNℓ​ count the points of the reduced curve, including its point at infinity, and set aℓ=ℓ+1−Nℓa_\ell=\ell+1-N_\ellaℓ​=ℓ+1−Nℓ​. These counts contribute factors

(1−aℓℓ−s+ℓ1−2s)−1\left(1-a_\ell\ell^{-s}+\ell^{1-2s}\right)^{-1}(1−aℓ​ℓ−s+ℓ1−2s)−1

to the Hasse–Weil function L(E,s)L(E,s)L(E,s). There are specified factors at bad primes as well. Modularity gives analytic continuation and a functional equation with center s=1s=1s=1. The analytic rank is the order of vanishing there, written ord⁡s=1L(E,s)\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)ords=1​L(E,s).

A Selmer group packages arithmetic compatibility conditions over Q\mathbb QQ, the real numbers, and all prime-adic completions. For a prime ppp, the full ppp-power Selmer group uses all powers pnp^npn, with the usual local conditions everywhere. It is larger than the information supplied by rational points alone.

The discrepancy is measured by the Tate–Shafarevich group, written Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q). Its elements describe principal homogeneous spaces for EEE: curves with an EEE-action which look like EEE after choosing a point. The classes in Sha have points over every completion but may have no rational point. Thus they record a failure of passing from local solvability to global solvability.

The standard exact sequence is

0⟶E(Q)⊗(Qp/Zp)⟶Sel⁡p∞(E/Q)⟶Sha⁡(E/Q)[p∞]⟶0.0\longrightarrow E(\mathbb Q)\otimes(\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sel}_{p^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)[p^\infty]\longrightarrow0.0⟶E(Q)⊗(Qp​/Zp​)⟶Selp∞​(E/Q)⟶Sha(E/Q)[p∞]⟶0.

Here [p∞][p^\infty][p∞] selects elements killed by some power of ppp. The corank sp(E)s_p(E)sp​(E) counts the copies of the divisible group Qp/Zp\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_pQp​/Zp​ in the Selmer group, ignoring finite parts. It counts the rational-point rank and potentially an additional divisible contribution from Sha. If Sha is finite, then sp(E)=rs_p(E)=rsp​(E)=r. Assuming r≤1r\leq1r≤1 alone does not establish the Selmer condition.

The factors in the leading coefficient

Write ΩE\Omega_EΩE​ for the integral of the absolute value of a minimal Néron differential over all real components of E(R)E(\mathbb R)E(R). A Néron differential is the invariant differential normalized by a minimal integral model. The finite Tamagawa number cℓc_\ellcℓ​ is the index of the subgroup reducing to the identity component inside E(Qℓ)E(\mathbb Q_\ell)E(Qℓ​); it is one at good primes.

The regulator Reg⁡E\operatorname{Reg}_ERegE​ measures the volume of the full free rational-point lattice using the canonical height pairing. To fix the convention used in these manuscripts, let hx(P)=log⁡max⁡(∣u∣,∣v∣)h_x(P)=\log\max(|u|,|v|)hx​(P)=logmax(∣u∣,∣v∣) when x(P)=u/vx(P)=u/vx(P)=u/v in lowest terms, and put

H(P)=lim⁡n→∞4−nhx([2n]P),B(P,Q)=H(P+Q)−H(P)−H(Q)2.H(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}4^{-n}h_x([2^n]P),\qquadB(P,Q)=\frac{H(P+Q)-H(P)-H(Q)}2.H(P)=n→∞lim​4−nhx​([2n]P),B(P,Q)=2H(P+Q)−H(P)−H(Q)​.

The regulator is the determinant of BBB on a basis of E(Q)/TE(\mathbb Q)/TE(Q)/T, and equals one in rank zero. A subgroup of index mmm has regulator m2Reg⁡Em^2\operatorname{Reg}_Em2RegE​. This distinction matters when a construction produces some independent points without proving that they form a full basis.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formulated their conjectures in the 1960s from computations relating rational points to point counts over finite fields. Their Notes on elliptic curves II is a primary source for this development. Tate placed the proposed rank and leading-term identities in a wider arithmetic framework, while Cassels explained how the combined expression behaves under isogeny.

The modularity work of Wiles, Taylor–Wiles, and Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor established the analytic setting for all elliptic curves over Q\mathbb QQ. The Gross–Zagier height formula relates derivatives of suitable L-functions to heights of Heegner points. Kolyvagin’s Euler systems then yield equality of analytic and arithmetic ranks, and finiteness of Sha, when analytic rank is zero or one.

Those results run from analytic information to arithmetic conclusions. A Selmer converse reverses the direction: small arithmetic Selmer corank must force a nonzero central value or derivative. That reversal is a separate problem, particularly when the curve has difficult reduction or a reducible representation on its torsion points.

Iwasawa theory, which studies arithmetic across towers of number fields, supplied increasingly strong converse and coefficient results. Kato’s zeta elements provide one direction of comparison; Skinner–Urban, Wei Zhang, and Jetchev–Skinner–Wan obtained major low-rank results under their respective local and residual hypotheses. Later work treated additional ordinary, supersingular, Eisenstein, and multiplicative cases. These labels distinguish how the curve and its torsion behave at the chosen prime; the manuscript’s historical sections explain the precise earlier restrictions.

Complex multiplication, meaning extra endomorphisms of the elliptic curve, provides another substantial theory. Burungale–Flach establish full rank-zero BSD for their class of CM curves, with consequences over Q\mathbb QQ. Exact two-primary formulas were also known in special CM and quadratic-twist settings. The family claims to remove the remaining curve and prime restrictions under the stated low-Selmer-corank hypothesis, while retaining every numerical factor in BSD.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The complete formula

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that, for every elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, if some prime qqq satisfies sq(E)∈{0,1}s_q(E)\in\{0,1\}sq​(E)∈{0,1}, then

r=rank⁡E(Q)=ord⁡s=1L(E,s)=sq(E),#Sha⁡(E/Q)<∞,r=\operatorname{rank}E(\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)=s_q(E),\qquad \#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)<\infty,r=rankE(Q)=ords=1​L(E,s)=sq​(E),#Sha(E/Q)<∞,

and

L(r)(E,1)r!=ΩEReg⁡E #Sha⁡(E/Q)∏ℓ finitecℓ(#T)2.\frac{L^{(r)}(E,1)}{r!}=\frac{\Omega_E\operatorname{Reg}_E\,\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\prod_{\ell\text{ finite}}c_\ell}{(\#T)^2}.r!L(r)(E,1)​=(#T)2ΩE​RegE​#Sha(E/Q)∏ℓ finite​cℓ​​.

Here L(r)L^{(r)}L(r) is the rrr-th derivative, so the left side is the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. The uncompleted L-function includes all finite Euler factors. The total real period already includes every real component; no extra real-component factor is inserted.

No additional assumption is imposed on reduction, rational torsion, rational isogenies, complex multiplication, or residual Galois representations. The prime qqq supplying the input condition need not equal a prime whose valuation is being checked in the output formula.

The roles of the three manuscripts

ManuscriptPrincipal contribution within the family
M1The exact full leading-term formula, completing the odd-prime comparisons and assembling all primes.
M2The low-corank Selmer converse at every prime, with finiteness of the entire Sha group.
M3The exact two-primary leading-term formula, with no restriction at two.

To state M3 precisely, define the normalized positive quantity

QE=L(r)(E,1)(#T)2r! ΩEReg⁡E∏ℓcℓ.Q_E=\frac{L^{(r)}(E,1)(\#T)^2}{r!\,\Omega_E\operatorname{Reg}_E\prod_\ell c_\ell}.QE​=r!ΩE​RegE​∏ℓ​cℓ​L(r)(E,1)(#T)2​.

It claims that s2(E)≤1s_2(E)\leq1s2​(E)≤1 gives the rank and finiteness conclusions, QE∈Q>0Q_E\in\mathbb Q_{>0}QE​∈Q>0​, and

v2(QE)=v2 ⁣(#Sha⁡(E/Q)).v_2(Q_E)=v_2\!\left(\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\right).v2​(QE​)=v2​(#Sha(E/Q)).

The valuation vpv_pvp​ counts the exponent of ppp in a nonzero rational number. Matching the valuation at two is one part of the full equality, not the whole equality.

M2 also derives the positive prime cube-sum cases ℓ≡4,7,8(mod9)\ell\equiv4,7,8\pmod9ℓ≡4,7,8(mod9): such primes are sums of two rational cubes, and the corresponding cubic has rank one and finite Sha. The paper acknowledges earlier direct treatments of these cases; this application illustrates its unrestricted converse at three.

Combining the family with the twist-density results discussed in family 006 gives the formula for a density-one set of signed squarefree twists of each fixed curve. That additional conclusion uses the distribution input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. BSD connects rational solutions, complex analysis, local arithmetic, and the failure of the local-to-global principle. An exact leading-term formula under an unrestricted low-Selmer-corank criterion would be a major advance on a central arithmetic problem.

The word “exact” has substantial content. Equality up to an unknown power of two, or up to factors at bad primes, leaves part of the conjecture unresolved. Likewise, proving that Sha is finite does not compute its order. The family claims to retain precisely the finite information that distinguishes these assertions.

Its reach is large but qualified: the initial Selmer condition remains essential. The density-one twist consequence means that exceptions have asymptotic proportion zero in the specified family; it does not eliminate every exceptional twist or prove BSD for arbitrary rank.

6. The main idea
