Force analytic nonvanishing from arithmetic smallness

For the converse, M2 reduces an odd-prime problem to showing that a certain Heegner point is not torsion. Heegner points arise from elliptic curves with complex multiplication mapped into the curve under study. The appropriate height formula then connects this point to an L-value or derivative.

Assuming the point is torsion, the paper obtains two incompatible measurements of the same auxiliary extension space. The low Selmer corank bounds how many Galois extensions satisfying specified local conditions can exist. A theta-series construction, transferred through congruences of automorphic forms, produces more such extensions than that bound permits.

A theta series is a structured generating function built from arithmetic data. Here the construction retains a truncated deformation parameter, so it records successive layers of extension information rather than only isolated character values. The stated contradiction forces the Heegner point to be non-torsion. The argument uses the separate two-converse and twist-density inputs identified in the manuscript.

Measure the error prime by prime

Once rank and finiteness are available, define

Xp(E)=vp(QE)−vp ⁣(#Sha⁡(E/Q)).X_p(E)=v_p(Q_E)-v_p\!\left(\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\right).Xp​(E)=vp​(QE​)−vp​(#Sha(E/Q)).

For odd ppp, M1 proves a nonnegative discrepancy for non-CM curves of analytic rank at most one. A second comparison pairs EEE with a suitable quadratic twist EDE^DED of complementary analytic rank and gives

Xp(E)+Xp(ED)=0.X_p(E)+X_p(E^D)=0.Xp​(E)+Xp​(ED)=0.

Two nonnegative numbers with sum zero must both vanish. CM curves are handled using the appropriate CM rank-zero input and a paired comparison. The same numerical idea appears in M3’s treatment at two, with additional machinery suited to that prime.

The difficult step is obtaining exact comparisons. The papers encode arithmetic in integral lattices and determinant lines, which track finite indices as well as vector-space dimensions. Their quotients must be units, elements with no unwanted divisibility, rather than merely integral elements. Theta comparisons and auxiliary deformation directions exclude possible extra factors. M3 treats the distinct torsion-representation cases and the real place explicitly.

Finally, M3 supplies positivity, rationality, and the correct valuation at two; M1 supplies every odd valuation. The positive rational number QE/#Sha⁡Q_E/\#\operatorname{Sha}QE​/#Sha then has exponent zero at every prime. Its prime factorization is empty, so it equals one. That last elementary observation turns the local comparisons into the full real-valued BSD formula.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These statements concern elliptic curves over Q\mathbb QQ. They do not assert unrestricted BSD over all number fields or in higher rank. In particular, a known Mordell–Weil rank of zero or one is not substituted for the full Selmer-corank assumption.

The precise normalizations of the period, height pairing, regulator, Euler factors, and local conditions are part of the result. Changing a height by a factor of two or using a sublattice of rational points changes the numerical formula unless the corresponding correction is made.

The family does not supply an efficient general algorithm to find a basis of rational points or compute Sha. Nor does its twist-density consequence imply a bound on every exceptional curve. Higher-corank cases and broader base fields remain outside the stated coverage.

8. Sources and further reading

The three Theorems 1.1 contain the principal assertions. M1’s introductory discrepancy calculation explains the final assembly; M2’s introduction describes the extension-length contradiction; M3’s first section distinguishes integrality from the stronger unit comparison needed at two.

The historical sources linked above explain the development from point-counting experiments to Heegner points and Iwasawa theory. Family 006 treats the complementary distribution question: how often the relevant small coranks occur among quadratic twists.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Exact Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer Formula from Low Selmer Corank (October 7, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Selmer converse for elliptic curves at every prime (October 7, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The two-primary Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula in Selmer corank at most one (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How arithmetic torus packets spread through spaces of lattices
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 015 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A lattice in the plane can be a square grid, a stretched rectangular grid, or a tilted one. In higher dimensions the variety of shapes is much larger. Number fields produce particularly structured lattices: apply all real embeddings of a field to its algebraic integers or ideals, then rescale to give a fundamental cell volume one.

These arithmetic lattices belong to compact families obtained by stretching the coordinate directions while preserving volume. The central question is whether complete collections of such families eventually spread uniformly through the space of all lattice shapes as their arithmetic complexity increases.

Family 015 reports three equidistribution results: one for every fixed prime degree at least five, one for primitive quartic fields, and one for primitive sextic fields. The objects being distributed are packets of orbits, with precise arithmetic membership and volume weights. This distinction is as important as the limiting uniformity.

2. Background and essential definitions

Number fields give lattices

A number field KKK is a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ. It is totally real of degree nnn if it has nnn embeddings σ1,…,σn\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_nσ1​,…,σn​ into R\mathbb RR. A full lattice M⊂KM\subset KM⊂K is a free abelian group of rank nnn spanning KKK over Q\mathbb QQ. Its image

σ(M)={(σ1(a),…,σn(a)):a∈M}\sigma(M)=\{(\sigma_1(a),\ldots,\sigma_n(a)):a\in M\}σ(M)={(σ1​(a),…,σn​(a)):a∈M}

is an ordinary lattice in Rn\mathbb R^nRn. Dividing it by the nnn-th root of its covolume makes its fundamental cell have volume one.

The space of these unimodular lattices is

Xn=SLn(Z)\SLn(R).X_n=\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb R).Xn​=SLn​(Z)\SLn​(R).

Changing an integral basis leaves the lattice unchanged, which explains the quotient. Its invariant probability mnm_nmn​, induced by Haar measure, is the natural meaning of “uniform distribution” on this space.

The positive diagonal group

An={diag⁡(eu1,…,eun):u1+⋯+un=0}A_n=\{\operatorname{diag}(e^{u_1},\ldots,e^{u_n}):u_1+\cdots+u_n=0\}An​={diag(eu1​,…,eun​):u1​+⋯+un​=0}

stretches coordinates without changing volume. Units of the appropriate number-theoretic order provide periods for this action. Dirichlet’s unit theorem makes the resulting arithmetic orbits compact tori of dimension n−1n-1n−1. The phrase “torus packet” refers to a finite arithmetic collection of these compact diagonal orbits.

Orders, ideal classes and local type

The ring of integers OK\mathcal O_KOK​ contains all algebraic integers in KKK. An order O⊆OK\mathcal O\subseteq\mathcal O_KO⊆OK​ is a subring containing one and having full rank. Its discriminant satisfies

∣Disc⁡(O)∣=∣Disc⁡(K)∣[OK:O]2.|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O)|=|\operatorname{Disc}(K)|[\mathcal O_K:\mathcal O]^2.∣Disc(O)∣=∣Disc(K)∣[OK​:O]2.

The discriminant therefore grows either because the field changes or because the order becomes thinner inside a fixed field.

Ideals are grouped into classes by multiplication by nonzero elements of KKK. For a nonmaximal order, an ideal is invertible if it has a fractional ideal inverse. Such ideals are locally free of rank one over that order; arbitrary full lattices need not have this property.

For a general full lattice, its multiplier order is

O(M)={a∈K:aM⊆M}.\mathcal O(M)=\{a\in K:aM\subseteq M\}.O(M)={a∈K:aM⊆M}.

Two full lattices have the same local homothety type if, after completing at every rational prime ℓ\ellℓ, they differ by multiplication by an invertible element of K⊗QQℓK\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ellK⊗Q​Qℓ​. Here Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​ is the completion for the ℓ\ellℓ-adic absolute value. Specifying the multiplier order alone can leave several local types possible.

Finally, a field is primitive if no field lies strictly between Q\mathbb QQ and KKK. Prime-degree fields are automatically primitive. Quartic and sextic fields require this as an additional hypothesis.

What is averaged?

For a packet P\mathcal PP, let νO\nu_OνO​ be uniform probability on an orbit OOO, and let vol⁡(O)\operatorname{vol}(O)vol(O) be its diagonal-group volume. The packet measure is

μP=∑O∈Pvol⁡(O)νO∑O∈Pvol⁡(O).\mu_{\mathcal P}=\frac{\sum_{O\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{vol}(O)\nu_O}{\sum_{O\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{vol}(O)}.μP​=∑O∈P​vol(O)∑O∈P​vol(O)νO​​.

Each distinct orbit appears once. The packet also includes the prescribed coordinate-sign translates, so ordinary ideal-class representatives do not introduce an artificial sign choice. In even dimensions all sign patterns are included, including determinant-negative sign matrices acting on the underlying lattice. In odd prime degree, determinant-positive sign patterns suffice because a common minus sign does not change a lattice.

3. Development history and previous partial results

For real quadratic fields, the related objects project to closed geodesics on the modular surface. Linnik’s dynamical approach, including Skubenko’s work, established distribution results with an auxiliary splitting condition. Duke removed that restriction for packets associated with fundamental discriminants using analytic methods. These are the two-dimensional origins of the problem, described in the introductions of M1–M3 and Duke’s cited 1988 paper.

Higher dimensions introduce a diagonal group with several independent directions. Einsiedler, Katok and Lindenstrauss proved a rigidity theorem: positive-entropy diagonal-invariant ergodic probabilities are algebraic in the relevant lattice spaces. Entropy measures the rate at which a dynamical system creates distinguishable orbit histories. This turns enough arithmetic spreading into a strong restriction on possible limit measures.

Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh connected arithmetic counting to that rigidity and proved the cubic analogue of Duke’s theorem, including packets arising from nonmaximal orders. Their 2011 paper is a central predecessor. It also explains why local homothety is finer than a multiplier-order condition and why composite dimensions allow additional limiting obstructions.

For higher prime degrees, Lemke Oliver, Thorner and Zaman proved equidistribution outside a small exceptional family of fields through progress on Artin LLL-functions. Their primary paper gives the surrounding analytic framework. Khayutin obtained entropy bounds under maximal-order and Galois-group hypotheses, while Wieser and Yang studied certain quartic packets with quadratic subfields and additional conditions.

The gaps addressed here are thus specific. M1 removes the exceptional-field restriction and admits arbitrary local module types. M2 and M3 tackle composite dimensions where positive entropy alone does not force the full uniform measure.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: fixed prime degree, every local type

Fix a prime n≥5n\ge5n≥5. For any sequence of totally real degree-nnn fields KiK_iKi​, full lattices Mi⊂KiM_i\subset K_iMi​⊂Ki​, and ordered real embeddings, M1 claims

D(Mi):=∣Disc⁡(O(Mi))∣⟶∞⟹μi⟶mn.D(M_i):=|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O(M_i))|\longrightarrow\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu_i\longrightarrow m_n.D(Mi​):=∣Disc(O(Mi​))∣⟶∞⟹μi​⟶mn​.

The packet consists of all global homothety classes in the prescribed local type, with the sign and volume conventions above. Nonmaximal orders can have unbounded index, and the lattices need not be invertible modules over their multiplier order. The fields may remain fixed while their multiplier-order discriminants grow. The degree is fixed throughout the limit.

M2: primitive quartic fields and arbitrary orders

For totally real primitive quartic fields KiK_iKi​ and arbitrary orders Oi\mathcal O_iOi​, M2 claims the same conclusion on X4X_4X4​ as

∣Disc⁡(Oi)∣⟶∞.|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O_i)|\longrightarrow\infty.∣Disc(Oi​)∣⟶∞.

Here the packet contains every class of proper invertible fractional Oi\mathcal O_iOi​-ideals. Proper means that the multiplier order is exactly Oi\mathcal O_iOi​. This is narrower than M1’s arbitrary full-lattice local types. It still includes sequences in one fixed primitive quartic field with increasing order index.

M3: primitive sextic fields, maximal orders

For totally real primitive sextic fields KiK_iKi​, M3 claims equidistribution of the complete ordinary ideal-class packets of OKi\mathcal O_{K_i}OKi​​ on X6X_6X6​, provided

∣Disc⁡(Ki)∣⟶∞.|\operatorname{Disc}(K_i)|\longrightarrow\infty.∣Disc(Ki​)∣⟶∞.

This statement concerns maximal orders. It does not extend M2’s arbitrary-order conclusion to degree six.

Uniformity includes keeping all the mass

For every continuous compactly supported test function fff, each theorem asserts

∫f dμi⟶∫f dmn.\int f\,d\mu_i\longrightarrow\int f\,dm_n.∫fdμi​⟶∫fdmn​.

It also asserts no escape of mass: given ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, a compact set contains at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon1−ε of every sufficiently late packet. This is necessary because XnX_nXn​ is noncompact. A lattice can become extremely thin in one direction while keeping volume one, moving into a cusp. Convergence observed only on bounded regions would otherwise allow some probability to disappear there.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, these theorems make major progress on higher-dimensional Duke equidistribution and on the interaction between number-field arithmetic and homogeneous dynamics.

M1’s force comes from treating every sequence in its degree range, including difficult local types and increasing conductor inside a fixed field. M2 and M3 overcome an additional structural issue: a spread-out limit in composite dimension can still live on a proper algebraic subspace. Excluding that possibility demands more information than a single entropy estimate.

The conclusion says that a highly constrained arithmetic construction eventually samples ordinary lattice geometry according to its invariant measure. It is a global distribution statement about complete packets, not a claim that an individual ideal produces a randomly chosen lattice.

6. The main idea

Count vectors, then use dynamics

The common first step averages lattice-vector counts over the packet. Ideal classes and local module choices convert this geometric average into an arithmetic ideal count. Short-vector bounds prevent escape into the cusp; bounds for vectors in small boxes show that limiting measures cannot concentrate too strongly in ordinary neighborhoods.

A key normalization is the residue

κK=Res⁡s=1ζK(s),\kappa_K=\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s),κK​=s=1Res​ζK​(s),

where ζK\zeta_KζK​ is the Dedekind zeta function. The class-number formula brings this residue into the packet volume. The papers retain the same factor in their counting estimates so that it cancels correctly, rather than replacing it prematurely by a rough field-dependent bound.

M1 handles nonmaximal local modules through containment probabilities: at each prime, how likely is a vector to belong to a unit translate of the prescribed module? A uniform small positive moment controls the local tails. Stark’s exceptional-zero information and short-interval estimates supply the global count; the absence of quadratic subfields is relevant here.

The resulting radius-rrr ball estimate has order rnr^nrn. Since the diagonal orbits have dimension n−1n-1n−1, this enforces positive entropy in almost every ergodic component. In prime degree, the existing measure-classification theorem then identifies the limit as Haar probability.

Quartic fields: detect the remaining block structure

In degree four, proper homogeneous limits can have two blocks of size two. M2 detects this through the exterior square of a lattice. Exterior coordinates vijv_{ij}vij​ record oriented two-dimensional areas, and the diagonal action preserves three products:

(v12v34,−v13v24,v14v23).(v_{12}v_{34},-v_{13}v_{24},v_{14}v_{23}).(v12​v34​,−v13​v24​,v14​v23​).

These products are organized by a cubic resolvent field associated with the quartic field. A two-block obstruction forces two product coordinates to be very small. Counting such thin configurations rules out concentration on the obstructing homogeneous pieces.

The hard extension to arbitrary orders is uniformity at primes dividing the order index. M2 uses local quadratic Fourier analysis, Poisson summation and a sieve to retain the correct conductor dependence and packet normalization.

Sextic fields: retain information before taking the limit

M3 uses ordinary vectors together with dual vectors to bound the mass of thin two-sided dynamical tubes. Primitivity ensures that every nonrational field element generates the full field, providing the arithmetic separation needed for these bounds.

A subtlety is that exact conditional measures of each finite packet along a transverse root direction are atomic. Taking such conditionals too early would hide spreading visible at growing scales. M3 instead conditions at intermediate resolutions before passing to a limit, proves a product rule, and tracks which root directions have nontrivial spread.

The root groups are elementary shears I+sEjkI+sE_{jk}I+sEjk​, where EjkE_{jk}Ejk​ has a single nonzero entry. The argument propagates activity among these directions and uses tube decay to force full activity. A proper homogeneous component would leave a direction inactive, giving the required contradiction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All three statements concern complete packets with the stated weights. They do not assert equidistribution of an individual orbit, an arbitrary subset of ideal classes, or an unweighted collection chosen by another rule. No quantitative convergence rate is part of the headline conclusions.

The permitted degrees and orders should remain separate: arbitrary local types in fixed prime degree at least five; invertible ideals of arbitrary orders in primitive quartic fields; maximal-order ideals in primitive sextic fields. General composite degrees, fields with intermediate subfields, and unrestricted sextic orders are outside these statements.

Primitivity is an arithmetic hypothesis on each field, but it does not automatically prohibit a sequence from approaching a proper homogeneous space. That is precisely why the additional quartic and sextic arguments are needed. Extending those arguments to broader settings is a natural further question.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 of each manuscript gives its packet definition and limiting statement. M1’s introduction and Sections 2–6 explain counting, local types and entropy. M2’s Sections 4–9 describe the quartic obstruction and cubic-resolvent method. M3’s introduction provides a detailed guide to the intermediate-resolution argument.

The cubic theorem and the approximate-Artin paper linked in section 3 are useful primary predecessors. The manuscripts’ bibliographies identify Duke’s original paper and the measure-rigidity and entropy results used here. For optional terminology, see Dirichlet’s unit theorem and equidistribution; the packet convergence above is a measure-valued version of that general idea.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Equidistribution of Prime-Degree Torus Packets with Arbitrary Local Type (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Equidistribution of primitive quartic torus packets for arbitrary orders (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Equidistribution of Primitive Sextic Torus Packets (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Margulis–Platonov: local origins of abstract normal subgroups
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 018 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A normal subgroup is the kernel of a possible quotient: it describes which elements become indistinguishable after passing to a simpler group. For matrix groups with entries in a number field, one can construct quotients by examining the entries locally, using completions of the field and congruence conditions.

Could there also be abstract normal subgroups that have no such local explanation? The word “abstract” is important. We do not assume that a subgroup is closed, continuous, finitely generated or initially related to congruences.

The Margulis–Platonov conjecture predicts that, apart from subgroups in the center, every normal subgroup of the rational points of a suitable simple algebraic group is detected by finitely many compact local groups. Family 018 claims this classification over number fields and over global function fields, including characteristic two.

2. Background and essential definitions

Global fields and their completions

A global field is either a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ, called a number field, or a finite extension of Fq(t)\mathbb F_q(t)Fq​(t), called a global function field. A place vvv specifies an absolute value, and completing the field gives kvk_vkv​.

For Q\mathbb QQ, the familiar real absolute value gives R\mathbb RR, while each prime ppp gives the field Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​. These latter, nonarchimedean completions measure divisibility rather than ordinary size. Function-field places are all nonarchimedean.

An algebraic group GGG is a group defined by polynomial equations. Its rational points G(k)G(k)G(k) consist of solutions with coordinates in kkk. The standard example is SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, the determinant-one matrices.

The hypotheses are that GGG is absolutely almost simple and simply connected. Absolutely almost simple means that, even over an algebraic closure, it has no proper positive-dimensional connected normal algebraic subgroup. Simply connected has its algebraic-group meaning: there is no nontrivial central isogeny onto it from another connected semisimple group. It does not assert topological simple connectedness of every group G(kv)G(k_v)G(kv​).

The compact local factors

The kvk_vkv​-rank of GGG is the dimension of its largest split torus over kvk_vkv​. A split torus looks like a product of multiplicative groups. If this rank is zero, the group is anisotropic at vvv.

For the nonarchimedean places in this setting, anisotropy corresponds to compactness of G(kv)G(k_v)G(kv​). Compact groups can have open normal subgroups and finite quotients. They are therefore natural sources of finite quotients of G(k)G(k)G(k).

Let

A={v nonarchimedean:rank⁡kvG=0},HA=∏v∈AG(kv).\mathcal A=\{v\text{ nonarchimedean}:\operatorname{rank}_{k_v}G=0\},\qquad H_{\mathcal A}=\prod_{v\in\mathcal A}G(k_v).A={v nonarchimedean:rankkv​​G=0},HA​=v∈A∏​G(kv​).

The set A\mathcal AA is finite. The diagonal map δA:G(k)→HA\delta_{\mathcal A}:G(k)\to H_{\mathcal A}δA​:G(k)→HA​ regards the same rational element in each completion. The product has its usual local topology.

The center Z(G(k))Z(G(k))Z(G(k)) consists of elements commuting with every element of G(k)G(k)G(k). A subgroup is noncentral if it is not contained in this center. If WWW is open and normal in HAH_{\mathcal A}HA​, its inverse image is an abstract normal subgroup of G(k)G(k)G(k). The conjecture says that this construction accounts for all noncentral normal subgroups.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem grew from Kneser’s simplicity question for norm-one groups of quaternion algebras and Platonov’s extension to simply connected simple groups. Margulis formulated the description using anisotropic local factors. His normal-subgroup results supplied a crucial finite-index reduction, but finite index alone did not identify which local topology detects the subgroup.

The isotropic case was settled through the global Kneser–Tits theorem and simplicity results based on unipotent generation. The anisotropic cases require different tools because those unipotent directions may be absent over the ground field.

For inner forms of type AAA, the groups are closely related to norm-one elements of division algebras. Work by Tomanov, Platonov–Rapinchuk, Raghunathan and Rapinchuk–Potapchik developed reductions to finite quotients. Segev and Segev–Seitz supplied finite-simple-group obstructions. Rapinchuk–Segev–Seitz then proved the stronger statement that every finite quotient of the multiplicative group of a finite-dimensional division algebra is solvable, and established Margulis–Platonov for inner type AAA over global fields. Their primary paper records this result.

Other classical and low-index unitary cases were known, as were substantial quadratic-splitting cases through Chernousov’s work. The number-field manuscript identifies the remaining groups as anisotropic outer type AAA, trialitarian type D4D_4D4​, and type E6E_6E6​. Over function fields, Harder’s structural results reduce the unresolved anisotropic case to outer type AAA, represented by special unitary groups.

The conjecture also matters to the congruence subgroup problem, which asks whether finite-index subgroups of arithmetic groups come from congruence conditions. Prasad and Rapinchuk’s survey explains this relationship. It is an input to that broader problem, not an automatic solution to all its cases.

M2 develops the number-field argument. M1 adapts its structure to function fields, replacing steps that depend on characteristic zero and treating characteristic two separately where necessary.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The normal-subgroup theorem over all global fields

M2 claims that, over every number field kkk, every noncentral abstract normal subgroup N◃G(k)N\triangleleft G(k)N◃G(k) has the form

N=δA−1(W)\boxed{N=\delta_{\mathcal A}^{-1}(W)}N=δA−1​(W)​

for some open normal subgroup W◃HAW\triangleleft H_{\mathcal A}W◃HA​. Only nonarchimedean anisotropic places enter the product. Compact real factors are not added to this formula.

M1 claims exactly the corresponding description for every global function field and every positive characteristic. It includes groups anisotropic over the global field and does not exclude characteristic two or power exponents divisible by the characteristic.

If A\mathcal AA is empty, the product is the trivial group. The conclusion then reads

N=G(k).N=G(k).N=G(k).

Thus there are no proper noncentral normal subgroups in that case. This is an exact abstract equality, stronger than saying that a subgroup is dense or merely has finite index.

In general, an open subgroup of the finite compact product has finite index, so the theorem explains the finite-index conclusion through a particular local source. It also means that every finite quotient of G(k)G(k)G(k) is continuous for the topology induced by these anisotropic local factors: its finite-index kernel is noncentral and hence arises from an open local subgroup.

A carefully delimited congruence consequence

M2 applies the normal-subgroup theorem to Rapinchuk’s positive-density congruence theorem. Let M/kM/kM/k be the minimal Galois extension over which GGG becomes an inner form of the split group. Let Spl⁡(M/k)\operatorname{Spl}(M/k)Spl(M/k) be the nonarchimedean places splitting completely in MMM.

Suppose a set of places SSS contains every archimedean place, contains no nonarchimedean anisotropic place, and satisfies

dk(S∩Spl⁡(M/k))>0,d_k\bigl(S\cap\operatorname{Spl}(M/k)\bigr)>0,dk​(S∩Spl(M/k))>0,

where the indicated Dirichlet density exists. Dirichlet density measures the asymptotic proportion of primes through their weighted prime sums. Under these hypotheses M2 claims that the SSS-congruence kernel is trivial.

Equivalently, in a fixed faithful matrix representation, every finite-index normal subgroup of G(O(S))G(\mathcal O(S))G(O(S)) contains a principal congruence subgroup of nonzero ideal level. Here O(S)\mathcal O(S)O(S) consists of elements integral outside SSS; a principal congruence subgroup is the kernel of reduction modulo an ideal. The conclusion retains the positive-density and anisotropic-place restrictions. It is not the unrestricted finite-SSS congruence conjecture.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, the family completes a major structural classification across all global fields. It says that an abstract quotient cannot hide information invisible to the designated local groups.

This is a strong connection between algebra and topology. The subgroup is introduced without continuity, yet the theorem forces a local topological description. The anisotropic factors are precisely where compactness permits finite information to survive.

The result also supplies a missing hypothesis in existing congruence theorems and unifies remaining unitary and exceptional-group cases. Its impact is broad within arithmetic groups, while the separate requirements of the full congruence subgroup problem remain significant.

6. The main idea

Isolate what local closure might miss

Starting with a finite quotient, choose a positive integer eee annihilating it and form the subgroup

R=⟨ge:g∈G(k)⟩.R=\langle g^e:g\in G(k)\rangle.R=⟨ge:g∈G(k)⟩.

This is the group generated by all eee-th powers, not merely the set of powers. Let

P0=δA(R)‾,V0=δA−1(P0),V=V0/R.P_0=\overline{\delta_{\mathcal A}(R)},\qquadV_0=\delta_{\mathcal A}^{-1}(P_0),\qquad V=V_0/R.P0​=δA​(R)​,V0​=δA−1​(P0​),V=V0​/R.

The finite group VVV measures a potential discrepancy: a rational point might lie in the local closure of the power subgroup without lying in the abstract subgroup itself. The central task is to prove V=1V=1V=1.

Ordinary approximation only gets close locally. The papers develop approximation within an exact prescribed coset of RRR, while simultaneously controlling finitely many places and avoiding unwanted reductions at the others. Products of conjugated torus powers retain the coset condition. A separate norm-torus calculation turns compatible local norm equations into exact rational solutions.

Exclude two kinds of finite obstruction

For an odd-degree division algebra with a unitary involution, a nontrivial discrepancy produces either a finite abelian character or a finite nonabelian simple quotient of the full unitary group. Passing from the special unitary subgroup to this full group requires commuting approximation and a central-extension argument; it is not automatic.

Finite abelian characters are handled by exact algebraic difference identities and elementary transformations, using the already known inner-type-AAA theorem.

A nonabelian simple quotient can be viewed as assigning finitely many colors to rational unitary elements. The color assignment is not assumed continuous. The papers construct an invariant probability law on finite color patterns that retains uniform distributions over all colors. This is essential: naive averaging could lose some of them.

Recurrence then forces membership in a carefully chosen proper subset of colors to be invariant under more transformations than is possible. Finite-simple-group structure supplies the obstruction, and generated rotations ultimately force that subset to be either empty or the entire group, contradicting its choice.

Adapt the argument to characteristic and group type

The number-field proof uses a multidimensional recurrence theorem of Furstenberg and Katznelson. In positive characteristic, additive groups have finite exponent, so the same integer-dilation argument does not apply. M1 replaces it with finite additive Fourier analysis. Odd characteristic uses a quadratic parametrization; characteristic two uses additive polynomials and coordinates over power subfields.

Another issue arises when the characteristic divides eee: taking eee-th powers need not be locally invertible. M1 separates the inseparable part and controls local power subgroups directly.

Induction then handles the remaining unitary degrees through smaller centralizers, quaternion factors and simultaneous norm equations. Degree four has a separate determinant correction. M2 additionally treats the remaining D4D_4D4​ and E6E_6E6​ groups by factorization into subgroups whose normal-subgroup behavior is already controlled. Finally the argument returns from the power subgroup to the original NNN.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The groups are absolutely almost simple and algebraically simply connected. Dropping those assumptions can change both the available quotients and the appropriate statement. Central subgroups are explicitly outside the classification of noncentral ones.

The theorem concerns G(k)G(k)G(k), the full rational-point group. An arithmetic subgroup such as G(Z)G(\mathbb Z)G(Z) is a different object and can have different normal-subgroup behavior. One should not replace it by G(k)G(k)G(k) in either direction without the relevant arithmetic argument.

The congruence consequence is limited to the stated positive-density range. It does not settle Serre’s finite-SSS conjecture, arbitrary infinite sets SSS, or all questions about the size and centrality of congruence kernels. Nor does the classification provide an explicit algorithm listing every open normal subgroup of each compact local factor.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 of M1 gives the function-field statement, including characteristic two. Theorem 1.1 of M2 gives the number-field statement; Corollary 1.2 gives the positive-density congruence consequence. Both introductions explain the finite discrepancy group and distinguish known type-AAA inputs from the remaining cases.

The Rapinchuk–Segev–Seitz paper and Prasad–Rapinchuk survey linked in section 3 provide primary background. Rapinchuk’s positive-density theorem is the separate input used for M2’s corollary. Optional background on normal subgroups and local fields can help connect the abstract and topological sides.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Margulis–Platonov conjecture over global function fields (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Margulis–Platonov conjecture over number fields (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Recovering p-adic points from fundamental-group sections
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 019 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Can the rational points of an algebraic curve be recognized purely from its groups of covering symmetries? Grothendieck’s section conjecture proposes a striking answer: a point should be equivalent to a certain splitting of the curve’s arithmetic fundamental group.

The distinction between a point and a splitting is substantial. A point is a solution of polynomial equations. A splitting is a continuous homomorphism between infinite profinite groups. The conjecture says that, for suitable curves and fields, the group-theoretic object cannot exist without a geometric point producing it.

Family 019 claims the local version over every finite extension of Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​. It also contains a geometric theorem constructing one étale cover with simultaneously prescribed behavior over several disks and their common exterior. The section manuscript gives global consequences under an additional finite-descent hypothesis, including stated modular-curve cases over Q\mathbb QQ.

2. Background and essential definitions

Covering spaces in algebraic geometry

A finite étale cover Y→XY\to XY→X is a finite algebraic map with no ramification. It is the algebraic counterpart of a finite covering space. The étale fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X)π1​(X) records how the sheets of every such cover can be permuted compatibly.

Unlike the usual fundamental group from elementary topology, it is profinite: an inverse limit of finite groups. Its topology is part of the data, so homomorphisms in the section conjecture must be continuous.

Let kkk be a finite extension of Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​, with algebraic closure kˉ\bar kkˉ. Its absolute Galois group is Gk=Gal⁡(kˉ/k)G_k=\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)Gk​=Gal(kˉ/k). For a smooth proper geometrically connected curve X/kX/kX/k, the fundamental group fits into

1⟶π1(Xkˉ)⟶π1(X)⟶rGk⟶1.1\longrightarrow\pi_1(X_{\bar k})\longrightarrow\pi_1(X)\overset{r}{\longrightarrow}G_k\longrightarrow1.1⟶π1​(Xkˉ​)⟶π1​(X)⟶r​Gk​⟶1.

The kernel records covers after the constants are algebraically closed. The quotient records arithmetic symmetry of the constants.

A section is a continuous group homomorphism s:Gk→π1(X)s:G_k\to\pi_1(X)s:Gk​→π1​(X) with r∘s=id⁡r\circ s=\operatorname{id}r∘s=id. A rational point a∈X(k)a\in X(k)a∈X(k) supplies a section. Choices of paths or base-point identifications change it by conjugation inside π1(Xkˉ)\pi_1(X_{\bar k})π1​(Xkˉ​), so the intrinsic object is a conjugacy class.

Here proper curves have no punctures, and “hyperbolic” means genus at least two. The genus measures the curve’s geometric complexity; this restriction is central to the conjecture’s stated form.

Valuations, disks and birational information

A valuation measures sizes of field elements. A decomposition group consists of Galois automorphisms preserving a chosen extension of a valuation. It can therefore locate group-theoretic information at a point or at a more general valued position.

The function field K=k(X)K=k(X)K=k(X) contains rational functions on the curve. Its absolute Galois group records all finite separable extensions, including covers ramified at points. The étale group records only unramified covers of the whole curve. Consequently, lifting an étale section to a birational section of the function-field Galois group is an additional task.

For geometric constructions the papers use Berkovich analytic curves over Ω=kˉ^\Omega=\widehat{\bar k}Ω=kˉ, the completed algebraic closure. These spaces include generalized points that make nonarchimedean curves connected and allow finite graph-like skeleta to describe their degeneration. An open disk has a single attachment point to its exterior; annuli become edges of a skeleton. This geometry makes it possible to cut, glue and control covers analytically before recovering algebraic covers.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Grothendieck formulated the section conjecture in his 1983 letter to Faltings for arithmetic fields, with the properness condition relevant to the version used here. The local ppp-adic problem keeps the full arithmetic and geometric fundamental groups but brings valuation theory into the foreground.

Koenigsmann established the birational ppp-adic section theorem: a birational section is located at a rational point. Pop later obtained a related criterion from suitable small quotients of the Galois group. These results do not automatically give the étale theorem because a section of a quotient need not lift through the larger group.

Pop and Stix proved that every étale section can be localized at a valuation extending the ppp-adic valuation. Their primary paper turns the question into one about which valuations can support a section. Pajwani developed this perspective using étale homotopy and fixed points in Berkovich spaces. The remaining issue is to force the relevant valuation to come from a rational point.

On the covering side, Tamagawa constructed resolution covers for points of stable marked models, Lepage treated Mumford curves, and Mochizuki–Tsujimura supplied positive-genus resolution for arbitrary hyperbolic curves over ppp-adic local fields. M1 builds on this geometry to impose exterior splitting and divisibility of disk-component degrees simultaneously.

For global applications, Harari–Stix connected sections with finite descent, while Stoll developed criteria under which finite descent cuts out exactly the rational points. Stoll’s paper, together with its corrections cited in M2, is the arithmetic input for several consequences. Betts–Stix also proved restrictions on local images of globally constrained Selmer sections; this concerns sections already arising from points at every completion, not the full local surjectivity claimed here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: one exterior sheet and nontrivial disk degrees

Let X/kˉX/\bar kX/kˉ be smooth, proper and connected of genus at least two. Choose finitely many disjoint open disks V1,…,VdV_1,\ldots,V_dV1​,…,Vd​, each with radius in ∣Ω×∣|\Omega^\times|∣Ω×∣ and with its closed disk strictly inside a larger local-coordinate disk. Set

U=Xan∖⋃i=1dVi.U=X^{\mathrm{an}}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{d}V_i.U=Xan∖i=1⋃d​Vi​.

Assume UUU is nonempty and contains an Ω\OmegaΩ-rational point. M1 claims the existence of a single connected finite étale surjective cover g:Y→Xg:Y\to Xg:Y→X such that one component of g−1(U)g^{-1}(U)g−1(U) maps isomorphically to all of UUU, while every connected component above every ViV_iVi​ has degree divisible by ppp.

The disks are the prescribed disks; they are not shrunk in the conclusion. Only one exterior sheet is required. The other sheets need not split, and the final cover need not be Galois.

M2: the full local section conjecture

For every prime ppp, finite extension k/Qpk/\mathbb Q_pk/Qp​, and smooth proper geometrically connected curve X/kX/kX/k of genus at least two, M2 claims a bijection

X(k)⟶{s:Gk→π1(X):r∘s=id⁡, s continuous}/π1(Xkˉ).X(k)\longrightarrow\{s:G_k\to\pi_1(X):r\circ s=\operatorname{id},\ s\text{ continuous}\}\big/\pi_1(X_{\bar k}).X(k)⟶{s:Gk​→π1​(X):r∘s=id, s continuous}/π1​(Xkˉ​).

The quotient is by conjugation by the full geometric étale fundamental group. The theorem both identifies every section with a point and distinguishes different points. No good-reduction assumption is imposed.

Its main intermediate theorem concerns completions. Let K~⊂Ksep\widetilde K\subset K^{\mathrm{sep}}K⊂Ksep be the compositum of the fields of all connected finite étale covers, retaining all embeddings. For a real-valued rank-one norm extending the normalized ppp-adic norm, choose a prolongation to KsepK^{\mathrm{sep}}Ksep. Inside the same completed field, M2 claims

Ksep⊆K~^⊆Ksep^.K^{\mathrm{sep}}\subseteq\widehat{\widetilde K}\subseteq\widehat{K^{\mathrm{sep}}}.Ksep⊆K⊆Ksep.

These are the specified embedded copies of the fields. The claim is about a completion; it does not say that every ramified cover was already an étale cover in the algebraic tower.

Global consequences retain an arithmetic condition

For a proper genus-at-least-two curve C/FC/FC/F over a number field, a global section now determines local points at finite places and connected components at real places. M2 identifies these modified adelic tuples with the finite-cover descent locus: tuples that survive every finite torsor test after an appropriate global twist.

If that locus equals the diagonal rational points,

C(AF)∙f-cov=C(F),C(\mathbb A_F)_{\bullet}^{\mathrm{f\text{-}cov}}=C(F),C(AF​)∙f-cov​=C(F),

M2 claims the global section conjecture for CCC. The equality is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of local point-theoreticity alone.

The stated sufficient cases include a nonconstant map to an abelian variety A/FA/FA/F with A(F)A(F)A(F) finite and no nonzero divisible subgroup in its Tate–Shafarevich group, or the analogous condition on the curve’s Jacobian. The Tate–Shafarevich group records torsors locally solvable everywhere; its divisible subgroup consists of elements divisible by every positive integer.

M2 also claims the conclusion for the smooth projective modular curves X0(N)X_0(N)X0​(N) and X1(N)X_1(N)X1​(N) over Q\mathbb QQ whenever their genus is at least two. These parametrize elliptic curves with a cyclic subgroup or a marked point of order NNN, with cusps added in their compactification. A further elliptic-target criterion uses the corank-zero Selmer converse from family 002. The modular-curve consequence is stated separately and does not depend on that Selmer specialization.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Taken as stated, the local theorem resolves a central problem in anabelian geometry: recovering arithmetic geometry from fundamental groups. It turns every abstract continuous splitting in the specified sequence into a unique ppp-adic point.

The completion theorem addresses the precise gap between étale and birational information. The global consequences then connect this local reconstruction with a different arithmetic problem, finite descent. M1 contributes a flexible geometric construction with simultaneous control over an entire exterior and every deleted disk.

The rating reflects this foundational local classification and its global applications. It does not imply that the unrestricted number-field section conjecture follows without further input.

6. The main idea

Make cycles inside the disks without disturbing the exterior

M1 first uses resolution covers to obtain positive-genus components above chosen positions inside each disk. An auxiliary prime ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p supplies residue-component torsors. Along suitable skeletal paths, edges multiply faster than endpoint vertices, forcing a cycle above every disk.

A cyclic graph cover of degree ppp can then change sheets around one of these cycles while remaining split above the whole exterior. Analytic covering theory and proper algebraization turn this into a finite étale algebraic cover. Taking all conjugate characters makes the construction compatible with the Galois action.

Finally, quotient by the stabilizer of a chosen exterior component. Its quotient sheet has degree one over UUU. Disk stabilizers retain a nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup, so every disk-component degree remains divisible by ppp. This explains why the two desired properties can coexist in one connected cover.

Replace branched disks by trivial pieces

M2’s completion argument uses analytic patching in two stages. Near a branch point a finite cover has a local form involving t=zet=z^et=ze. If another cover supplies a sufficiently divisible root of ttt on a surrounding annulus, the pulled-back cover splits there. The part over the inner disk can then be replaced by a trivial cover and glued to the exterior.

The roots must exist on every inverse-image sheet of the annulus. One favorable sheet would not trivialize the full covering algebra needed for this replacement.

First, stable reduction and an odd prime ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p supply prime-to-ppp collar roots, after moving suitable collars into stable skeleta. Second, an auxiliary curve with parallel skeletal edges gives a Jacobian torus character of slope one. Pullback by multiplication by an arbitrary integer mmm on the Jacobian supplies an mmm-th root of that character. On a sufficiently long collar, logarithms and exponentials handle the remaining analytic unit.

The auxiliary covers in the second stage retain horizontal ramification indices covered by the first stage. Repeating the replacement therefore places arbitrary finite separable extensions into the same completion. Horizontal ramification here is at closed points over kˉ\bar kkˉ, whose residue characteristic is zero; it is distinct from wild behavior in characteristic-ppp reduction models.

Convert localization into a rational point

The completion inclusion identifies the relevant absolute and étale decomposition groups. A section localized at a rank-one valuation can consequently be lifted birationally. Koenigsmann’s theorem places that lift at a rational point, producing incompatible henselian valuations unless the localization has the required point-type form.

After excluding the other valuative cases, surjectivity onto GkG_kGk​ forces the remaining closed point to have residue field exactly kkk. A Kummer-theoretic argument on the Jacobian proves uniqueness. The global step then uses finite descent and Stix’s finite-support theorem, rather than assuming that matching local points automatically gives a global point.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The local theorem concerns proper smooth curves of genus at least two over finite extensions of Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​, using the full profinite groups. Open curves have cuspidal phenomena and are not covered by this statement. Geometrically abelian or other smaller quotients are different problems.

The global conclusion remains conditional on the stated finite-cover equality except in the cases where the manuscript invokes an established criterion. Local point existence at every place alone does not supply that equality.

M1 and M2 have distinct geometric statements. M1’s prescribed exterior-sheet theorem should not be substituted for M2’s all-sheet collar-root construction; the latter is the route explicitly used in the current section manuscript. Neither theorem supplies an effective algorithm to list all sections or rational points from a finite group presentation.

8. Sources and further reading

M1, Theorem 1.1, specifies the disk radii, exterior and simultaneous cover properties. M2, Theorems 1.1–1.2, states the section and completion claims. Its Theorem 8.2 and Corollaries 8.3–8.5 give the finite-descent, abelian-target and modular-curve consequences.

The Pop–Stix and Stoll papers linked in section 3 explain the valuative and descent inputs. M2’s references include the corrections to Stoll’s covering arguments and the current Selmer-converse source. Optional background on the étale fundamental group and Berkovich spaces can supplement the definitions here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Étale covers with a prescribed exterior sheet (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The p-adic section conjecture (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Squarefree quartic values and the large-prime obstacle
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 020 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An integer is squarefree if no prime square divides it. The numbers 666 and 101010 are squarefree; 121212 is not, because 4∣124\mid124∣12. Among all positive integers, squarefree numbers have a familiar positive density. But what happens in a sparse polynomial sequence such as

14+2, 24+2, 34+2,…?1^4+2,\ 2^4+2,\ 3^4+2,\ldots?14+2, 24+2, 34+2,…?

There is no obvious reason a positive fraction of these values should avoid every prime square at once. Testing divisibility by a fixed finite list of primes is straightforward. The difficulty is excluding square factors from very large primes, whose squares can divide a polynomial value even when the input is much smaller than the prime.

Family 020 claims the expected squarefree density for every irreducible quartic with no local obstruction. More generally, it fills the low-degree gaps for values free of (d−2)(d-2)(d−2)-th prime powers. Combined with an established higher-degree theorem, this yields that density for every degree d≥4d\ge4d≥4.

2. Background and essential definitions

For an integer k≥2k\ge2k≥2, a nonzero integer is kkk-power-free if no prime power pkp^kpk divides it. Negative values are treated through divisibility in exactly the same way. Zero is excluded because every prime power divides zero. The case k=2k=2k=2 is squarefreeness.

For a polynomial f∈Z[x]f\in\mathbb Z[x]f∈Z[x], define

ρf(q)=#{a mod q:f(a)≡0(modq)}.\rho_f(q)=\#\{a\bmod q:f(a)\equiv0\pmod q\}.ρf​(q)=#{amodq:f(a)≡0(modq)}.

This counts the residue classes that fail the divisibility test modulo qqq. A necessary condition for kkk-power-free values is

ρf(pk)<pkfor every prime p.\rho_f(p^k)<p^k\qquad\text{for every prime }p.ρf​(pk)<pkfor every prime p.

If equality holds for one prime, every input gives a value divisible by that same pkp^kpk. Such a prime power is a fixed divisor obstruction.

When no obstruction occurs, the predicted density is

cf,k=∏p(1−ρf(pk)pk).c_{f,k}=\prod_p\left(1-\frac{\rho_f(p^k)}{p^k}\right).cf,k​=p∏​(1−pkρf​(pk)​).

For any finite set of primes, the Chinese remainder theorem makes this product exact: residue conditions at different prime powers combine independently. The hard step is justifying the passage to infinitely many primes while the input bound grows.

An irreducible polynomial over Q\mathbb QQ cannot be factored there into two positive-degree polynomials. In characteristic zero it has distinct complex roots. This separability ensures that, outside finitely many exceptional primes, roots modulo ppp lift uniquely to roots modulo pkp^kpk, and ρf(pk)≤deg⁡f\rho_f(p^k)\le\deg fρf​(pk)≤degf. Thus the infinite product converges to a positive number once every local factor is positive.

Write

Sf,k(X)=#{1≤n≤X:f(n) is k-power-free}.S_{f,k}(X)=\#\{1\le n\le X:f(n)\text{ is }k\text{-power-free}\}.Sf,k​(X)=#{1≤n≤X:f(n) is k-power-free}.

An asymptotic Sf,k(X)=cf,kX+o(X)S_{f,k}(X)=c_{f,k}X+o(X)Sf,k​(X)=cf,k​X+o(X) says that the proportion approaches cf,kc_{f,k}cf,k​. The notation o(X)o(X)o(X) means an error whose ratio to XXX tends to zero. It does not, by itself, promise a particular rate.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical work of Ricci obtained power-free asymptotics when the excluded power was at least the polynomial degree. Erdős proved infinitude in the k=d−1k=d-1k=d−1 range, and Hooley obtained its asymptotic form. The cubic squarefree case belongs to that range. Erdős explicitly highlighted n4+2n^4+2n4+2 as an unresolved quartic example in 1953 and returned to the degree-minus-two obstacle in his later survey, both cited by the manuscript.

Nair and Huxley–Nair extended the accessible range. Heath-Brown’s determinant method reached k≥(3d+2)/4k\ge(3d+2)/4k≥(3d+2)/4. Browning improved this to

k≥3d+14,k\ge\frac{3d+1}{4},k≥43d+1​,

which already includes k=d−2k=d-2k=d−2 for d≥9d\ge9d≥9. See Browning’s 2011 paper. This is why the new manuscript concentrates on degrees four through eight rather than claiming that every degree requires a new argument.

Special polynomial shapes can admit stronger results. Heath-Brown obtained power-saving asymptotics for irreducible binomials xd+cx^d+cxd+c in a better range, and Reuss obtained power-saving results at exponent d−1d-1d−1 for general fixed polynomials. The determinant and number-field techniques developed in these works are direct methodological predecessors.

There are also results with different quantifiers. Squarefree binary forms vary two integer inputs, while the present problem fixes one input to one. Averaging over many coefficient choices is different from proving a theorem for each fixed polynomial. Neither automatically resolves an individual quartic sequence.

Granville showed that the abc conjecture would give the predicted squarefree-value density for general separable polynomials satisfying the local condition. His primary paper explains that conditional landscape. The present manuscript states an unconditional result in its degree and power range, without using abc.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The new low-degree theorem

Theorem 1.1 concerns an integer polynomial irreducible over Q\mathbb QQ, of degree 4≤d≤84\le d\le84≤d≤8, with k=d−2k=d-2k=d−2. Assuming no fixed prime kkk-th power divisor, it claims

Sf,k(X)=cf,kX+of(X),cf,k>0.S_{f,k}(X)=c_{f,k}X+o_f(X),\qquad c_{f,k}>0.Sf,k​(X)=cf,k​X+of​(X),cf,k​>0.

The powers are as follows:

Degree dddExcluded prime power
4p2p^2p2: squarefree values
5p3p^3p3: cube-free values
6p4p^4p4
7p5p^5p5
8p6p^6p6

Inputs are positive integers. The polynomial is fixed, with no bound imposed on its coefficient sizes. It need not be primitive, meaning its coefficients may have a common factor, and its leading coefficient may be negative. The exact local factors retain this content and sign generality.

Combining this theorem with Browning’s higher-degree result gives Corollary 1.2: the same (d−2)(d-2)(d−2)-power-free density for every irreducible degree d≥4d\ge4d≥4 satisfying the corresponding local condition.

Products and simultaneous values

For fixed k≥2k\ge2k≥2, Corollary 1.3 treats a separable polynomial whose nonconstant irreducible factors each have degree at most k+2k+2k+2. Here separable means no repeated nonconstant factor. Under the joint local admissibility condition, its whole value is kkk-power-free with the predicted density.

The corollary also treats finitely many fixed polynomials F1,…,FrF_1,\ldots,F_rF1​,…,Fr​ of this kind, requiring each value separately to be kkk-power-free. Let

Ωp={a mod pk:pk∣Fi(a) for at least one i}.\Omega_p=\{a\bmod p^k:p^k\mid F_i(a)\text{ for at least one }i\}.Ωp​={amodpk:pk∣Fi​(a) for at least one i}.

If ∣Ωp∣<pk|\Omega_p|<p^k∣Ωp​∣<pk for all primes, the density is

∏p(1−∣Ωp∣pk)>0.\prod_p\left(1-\frac{|\Omega_p|}{p^k}\right)>0.p∏​(1−pk∣Ωp​∣​)>0.

Different polynomials may share factors. Requiring each value separately to be power-free is different from requiring their product to be power-free. A shared prime can appear once in each of two squarefree values and twice in their product. The local union Ωp\Omega_pΩp​ correctly captures the separate-value question.

Two concrete quartics

The theorem includes x4+2x^4+2x4+2, irreducible by Eisenstein’s criterion at two, and the cyclotomic polynomial x4+1x^4+1x4+1. Both satisfy the local obstruction condition.

For x4+1x^4+1x4+1, the manuscript works out the exact density:

c8=∏p≡1(mod8)(1−4p2)>34.c_8=\prod_{p\equiv1\pmod8}\left(1-\frac4{p^2}\right)>\frac34.c8​=p≡1(mod8)∏​(1−p24​)>43​.

There are no roots modulo four. For odd ppp, a root modulo ppp has multiplicative order eight, so roots exist precisely when p≡1(mod8)p\equiv1\pmod8p≡1(mod8), with four simple roots then lifting modulo p2p^2p2. Corollary 12.1 consequently claims that, for all sufficiently large real NNN, at least N/2N/2N/2 integers in [N,2N][N,2N][N,2N] give squarefree values of n4+1n^4+1n4+1.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, the quartic theorem resolves a classical barrier in polynomial squarefreeness, including Erdős’s example n4+2n^4+2n4+2. The family also completes the degree-minus-two range by connecting the new low-degree argument to established higher-degree work.

The result gives the full predicted positive density, stronger than merely proving infinitely many examples. Its hypotheses match the unavoidable local obstruction for the stated class of polynomials.

Methodologically, the manuscript combines number-field factorization with determinant estimates that adapt their auxiliary primes as the geometry changes. Its special quartic analysis explains why the first unresolved degree needs more than a routine substitution into general estimates.

6. The main idea

Separate small primes from large primes

Fix a cutoff YYY. Divisibility by primes p≤Yp\le Yp≤Y is handled exactly by residue classes and the Chinese remainder theorem. Medium primes can be bounded using root counts and lifting. The hard tail is

#{X<n≤2X:pk∣f(n) for some prime p>X}.\#\{X<n\le2X:p^k\mid f(n)\text{ for some prime }p>X\}.#{X<n≤2X:pk∣f(n) for some prime p>X}.

For primitive irreducible polynomials with positive leading coefficient in degrees four through eight, Proposition 1.4 claims that this is Of(X1−δ)O_f(X^{1-\delta})Of​(X1−δ) for some δ>0\delta>0δ>0. It does not require the local admissibility condition.

This power saving is an intermediate large-prime estimate. The final density proof first lets XXX grow with YYY fixed, then lets YYY grow. The manuscript does not promote that procedure to a power-saving error for the complete asymptotic.

Factor the equation inside a number field

If pk∣f(n)p^k\mid f(n)pk∣f(n), write f(n)=ypkf(n)=yp^kf(n)=ypk. The triples lie on the surface

f(x)=yzk.f(x)=yz^k.f(x)=yzk.

For some prime-size ranges, a weighted determinant estimate on this surface suffices. In the harder range, choose a root θ\thetaθ of fff and work in K=Q(θ)K=\mathbb Q(\theta)K=Q(θ). Ideal factorization and units lead to relations of the form

αkβ=μ(n−θ),\alpha^k\beta=\mu(n-\theta),αkβ=μ(n−θ),

with integral field elements α,β\alpha,\betaα,β and a fixed denominator-clearing integer μ\muμ. Units balance their sizes at the different embeddings. Coordinates in an integral basis then place α\alphaα and β\betaβ in paired boxes.

Their directions are not independent: near a balanced point, either direction determines the other analytically once 1/n1/n1/n is specified. This is the extra arithmetic structure missing from the original surface equation.

Force the points onto smaller algebraic sets

The determinant method arranges monomial values at integer points into a matrix. Integrality or divisibility gives a lower bound for a nonzero determinant; sufficiently strong analytic bounds force it to vanish. Vanishing produces an auxiliary polynomial containing the points.

The manuscript repeatedly cuts the dimension in paired boxes. It distinguishes equations involving both coordinate groups from those involving only one group, because the available Taylor monomials differ. Reduced lattice bases shrink the coordinates, while unusually short vectors restrict how many boxes can contain them.

The auxiliary varieties depend on earlier cuts, so a fixed list of good primes cannot simply be assumed. The adaptive-prime counting argument controls primes where smooth coordinates fail as the construction proceeds.

Quartics require sharper surface and curve geometry. Exceptional projections and low-degree maps are treated separately. One limiting case involves degree-five polynomials with prescribed critical values; their relevant integer values form a single small exceptional set removed before summing over boxes. This avoids repeatedly charging the same exceptional inputs.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The general degree-ddd conclusion excludes pd−2p^{d-2}pd−2. It does not prove squarefree values for every degree. For example, the degree-five theorem is cube-free, not squarefree. The unrestricted squarefree-value conjecture for higher-degree irreducible polynomials remains beyond this statement.

The polynomials, their number in a simultaneous family, and the exponent kkk are fixed. No uniform coefficient bound or uniform error term is asserted. The final asymptotic has an o(X)o(X)o(X) error, even though a particular large-prime tail has a power saving.

The local condition is indispensable. It must be checked for the whole polynomial or the simultaneous family, rather than inferred from separate factors without accounting for shared residue obstructions. Repeated factors are excluded from the separable-product corollary.

Further questions include effective rates in the full asymptotic, squarefree values in higher degrees, uniformity over coefficient families and values at prime rather than unrestricted integer inputs.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 states the new degree-four-through-eight result; Corollaries 1.2–1.3 give the higher-degree and simultaneous consequences. Proposition 1.4 isolates the large-prime estimate. Section 12 supplies the worked n4+1n^4+1n4+1 example and its Euler product.

Browning’s and Granville’s papers linked in section 3 explain the established higher-degree range and the abc-based general prediction. The manuscript’s bibliography identifies the earlier Erdős, Hooley, Nair, Heath-Brown and Reuss contributions. Optional background on squarefree integers and the Chinese remainder theorem helps interpret the local factors.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Squarefree values of quartics and power-free values of polynomials (2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Rational approximation with any fixed shift
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 022 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Suppose we try to approximate a real number xxx by fractions, but move each numerator by the same fixed real shift γ\gammaγ. For denominator qqq, the available centers are

a+γq,a∈Z.\frac{a+\gamma}{q},\qquad a\in\mathbb Z.qa+γ​,a∈Z.

We may choose a different error tolerance for every denominator. Some denominators can receive a generous tolerance, others a tiny one, and most can be ignored altogether. Under what condition does almost every real number lie near infinitely many of these shifted fractions?

Family 022 claims the weak inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture for every prescribed real shift. Its divergence condition uses Euler’s totient function to account for arithmetic redundancy among denominators. It requires no monotonicity or regular spacing of the tolerances.

The qualification “weak” matters: the integer aaa is unrestricted. The theorem does not require aaa and qqq to be coprime.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a real number ttt, let

∥t∥=min⁡a∈Z∣t−a∣.\|t\|=\min_{a\in\mathbb Z}|t-a|.∥t∥=a∈Zmin​∣t−a∣.

Then ∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q)\|qx-\gamma\|<\psi(q)∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q) means that some integer aaa satisfies

∣x−a+γq∣<ψ(q)q.\left|x-\frac{a+\gamma}{q}\right|<\frac{\psi(q)}q.​x−qa+γ​​<qψ(q)​.

The nonnegative function ψ:N→[0,∞)\psi:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)ψ:N→[0,∞) supplies the tolerances. Finite-valued means each ψ(q)\psi(q)ψ(q) is finite; the function need not be bounded globally. A zero value simply makes that denominator unavailable.

Euler’s totient φ(q)\varphi(q)φ(q) counts integers between one and qqq that are coprime to qqq. Its ratio

φ(q)q=∏p∣q(1−1p)\frac{\varphi(q)}q=\prod_{p\mid q}\left(1-\frac1p\right)qφ(q)​=p∣q∏​(1−p1​)

measures the proportion of reduced residue classes. For q=12q=12q=12, these are 1,5,7,111,5,7,111,5,7,11, so the ratio is 1/31/31/3. Denominators divisible by many different small primes have a smaller ratio.

For each qqq, the approximation event is a periodic union of intervals centered at (a+γ)/q(a+\gamma)/q(a+γ)/q, each of radius ψ(q)/q\psi(q)/qψ(q)/q. When ψ(q)≤1/2\psi(q)\le1/2ψ(q)≤1/2, its total length in one period is 2ψ(q)2\psi(q)2ψ(q). However, events for different denominators can overlap strongly. Summing their lengths does not by itself prove that infinitely many occur.

Lebesgue-almost every means all real numbers except a set of Lebesgue measure zero. It is a statement about length, not every individual real number. The exceptional set is allowed to depend on both γ\gammaγ and ψ\psiψ.

The relevant infinite-occurrence set is

Wγ(ψ)={x:∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q) for infinitely many q}.W_\gamma(\psi)=\{x:\|qx-\gamma\|<\psi(q)\text{ for infinitely many }q\}.Wγ​(ψ)={x:∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q) for infinitely many q}.

It is a limsup set: a point belongs if it survives in approximation events arbitrarily far along the denominator sequence.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Khintchine’s theorem gives a clean answer in the homogeneous case γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 when ψ\psiψ is non-increasing: divergence of ∑qψ(q)\sum_q\psi(q)∑q​ψ(q) gives full measure. Szüsz extended the monotone theory to fixed inhomogeneous shifts. Removing monotonicity makes overlapping denominators a serious obstacle.

Duffin and Schaeffer exhibited the failure of a naive unweighted criterion in the homogeneous setting and proposed a theorem for reduced fractions, weighted by φ(q)/q\varphi(q)/qφ(q)/q. Koukoulopoulos and Maynard proved that conjecture in their 2020 Annals paper, cited by the manuscript. It is a major antecedent, but does not automatically settle arbitrary shifted centers.

Inhomogeneous overlap is difficult even when numerators are unrestricted. Ramírez constructed nonmonotone counterexamples to unweighted divergence for prescribed countable collections of shifts. These have finite totient-weighted sum, so they do not contradict the statement considered here. His primary paper explains the distinction.

Yu obtained results with additional divergence or size assumptions and restrictions on the shift. Chow and Technau proved the weak conjecture for certain structured approximation functions arising in multiplicative approximation. Beresnevich, Hauke and Velani proved the weak statement for every rational shift and obtained further irrational-shift results under additional conditions. Their 2024 paper is the immediate predecessor for the arbitrary-shift question.

There is also a crucial warning about the stronger numerator condition. The manuscript cites September 2026 counterexamples by Hauke-Treuer–Maynard–Pollington and independently He–Liao to the ordinary coprime-numerator formulation for broad classes of shifts. Thus “weak” is not a cosmetic adjective.

For a rational shift γ=A/B\gamma=A/Bγ=A/B, the earlier positive theorem can impose the adapted condition gcd⁡(A+aB,q)=1\gcd(A+aB,q)=1gcd(A+aB,q)=1. This is different from gcd⁡(a,q)=1\gcd(a,q)=1gcd(a,q)=1. Family 022’s stated advance is to allow a completely arbitrary fixed irrational shift together with an arbitrary sparse, nonmonotone tolerance function, while leaving numerators unrestricted.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript. Theorem 1.1 states that, for every fixed γ∈R\gamma\in\mathbb Rγ∈R and finite-valued ψ\psiψ,

∑q=1∞φ(q)qψ(q)=∞\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(q)}q\psi(q)=\inftyq=1∑∞​qφ(q)​ψ(q)=∞

implies

∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q)for infinitely many q\|qx-\gamma\|<\psi(q)\quad\text{for infinitely many }q∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q)for infinitely many q

for Lebesgue-almost every x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R.

There is no Diophantine restriction on γ\gammaγ. It may be rational, badly approximable, or extremely well approximated by rationals. No monotonicity is required of ψ\psiψ, even on its support. The conclusion is a divergence implication, not an asymptotic count of solutions.

The quantifiers are worth keeping explicit: first fix γ\gammaγ and ψ\psiψ; then almost every xxx works. The theorem does not give one universal exceptional null set valid simultaneously for all real shifts and all tolerance functions.

A Hausdorff-measure consequence

Corollary 1.2 extends the divergence statement to a finer measure of size. A gauge f(r)f(r)f(r) assigns a cost to a covering interval of small diameter rrr; Hausdorff fff-measure is obtained by minimizing total cost over increasingly fine covers. The familiar Hausdorff dimension uses gauges f(r)=rsf(r)=r^sf(r)=rs.

Assume fff is continuous, positive and nondecreasing on positive arguments, tends to zero as r↓0r\downarrow0r↓0, and has monotone ratio f(r)/rf(r)/rf(r)/r. If

∑q=1∞φ(q)f ⁣(ψ(q)q)=∞,\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\varphi(q) f\!\left(\frac{\psi(q)}q\right)=\infty,q=1∑∞​φ(q)f(qψ(q)​)=∞,

then for every bounded interval III,

Hf(I∩Wγ(ψ))=Hf(I).\mathcal H^f(I\cap W_\gamma(\psi))=\mathcal H^f(I).Hf(I∩Wγ​(ψ))=Hf(I).

The corollary uses the mass transference principle of Beresnevich and Velani. It retains the fixed shift and unrestricted numerators, and asserts no convergence converse.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, this settles a major general form of metric approximation with an additive shift. Both sources of irregularity remain unrestricted: the shift can have any rational-approximation behavior, and the denominator support can be arbitrarily sparse.

The conclusion shows that the totient-weighted divergence condition is robust enough to overcome the resulting overlaps for unrestricted numerators. The Hausdorff consequence connects the theorem to fractal-size questions as well as ordinary length.

The mathematical significance lies in the uniformity of the hypotheses, not in a pointwise claim for every real number. This is a broad theorem about almost-everywhere approximation, with arithmetic correlations replacing the independence that elementary probability would prefer.

6. The main idea

Keep enough mass while controlling overlap

For independent events, divergent total probability often implies infinitely many occurrences. These approximation events are far from independent. A standard replacement is a second-moment estimate: if a nonnegative counting function has substantial average and its squared average is controlled, it cannot concentrate all its mass on an arbitrarily tiny set.

The paper works with arbitrarily late finite blocks of denominators whose totient-weighted mass lies in a fixed small range. Within each block it constructs a weighted sum of interval indicators, supported inside the original approximation events. It aims to retain enough first-moment mass while bounding the second moment.

A comparison sum follows the same prime-step updates but omits certain additional deletions. This sum is equidistributed on fixed spatial intervals. Small loss of mass and control of the retained second moment then rule out a positive-measure set avoiding every sufficiently late block. The argument approximates such an avoided set by one fixed finite union of intervals, rather than assuming an unproved zero-one principle for the shifted problem.

Close shifted fractions reveal denominator structure

Two centers can be close only when an integer combination of their numerators and shifted denominators is small. At very small scales there is too little room for direct averaging.

An inverse estimate shows that large weighted overlap forces the prime-exponent patterns of the denominators to cluster around a common integer. This builds on the common-pivot ideas from homogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer proofs, but the shifted phases require additional analysis.

Varying permitted factors then gives either a rotation estimate controlling the overlap or a precise rational model for the phase offsets. Exact coincidences in those models are handled by explicit numerator restrictions. Those restrictions are tools used on selected weighted subevents; the final theorem still permits all numerators.

Expose primes without pretending the tests are independent

Large common primes can create repeated correlations when previously separate collections of rows begin to interact. The manuscript assigns each denominator an integer multiple and exposes its prime factors in stages. Before all factors are exposed, a row is represented on a finer projected grid containing its eventual true centers.

At a prime step, nearby grid entries are grouped. Some weights survive only when a numerator passes a divisibility test; linked portions of other weights are suppressed to offset the strongest correlated contributions. The rules preserve the required first-moment normalization.

The construction also remembers earlier alignments when intermediate labels disappear. At the first meeting of two previously separate collections, a backward comparison accounts for covariance through entries that passed their tests. A squared-mass bound limits the total contributions assigned to them.

This history-sensitive accounting is the paper’s response to dependencies across many scales. It averages common residue translations, while keeping γ\gammaγ fixed throughout; it does not assume independent outcomes or randomize the shift. Once the finite-block estimates are established, the almost-everywhere conclusion follows, and mass transference yields the Hausdorff version.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem does not impose ordinary numerator coprimality. Adding gcd⁡(a,q)=1\gcd(a,q)=1gcd(a,q)=1 changes the statement and, according to the cited counterexamples, can make it false.

Convergence of the totient-weighted sum is not claimed to force a null approximation set. A simple sufficient null-set criterion comes instead from convergence of the unweighted sum ∑qψ(q)\sum_q\psi(q)∑q​ψ(q), by the first Borel–Cantelli lemma and interval-length bounds. The gap between these conditions should not be erased by calling the new result a complete convergence-divergence law.

The result gives no rate or asymptotic formula for the number of successful denominators. It also does not treat an arbitrary changing sequence of shifts γq\gamma_qγq​, nor recover the approximation behavior of a specified exceptional real number.

Further questions include quantitative counting, finer dependence on the tolerance support, and meaningful numerator restrictions adapted to particular shifts.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 gives the Lebesgue-measure statement; Corollary 1.2 and Section 11 give the Hausdorff consequence. The introduction carefully distinguishes unrestricted, reduced and shift-adapted numerators. Sections 5–10 develop the weighted finite-block construction and overlap estimates.

The Ramírez and Beresnevich–Hauke–Velani papers linked in section 3 explain the earlier obstruction and rational-shift theorem. The cited counterexample preprints explain why the stronger coprime formulation must remain separate. Optional background on the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture and Hausdorff measure provides additional context.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Weak Inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer Conjecture (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Jacobsthal’s function: how long can primes cover an interval?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 021 · Number theory
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Choose a positive integer nnn and scan consecutive integers until one is coprime to it. How long might the wait be? For n=6n=6n=6, the integers coprime to nnn are those avoiding divisibility by two and three. Larger moduli can create longer stretches in which every integer shares a prime factor with nnn.

The size of nnn is not the most natural parameter. Replacing nnn by the product of its distinct prime divisors leaves coprimality unchanged. The real resource is the number kkk of available primes: how long an interval can they cover by their divisibility classes?

Family 021 claims a uniform bound of order

k2(log⁡log⁡(3k))2.\frac{k^2}{(\log\log(3k))^2}.(loglog(3k))2k2​.

It answers Jacobsthal’s quadratic-bound question and includes a further slowly growing saving. The primes may be arbitrarily large, and the interval may start anywhere.

2. Background and essential definitions

Jacobsthal’s function j(n)j(n)j(n) is the least positive integer mmm such that every interval of mmm consecutive integers contains an integer coprime to nnn. Let ω(n)\omega(n)ω(n) count distinct prime divisors, with ω(1)=0\omega(1)=0ω(1)=0, and define

h(k)=sup⁡n≥1ω(n)≤kj(n).h(k)=\sup_{\substack{n\ge1\\\omega(n)\le k}}j(n).h(k)=n≥1ω(n)≤k​sup​j(n).

Thus h(k)−1h(k)-1h(k)−1 is the longest possible interval covered by divisibility by at most kkk primes. Prime powers do not add covering power: divisibility by ppp already detects every failure of coprimality caused by pap^apa.

For example, j(6)=4j(6)=4j(6)=4. The interval 2,3,42,3,42,3,4 contains no integer coprime to six, while every four consecutive integers include an integer congruent to one or five modulo six. This small example illustrates that the question concerns the worst translated interval, not just the interval starting at one.

A useful equivalent formulation assigns one forbidden residue class ap(modp)a_p\pmod pap​(modp) to each chosen prime. The Chinese remainder theorem supplies an integer bbb satisfying all these congruences. Then

m≢ap(modp) for every chosen p⟺gcd⁡ ⁣(m−b,∏p)=1.m\not\equiv a_p\pmod p\text{ for every chosen }p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gcd\!\left(m-b,\prod p\right)=1.m≡ap​(modp) for every chosen p⟺gcd(m−b,∏p)=1.
