Some bounded product fan-in; others assumed multilinearity or restricted the support of bottom linear forms. Bera and Chakrabarti’s depth-five result allowed growing matrix width but imposed a bottom-support restriction. Kumar and Saraf obtained strong homogeneous depth-four bounds in a different width–degree regime.

Unrestricted bottom linear forms at depth five were also studied over finite fields for other hard polynomials. Those results have different field assumptions and target families, so they do not directly give the balanced characteristic-zero IMM statement here.

Crucially, superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted-bottom constant-depth circuits over characteristic zero already existed. Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas’s constant-depth theorem implies such bounds for the target considered here. The new manuscript is not the first superpolynomial result in this setting.

Its stated contribution is the sharper nΩ(n)n^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}nΩ(n​) scale when width and degree both equal nnn. The shifted-partials work of Amireddy and coauthors provides a close methodological predecessor, but its cited width conditions and degree-dependent losses prevent directly substituting w=d=nw=d=nw=d=n.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For all sufficiently large nnn, every syntactically homogeneous ΣΠΣΠΣ\Sigma\Pi\Sigma\Pi\SigmaΣΠΣΠΣ circuit computing IMM⁡n,n\operatorname{IMM}_{n,n}IMMn,n​ over any characteristic-zero field is claimed to require at least

nn/400n^{\sqrt n/400}nn​/400

gates. The threshold for sufficiently large nnn is absolute and independent of the field.

The lower bound permits arbitrary support in bottom linear forms, arbitrary finite fan-in and fan-out, constants, repeated inputs, and shared gates. It concerns equality as formal polynomials, rather than agreement only on a finite collection of evaluations.

The manuscript also gives an upper construction, valid over every field, with at most

nn+4n^{\sqrt n+4}nn​+4

gates for n≥2n\ge2n≥2. It is homogeneous of depth four; inserting unary bottom sums places it in the stated depth-five model. Therefore the claimed gate complexity over characteristic-zero fields is

nΘ(n).n^{\Theta(\sqrt n)}.nΘ(n​).

The notation hides constant factors in the exponent. It does not mean the lower and upper leading constants match. Likewise, the all-field upper bound does not extend the lower bound to positive characteristic.

The paper first works over the complex numbers and then transfers the lower bound to all characteristic-zero fields. No field-specific advice or characteristic-dependent threshold is included in the final stated theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 2/5. This is a sharp-scale advance within a specialized arithmetic circuit model. Its significance lies in closing a quantitative gap for a canonical explicit polynomial, while removing bottom-support restrictions in the balanced width–degree regime.

The target is especially informative because it remains easy with unrestricted depth. A lower bound here measures the price of organizing a computation into a small number of homogeneous layers, rather than the intrinsic difficulty of evaluating the polynomial by every possible method.

The rating is relative to the broader collection. Existing constant-depth results already supplied superpolynomial lower bounds, and the new theorem retains homogeneity, depth, and characteristic restrictions. Matching the square-root scale is substantial within that setting, but its direct implications are narrower than a general arithmetic circuit separation.

The derivative–multiplication operator and path-moment analysis may also offer techniques for other lower bounds. Such applications remain possibilities unless separately proved; they are not included in the score as established consequences.

6. The main idea

Assign a rank to each polynomial

A common lower-bound strategy finds a measure that is small for every small circuit but large for the target polynomial. Here the measure is the rank of a linear operator built from differentiation and multiplication.

Partition the matrix layers into two groups, with variable sets VVV and UUU. Keep the part of a polynomial ggg having degree kkk in VVV and degree mmm in UUU, where k+m=nk+m=nk+m=n. Replace variables in VVV by partial derivatives and variables in UUU by multiplication operators.

Acting on a finite-dimensional space of homogeneous polynomials gives a linear map FgF_gFg​. Define R(g)=rank⁡FgR(g)=\operatorname{rank}F_gR(g)=rankFg​. Since differentiation in VVV commutes with multiplication in the disjoint variables UUU, products can be analyzed through compositions. Linearity also makes rank subadditive under sums.

Show shallow products pass through smaller spaces

For a product of homogeneous factors, each factor distributes its degree between VVV and UUU. The ideal proportional share need not be an integer. These small degree discrepancies force certain operator compositions through intermediate polynomial spaces with smaller dimensions.

If all factors have small degree, accumulating these losses controls the rank. If a factor has large degree, the manuscript expands one such factor into its bottom products of linear forms and pays an additional factor related to circuit size. This selective expansion avoids turning the entire circuit into a huge formula merely to analyze it.

The resulting upper estimate has the schematic form

R(g)≤2S2D exp⁡(Cn) n−n/100,R(g)\le 2S^2D\,\exp(C\sqrt n)\,n^{-\sqrt n/100},R(g)≤2S2Dexp(Cn​)n−n​/100,

where SSS is circuit size, DDD the source-space dimension, and CCC an absolute constant. The decisive feature is the negative power of nnn proportional to n\sqrt nn​.

Count matrix-product paths to obtain large rank

For IMM, the operator has a combinatorial structure coming from paths through the matrix layers. With a factorially normalized monomial basis, traces of Fg∗FgF_g^*F_gFg∗​Fg​ and its square become weighted counts of paths and quadruples of paths.

At each layer, a contributing quadruple has one of two pairing patterns. Switching patterns forces several vertex labels to agree, reducing the number of free choices. A balanced ordering of the two variable groups controls how weights accumulate along runs with a fixed pattern.

The paper uses the elementary positive-semidefinite rank estimate

rank⁡H≥(tr⁡H)2tr⁡(H2)\operatorname{rank}H\ge\frac{(\operatorname{tr}H)^2}{\operatorname{tr}(H^2)}rankH≥tr(H2)(trH)2​

for nonzero PSD HHH. Its path-count estimates give R(IMM⁡n,n)≥Dexp⁡(−C′n)R(\operatorname{IMM}_{n,n})\ge D\exp(-C'\sqrt n)R(IMMn,n​)≥Dexp(−C′n​). Comparing this with the circuit upper bound forces SSS to be at least ncnn^{c\sqrt n}ncn​.

The matching upper construction groups the matrix chain into blocks of length about n\sqrt nn​, expands each block, and then combines block entries. This explains why the same square-root scale arises from both directions, even though the constants differ.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Homogeneity is a real restriction. General circuits can mix degrees and use cancellation in ways excluded by the formal-degree rules. The theorem does not establish the same bound for arbitrary depth-five circuits without homogeneity.

The characteristic-zero hypothesis also matters to the lower-bound argument. Related finite-field results cited in the history concern different families or regimes; the all-field upper construction alone cannot bridge that gap.

The target has width equal to degree. Other width–degree relationships may have different best bounds, and a theorem in one regime should not be substituted into another without checking its losses and hypotheses.

Further questions include extending the sharp scale to broader circuit models, improving constants, and understanding which parts of the rank method survive in positive characteristic. The digest reports the manuscript’s quantitative comparisons without auditing its operator or moment estimates.

8. Sources and further reading

Nisan–Wigderson introduces the derivative-space viewpoint, Tavenas explains the depth-reduction scale, and Bera–Chakrabarti gives the earlier support-restricted depth-five result. Limaye–Srinivasan–Tavenas and Amireddy and coauthors locate the quantitative advance relative to existing unrestricted-bottom bounds. The source manuscript below states the balanced-regime theorem and matching upper construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Homogeneous depth-five lower bounds for iterated matrix multiplication (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: PCP for PPAD: preserving a search problem despite many failed constraints
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 136 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Some computational problems are guaranteed to have a solution for a simple mathematical reason, yet finding one can be difficult. Following a directed path from a known starting point illustrates the issue: another endpoint must exist, but the path may be exponentially long and only implicitly described.

The complexity class PPAD organizes search problems whose existence guarantees arise from this directed endpoint principle. It includes central equilibrium-computation problems. A major question asks whether PPAD difficulty survives when a proposed solution is allowed to violate a small but fixed fraction of its local conditions.

Allowing small numerical errors is already one relaxation. Allowing some conditions to fail completely is stronger: an adversary may concentrate failures at the most damaging places. A robust reduction must recover a valid answer even from such an imperfect assignment.

This manuscript claims a quasilinear-size PCP theorem for PPAD. It transforms an End-of-Line instance of length NNN into a system of approximate local constraints of total encoded size N(log⁡N)O(1)N(\log N)^{O(1)}N(logN)O(1). Any assignment satisfying sufficiently many constraints yields an endpoint of the original instance. Both the numerical tolerance and the permitted failure fraction are fixed positive constants.

2. Background and essential definitions

An End-of-Line instance gives Boolean circuits S,P:{0,1}n→{0,1}nS,P:\{0,1\}^n o\{0,1\}^nS,P:{0,1}n→{0,1}n, interpreted as proposed successor and predecessor functions. They describe an enormous graph without listing its vertices. The all-zero string is a designated source, with consistency promises ensuring that its first outgoing edge is legitimate.

The task is to find v≠0nv e0^nv=0n such that

P(S(v))≠vorS(P(v))≠v.P(S(v)) e v\quad ext{or}\quadS(P(v)) e v.P(S(v))=vorS(P(v))=v.

Such a vertex witnesses another endpoint or a failure of predecessor–successor consistency. The input length NNN includes the full circuit descriptions, not the number 2n2^n2n of potential vertices.

A generalized circuit assigns values in [0,1][0,1][0,1] to nodes. Gates impose local conditions such as copying, scaling, clipped addition, comparison, and Boolean operations. Cycles are allowed, unlike in an ordinary acyclic evaluation circuit. The problem is to find a globally consistent assignment approximately satisfying the gate relations.

For example, an addition gate with inputs xa,xbx_a,x_bxa​,xb​ and output xzx_zxz​ is ε\varepsilonε-satisfied if

∣xz−min⁡{xa+xb,1}∣≤ε.|x_z-\min\{x_a+x_b,1\}|\le\varepsilon.∣xz​−min{xa​+xb​,1}∣≤ε.

A comparison gate constrains its answer when its inputs are separated by more than the tolerance; near a tie it can leave the output unrestricted. Boolean gates similarly use explicitly specified low and high value regions.

The theorem allows at most a δ\deltaδ fraction of gates to fail. Every gate has equal weight, and even failed gates share the same single value for each circuit node. Failures do not permit assigning contradictory values to the same node at different occurrences.

“Quasilinear size” means linear input size times a fixed power of a logarithm. The complete encoding includes wiring indices, rational parameters, and auxiliary gates, rather than just a count of abstract components.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Papadimitriou introduced PPAD to classify total search problems based on directed parity arguments. The complexity of Nash equilibrium computation made the class especially influential. Chen, Deng, and Teng developed generalized circuits as an intermediary in two-player equilibrium reductions, while Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou used related arithmetic and logical gadgets in their equilibrium-complexity work.

Later results established hardness with constant numerical error while requiring every gate to satisfy its approximate relation. The PureCircuit framework gives strong constant-error results in this direction. But an assignment allowed to violate a positive fraction of gates could bypass important parts of a reduction, so ordinary constant-error hardness does not imply robust hardness.

Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein formulated the quasilinear PCP-for-PPAD conjecture in Can Almost Everybody Be Almost Happy?. Its two requirements are separate: tolerate a constant fraction of arbitrary gate failures, and keep the complete reduction nearly linear in size.

Rubinstein’s encoded-path and holographic-proof approach supplied important ingredients and conditional hardness for approximate two-player Nash equilibria, while leaving the required robust composition unresolved. More recent fine-grained equilibrium work uses PCP for PPAD together with an additional exponential-time hypothesis for PPAD.

The new manuscript claims the conjectured reduction itself. Consequences that also assume an exponential-time hypothesis retain that assumption; a PCP reduction alone does not establish every fine-grained running-time lower bound appearing in the surrounding literature.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

There are fixed rational constants 0<ε<1/100<\varepsilon<1/100<ε<1/10 and 0<δ<10<\delta<10<δ<1, fixed integers A,bA,bA,b, a fixed polynomial ppp, and deterministic construction and decoding algorithms with the following properties.

For an End-of-Line instance of binary length NNN, the construction outputs a generalized circuit of complete binary length MMM satisfying

M≤AN⌈log⁡2(N+2)⌉b.M\le A N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2) ight ceil^b.M≤AN⌈log2​(N+2)⌉b.

The construction takes polynomial time. Quasilinear output size is not a claim that the construction itself runs in quasilinear time.

From every rational assignment of total encoding length at most p(M)p(M)p(M) that ε\varepsilonε-satisfies at least a 1−δ1-\delta1−δ fraction of gates, the decoder returns an End-of-Line solution in polynomial time. Its guarantee is universal over which gates fail and how badly they fail, subject to node values remaining in [0,1][0,1][0,1].

The manuscript also establishes totality of the target finite search relation: acceptable rational assignments of the prescribed polynomial encoding length always exist. Its stated totality argument supplies an assignment satisfying every gate on a fixed rational mesh. Rationality makes the witness and decoder finite computational objects; the soundness argument is stated more broadly for real assignments meeting the failure budget.

All constants and algorithms are chosen once. The reduction is deterministic and uses no advice depending on input length. Neither tolerance shrinks as NNN grows.

The paper applies the robust circuit theorem to previously developed reductions for several equilibrium and allocation problems. Those applications retain their own approximation, payoff, and encoding conventions; they are not a universal hardness statement for every notion of approximate equilibrium.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The claim addresses a central conjecture connecting total search, robust local constraints, and equilibrium approximation. It would provide a broadly reusable source of PPAD hardness that survives concentrated local failures while preserving nearly linear instance size.

Robustness changes the qualitative interpretation of approximation. Requiring every participant or constraint to be approximately satisfied differs from allowing a small fraction to behave arbitrarily. A reduction that survives the latter must distribute its essential information so that a few failures cannot destroy it.

The size bound matters independently. A large polynomial blowup may preserve qualitative hardness but weaken quantitative consequences. Quasilinear complete encoding preserves far more of the source problem’s scale, supporting applications that need accurate size accounting.

The rating reflects the conjecture’s centrality and the range of established reduction frameworks it can feed. It does not turn PPAD-hardness into an unconditional assertion that no efficient algorithm exists, and it does not remove additional assumptions from conditional fine-grained consequences.

6. The main idea

Encode paths as a geometric fixed-point problem

The manuscript first replaces End-of-Line by a locally evolving graph with the same useful endpoints. Vertices are represented by separated encoded words. Each directed edge becomes a geometric path between the corresponding encodings, with extra coordinate blocks controlling the motion.

A bounded displacement field points along a path and inward toward it. Away from the desired endpoints, a clipped step retains a definite displacement. Therefore an accurate enough approximate fixed point must lie near an endpoint from which the original answer can be decoded.

This geometric idea has precedents. The new task is to compute its local information robustly while keeping all stored representations and wiring quasilinear.

Keep a large representation locally updateable

The outer representation has nearly linearly many symbols, each of polylogarithmic bit length. Error-correcting structure separates distinct valid words and supports local tests, local correction, and global decoding.

A single logical tape edit can change many encoded values. The construction stores certificates for the computations producing those values and prepares their finite differences before an edit. Differences of newly introduced certificates have lower assigned polynomial degree, so this recursive preparation has bounded depth.

Long linear computations are performed in small frequency groups with reusable scratch storage. Their time lengthens the represented path rather than the amount of information stored at each represented vertex. This separation is part of the quasilinear size accounting.

Compose through one fixed small input encoding

Applying a large polynomial-size robust construction directly to an NNN-bit object would lose the desired size. Instead, an inner construction operates on the polylogarithmic-size outer symbols.

The inner encoding and its positive correction radius are fixed before the number of inputs inspected by a later local function is chosen. It supports increasingly accurate correction in an average sense without requiring a new encoding for each use. Polynomial costs in the symbol length remain polylogarithmic in NNN.

The distinction between average correction and perfect correction of every coordinate is important. The geometric estimator prepares a bounded list of candidate pieces and estimates their statistics before selecting one. That order allows the stated average guarantees to support the later choice without silently assuming stronger pointwise accuracy.

Make arbitrary gate failures expensive to exploit

The generalized circuit contains many replicas of each geometric coordinate. A sparse expander averaging operation couples them, forcing most replicas close to their mean even before assuming that their local decisions are correct.

The analysis then charges inaccurate reads, ambiguous comparisons, and failed gates to controlled error budgets. Every physical read is routed with bounded load. Expensive decision gadgets are shared carefully and have many designated outputs, so an adversary cannot corrupt an entire group merely by breaking one cheaply placed extraction wire.

On reliable outputs, the update follows the intended displacement field. On unreliable outputs, boundedness still limits the damage. A mean-displacement argument keeps clipping inside the estimate and forces the average state near a valid endpoint. Global decoding then extracts the End-of-Line answer.

The printed circuit is deterministic. Random tapes used to analyze local choices are replaced by explicitly enumerated finite lists. Counting those lists, all hypothetical branches, and their wiring is part of the theorem’s complete-output bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The numerical gate conventions are fixed. Boolean implications can behave nonmonotonically as the tolerance changes, so a gate satisfied at one tolerance cannot simply be reclassified at another without checking its conditions. The manuscript uses one actual tolerance with explicit margins.

The theorem guarantees a robust reduction and a polynomial-time decoder from an acceptable assignment. It does not supply an efficient algorithm to find that assignment. Totality ensures existence, not easy search.

The fixed constants may be small and the polylogarithmic powers large. The claim is an asymptotic complexity result, not an implementable recipe for solving practical equilibrium instances more quickly.

Sharper size bounds, simpler robust encodings, and improved application-specific approximation thresholds remain separate questions. Fine-grained consequences based on PPAD exponential-time assumptions remain conditional. The digest reports the construction and consequences as stated, without verifying the lengthy coding, geometric, or gate-level arguments.

8. Sources and further reading

Babichenko–Papadimitriou–Rubinstein states the conjecture and its original equilibrium motivation. Chen–Deng–Teng, Daskalakis–Goldberg–Papadimitriou, and PureCircuit develop the generalized-circuit background. The source manuscript below provides the quasilinear construction, rational-witness totality, universal decoder, and separately specified game and market applications.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The PCP-for-PPAD conjecture: a quasilinear reduction (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Log-concave sampling: a zero dimension exponent for exact oracle queries
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 139 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 2/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Suppose a probability density is known only through a function and its gradient. How many evaluations are needed to draw a sample approximately from that density?

For a potential V:Rd→RV:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb RV:Rd→R, the target density is proportional to e−V(x)e^{-V(x)}e−V(x). A convex potential has one broad basin rather than many separated wells, making sampling more approachable. Yet common numerical schemes still need a number of gradient evaluations that grows as a positive power of dimension.

Is that dependence intrinsic to the information obtained from the oracle, or partly a consequence of how the algorithm processes it?

This manuscript claims that, for a fixed well-conditioned class with a known minimizer, every positive power of dimension can be beaten in exact first-order query complexity. More precisely, for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, at most CεdεC_\varepsilon d^\varepsilonCε​dε queries suffice for a fixed total-variation accuracy. A logarithmic lower bound remains.

The distinction from running time is decisive. Computation between queries is unrestricted, exact real-valued responses are available, and no arithmetic or bit-cost bound is supplied. The theorem concerns the number of contacts with the unknown potential.

2. Background and essential definitions

Assume VVV is twice continuously differentiable and normalized by V(0)=0V(0)=0V(0)=0 and ∇V(0)=0\nabla V(0)=0∇V(0)=0. The origin is therefore a known minimizer. Its Hessian satisfies

Id⪯∇2V(x)⪯2Idfor every x∈Rd.I_d\preceq\nabla^2V(x)\preceq2I_d\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^d.Id​⪯∇2V(x)⪯2Id​for every x∈Rd.

The matrix inequality means that every directional curvature lies between one and two. This combines strong convexity, which prevents flat directions, with smoothness, which limits curvature. The condition number is at most two.

The target Gibbs law is

πV(dx)=ZV−1e−V(x) dx,ZV=∫Rde−V(x) dx.\pi_V(dx)=Z_V^{-1}e^{-V(x)}\,dx,\qquadZ_V=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-V(x)}\,dx.πV​(dx)=ZV−1​e−V(x)dx,ZV​=∫Rd​e−V(x)dx.

The unknown normalizing constant makes the density integrate to one. A first-order query at xxx returns both V(x)V(x)V(x) and the entire gradient vector ∇V(x)\nabla V(x)∇V(x), exactly. One query therefore contains ddd real gradient coordinates; query count is not coordinate-operation count.

The distance requirement is total variation at most 1/101/101/10. Total variation is the largest difference in probabilities assigned to the same measurable event by two laws. It controls all events, not just expectations of smooth functions.

Let Q(d)Q(d)Q(d) be the smallest worst-execution query budget sufficient for every potential in the class. Algorithms may choose later queries adaptively from earlier replies and use private randomness. Their only information about VVV comes from oracle replies.

The optimal dimension exponent is the limiting upper growth rate of log⁡Q(d)/log⁡d\log Q(d)/\log dlogQ(d)/logd. Exponent zero permits growth slower than every fixed positive power. It does not necessarily mean constant or polylogarithmic query complexity.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Langevin sampling connects gradients with stochastic dynamics whose equilibrium is the target distribution. Nonasymptotic analyses by Dalalyan and Durmus–Moulines quantify how discretization and finite running time affect sampling accuracy. Underdamped dynamics and randomized midpoint methods improve dimension dependence under appropriate assumptions.

Accuracy metrics matter in these comparisons. A Wasserstein bound controls transportation cost, while total variation controls all measurable events. A rate in one metric cannot be silently assigned to another without a conversion theorem and its parameter losses.

The source cites recent methods with roughly d1/3d^{1/3}d1/3 query dependence at fixed conditioning and total-variation accuracy. Chen and coauthors’ smoothed Picard HMC improves the relevant fixed-accuracy exponent to 1/61/61/6 through a relative-entropy guarantee. Its expected query bound can be capped with a controlled additional error to obtain a fixed worst-run budget at the accuracy used here.

The manuscript also discusses a subsequent Gaussian-cloud correction preprint, which improves a different high-accuracy tradeoff while retaining polylogarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy. This is not the same objective as fixing accuracy and driving the dimension exponent to zero.

High-order Hamiltonian methods already exploit additional smoothness or structure. The new claim instead keeps only the stated C2C^2C2 regularity and two-sided Hessian bounds. Higher derivatives arise after Gaussian smoothing, and the challenge is to implement the resulting conditional means through finitely many queries to the original gradient.

For lower bounds, Chewi and coauthors developed rotationally invariant Gaussian constructions and already obtained logarithmic dimension dependence in a related fixed-parameter setting. The new paper adapts that strategy to its exact spectral interval and accuracy threshold rather than presenting the general lower-bound method as new.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there is a constant CεC_\varepsilonCε​ such that

Q(d)≤Cεdε(d≥2).Q(d)\le C_\varepsilon d^\varepsilon\qquad(d\ge2).Q(d)≤Cε​dε(d≥2).

The algorithm makes at most this many exact first-order queries on every execution. Its output law is within total variation 1/101/101/10 of πV\pi_VπV​ for every potential satisfying the stated assumptions.

The approximation orders and constants may depend on ε\varepsilonε. This family of guarantees does not provide one explicit polylogarithmic bound, and it does not supply a uniform small constant as ε\varepsilonε tends to zero.

The manuscript also states that there are absolute c>0,d0c>0,d_0c>0,d0​ with

Q(d)≥clog⁡d(d≥d0),Q(d)\ge c\log d\qquad(d\ge d_0),Q(d)≥clogd(d≥d0​),

even for arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms with unrestricted computation between queries. The lower bound already holds for centered Gaussian targets whose potentials have the form V(x)=xTAx/2V(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax/2V(x)=xTAx/2, with Id⪯A⪯2IdI_d\preceq A\preceq2I_dId​⪯A⪯2Id​.

Together the claims determine the optimal dimension exponent as zero, while leaving a gap in the finer growth rate between logarithmic and general subpolynomial behavior.

The oracle returns exact real values, and the model permits generation of random real variables. Algorithms may depend on dimension and must be measurable. There is no claim about the number of bit operations needed to represent queries, process answers, or write the sample to finite precision.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 2/5. The result would sharply separate information requirements from the costs of familiar numerical sampling schemes in a specialized, well-conditioned oracle model. It says that a positive power of dimension is not forced by the number of exact gradient evaluations alone.

The known-minimizer and fixed-conditioning assumptions isolate discretization and information issues from the problem of first locating a useful region. The C2C^2C2 scope is also meaningful: the method does not assume a full collection of uniformly bounded higher derivatives of the original potential.

The rating is relative to the collection and reflects the model’s limits. Arbitrary computation and exact real arithmetic between queries can hide enormous practical cost. A subpolynomial count of whole-gradient queries is therefore narrower than a subpolynomial-time sampling algorithm.

The matching exponent classification remains valuable despite that limitation. It identifies where a positive dimension exponent can and cannot be justified by an oracle lower bound, and suggests which additional resource restrictions would be needed for stronger practical conclusions.

6. The main idea

Turn the target into nearly Gaussian conditional laws

Add a small Gaussian perturbation to a target sample. Conditional on the noisy observation yyy, the original sample has density proportional to

exp⁡ ⁣(−V(x)−∥x−y∥22h).\exp\!\left(-V(x)-\frac{\|x-y\|^2}{2h}\right).exp(−V(x)−2h∥x−y∥2​).

After rescaling around yyy, this is a standard Gaussian multiplied by a weak perturbation. Small hhh reduces the perturbation’s curvature, making it a reusable auxiliary sampling problem.

This Gaussian conditional framework has established precedents. The new construction needs two related operations: a sample with added Gaussian noise and a conditional gradient mean with added Gaussian noise. The added noise is used as part of the recursive implementation, not merely tolerated as an uncontrolled output error.

Obtain high-order structure by smoothing

Gaussian conditioning makes conditional means smoother than the original C2C^2C2 potential. Their higher derivatives form tensors, which can be viewed as matrices by dividing their coordinate slots into two groups.

The manuscript bounds these matrices for every such division. This controls the contractions appearing in high-order flow approximations without paying an additional large power of dimension at each derivative. The relevant flows interpolate between Gaussian and target-like distributions and express their velocities through conditional gradient means.

A second stationary flow uses an auxiliary Gaussian momentum variable. Its displacement converts an integral of conditional means into a Gaussian centered at the desired mean. High-order quadrature then represents the needed operations as finite nested expressions in conditional means.

Implement noisy means with actual oracle calls

Writing a formula involving an exact conditional mean is not enough: that mean is itself unknown. The manuscript recursively replaces mean calls by procedures using only the original gradient oracle.

Its key mechanism is a translation property of random seeds. A shift in a conditional center can be compensated by a specified shift of Gaussian seeds while leaving the primitive query locations unchanged. Reducing the seed covariance then absorbs independent Gaussian uncertainty in the center.

The construction controls both the dependency depth of the finite expressions and the height of the routines evaluating their means. With approximation orders chosen for the desired ε\varepsilonε, this yields the claimed arbitrarily small positive query exponent.

The final output must approximate the original target, not a Gaussian-blurred version. A further sequence of conditioning steps reduces the auxiliary variance, followed by a Gaussian approximation centered at the appropriate mode. This removal of noise is necessary for the total-variation conclusion.

Hide a Gaussian covariance from too few queries

For the lower bound, take a quadratic potential. A gradient query returns AxAxAx, so sampling the target N(0,A−1)N(0,A^{-1})N(0,A−1) is a matrix-vector information problem.

Randomly rotate a carefully selected spectrum inside [1,2][1,2][1,2]. With few adaptive queries, much of the rotation remains unexposed. A deferred-revelation argument places even an unrestricted randomized output within an enlarged random span generated by matrix powers and auxiliary Gaussian vectors.

A separating statistic behaves differently on that information-limited output and on a true target sample. The argument yields a logarithmic query obstruction. It is independent of the upper-bound construction and does not claim that every sampler must follow a particular iterative scheme.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The minimizer is supplied and normalized to the origin. Finding it is not part of the query budget. The condition number is fixed at two, and the target accuracy is fixed at 1/101/101/10; general dependence on conditioning and arbitrary accuracy is not determined by the headline theorem.

Exact gradients can carry much more information than noisy or finite-precision responses. The result does not directly cover stochastic gradients, limited precision, or a realistic bit-cost model.

Exponent zero leaves a quantitative gap. The upper bound does not establish O((log⁡d)C)O((\log d)^C)O((logd)C), while the lower bound rules out a bounded query count. Determining the finer optimal rate remains open in the manuscript.

Finally, high approximation orders and unrestricted inter-query computation can make the construction unsuitable for implementation. Turning the information-theoretic improvement into an efficient numerical sampler would require additional complexity and stability analysis. The digest reports the claimed smoothing, recursion, and lower-bound mechanisms without independently checking them.

8. Sources and further reading

The Langevin papers introduce finite-time sampling analysis; smoothed Picard HMC and Gaussian-cloud correction provide the immediate high-order context. Chewi and coauthors supply the Gaussian oracle lower-bound framework. The source manuscript below states the subpolynomial query theorem and its logarithmic obstruction in one precise model.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Subpolynomial query complexity for well-conditioned log-concave sampling (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One-tape computation: trading unrestricted time for two-fifths-power space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 137 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 2/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A computation that runs for TTT steps can visit and modify as many as TTT tape cells. To reproduce its final answer, must a simulator remember all those cells at once?

If time is unlimited, the simulator can recompute information instead of retaining it. This creates a time–space tradeoff: repeated reconstruction may save memory at the cost of an enormous increase in running time.

For deterministic machines with one writable tape, a classical simulation uses roughly the square root of the original time as space. The manuscript in this family claims a smaller exponent:

O ⁣(T2/5polylog⁡(T+2))O\!\left(T^{2/5}\operatorname{polylog}(T+2)\right)O(T2/5polylog(T+2))

work-space bits. Here polylog⁡\operatorname{polylog}polylog means a fixed power of a logarithm.

The machine model and output are essential. The source has one writable tape and one writable head moving locally. A fixed number of additional read-only heads are allowed. The simulator reports the finite-control and halting outcome by the supplied time cap; it need not materialize the entire final tape. No useful simulation-time bound is asserted.

2. Background and essential definitions

A deterministic Turing machine has a finite control state, a finite tape alphabet, and a head that reads a symbol, writes a symbol, changes state, and moves locally. In this theorem the writable tape is indexed by integers and its head moves at most one cell per step.

The machine itself is fixed. The varying inputs are a public input xxx and a binary-encoded time cap T≥2T\ge2T≥2. Halting states are made absorbing, so asking for the state after TTT steps also records whether the machine halted earlier and what its outcome was.

Work space counts bits used by the simulator, excluding the read-only input. The simulator may rescan that input and recompute intermediate objects. Its time can be much larger than TTT.

The theorem includes a precise access condition for initial tape symbols. A fixed procedure must supply the symbol at any displacement ∣q∣≤T|q|\le T∣q∣≤T from a relevant head origin using polylogarithmic space. The underlying initial symbol functions are fixed independently of the cap. This rules out hiding a cap-dependent computation inside the initial tape description.

Ordinary explicit inputs satisfy the access condition: keep a counter and rescan the input to the requested position or an endmarker. The condition also permits some implicit encodings, provided they admit the same small-space access throughout the entire numerical range that local simulations may inspect.

A bound O~(T2/5)\widetilde O(T^{2/5})O(T2/5) abbreviates T2/5T^{2/5}T2/5 times logarithmic factors. It implies O(T2/5+η)O(T^{2/5+\eta})O(T2/5+η) for every fixed η>0\eta>0η>0, but not a log-free O(T2/5)O(T^{2/5})O(T2/5) endpoint.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical work on tape bounds and time–space tradeoffs asked how a long sequential computation could be reconstructed with less stored information. Paterson’s 1972 tape-bound paper, Ibarra and Moran’s single-tape tradeoffs, and Liśkiewicz and Loryś’s 1990 simulations form part of this background.

Williams’s account attributes the classical one-read/write-tape square-root-space simulation to Hopcroft and Ullman. More recently, Williams proved a broader multitape time-to-space simulation using O(tlog⁡t)O(\sqrt{t\log t})O(tlogt​) space under the stated time assumptions. His work asks whether the one-tape square-root exponent can be reduced by a fixed positive amount.

A key ingredient is the Cook–Mertz tree-evaluation algorithm. Its use of shared storage can avoid paying the full size of a value at every recursive level. Goldreich’s exposition explains the role of interpolation and a global register pool.

The present manuscript adapts this kind of recomputation to the special geometry of one writable head. Its proposed gain comes from organizing visits to tape blocks into epochs and arranging that large guesses are retained only on selected recursive dependencies.

The claim is therefore more specific than a new general multitape simulation. It answers the one-tape exponent question in the supplied-cap and symbol-access model, while separately retaining a square-root-type result for a fixed number of writable tapes.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Fix a deterministic machine with one writable tape and head, a fixed number of read-only heads, fixed head origins, local movement, and a fixed initial-symbol accessor satisfying the stated polylogarithmic-space condition. For every allowed (x,T)(x,T)(x,T), the manuscript claims a deterministic simulation of the finite-control and halting outcome by time TTT using

O~(T2/5)\widetilde O(T^{2/5})O(T2/5)

work-space bits.

Constants may depend on the fixed machine and accessor but not on the varying input or cap. The bound includes the simulator’s working storage, while the public read-only input itself is excluded. The full final writable tape is not required as output.

If the access condition holds at every cap and the original machine halts after ttt steps, no running-time bound need be supplied in advance. Trying successively larger caps gives the outcome in O~((t+2)2/5)\widetilde O((t+2)^{2/5})O((t+2)2/5) space.

For every fixed 0<δ<1/100<\delta<1/100<δ<1/10, the logarithmic factors can be absorbed to give O(T1/2−δ)O(T^{1/2-\delta})O(T1/2−δ). This is the claimed fixed improvement over the square-root exponent. The theorem does not assert the endpoint δ=1/10\delta=1/10δ=1/10 without logarithmic losses.

The manuscript also discusses space-hierarchy consequences for suitable decision languages in the one-writable-head model. Those are class nonmembership statements, not lower bounds at every input length, and do not extend to arbitrary multitape or random-access machines. The core theorem is the simulation with its explicit access and output conventions.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 2/5. The result would improve a longstanding space exponent in a fundamental but restricted computation model. It shows how local tape motion can support more aggressive recomputation than the standard square-root organization.

The exponent reduction is mathematically meaningful even with logarithmic factors. For sufficiently large caps, a fixed power saving dominates any fixed logarithmic overhead. The theorem also handles ordinary explicit input access and additional read-only heads, making the model broader than a completely isolated blank-tape computation.

The rating reflects the specialization of the conclusion. Simulation time is unrestricted, there is only one writable head, and the output is a finite-control outcome. These restrictions limit direct algorithmic applications compared with a fast general-purpose simulation or a bound for arbitrary writable tapes.

The main methodological interest is the accounting of suspended information along recursive calls. Reducing memory requires controlling not only the size of each local object but also which objects must remain live together while deeper computations run.

6. The main idea

Cut the tape where the head crosses infrequently

Partition the writable tape into blocks of width bbb, allowing the partition’s offset to vary. Averaging over offsets shows that one choice has only O(T/b)O(T/b)O(T/b) block visits. The head moves one cell at a time, so it cannot cross many block boundaries without spending steps.

During one visit, a long block of tape interacts with the rest of the computation through a short controller description: machine state, head positions, elapsed time, and terminal flags. Once a candidate controller transcript is fixed, all visits to an individual block can be replayed from that block’s initial contents.

This factors consistency over blocks. Rather than store the whole tape, the simulator can enumerate proposed transcripts and check their local consequences, using recomputation whenever old block contents are needed.

Separate epochs from smaller rounds

Group about bbb block visits into an epoch. Within an epoch, append controller information in rounds of about b\sqrt bb​ visits. A block and the relevant history each fit in O~(b)\widetilde O(b)O(b) bits.

A naive recursive evaluation would keep a large round guess on every call stack level. The manuscript instead uses interpolation to evaluate a history update without retaining that guess during calls to the preceding history. The guess is kept only when calling for a block state at the start of an epoch.

That selected call moves immediately to earlier epochs. Consequently a dependency path pays for at most one retained round guess per epoch, rather than once for every step of the history reconstruction.

Borrow registers and restore their contents

The evaluator implements an additive update to one chosen register while restoring every other register, even when the shared pool initially contains arbitrary data. A recursive descendant can therefore borrow registers holding the caller’s inputs or partially accumulated output, provided it restores them before returning.

Finite-field interpolation supplies this controlled evaluation. The fields and local arithmetic can be generated with polylogarithmic space, and the procedure may enumerate large finite sets because time is not the constrained resource.

The claimed space accounting becomes

O~ ⁣(b+(1+Tb2)b).\widetilde O\!\left( b+\left(1+\frac{T}{b^2}\right)\sqrt b\right).O(b+(1+b2T​)b​).

The first term pays for local block and history storage. The second pays for retained guesses along the epoch dependencies. Its main contribution is T/b3/2T/b^{3/2}T/b3/2. Balancing that with bbb gives b5/2b^{5/2}b5/2 of order TTT, hence

b≍T2/5.b\asymp T^{2/5}.b≍T2/5.

This calculation explains the exponent once the evaluator and dependency claims are available. It is not a proof that two fifths is optimal for every possible simulation strategy.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem’s unrestricted simulation time is essential to its interpretation. The simulator repeatedly enumerates and reconstructs information. Its own time may be enormous, so the result cannot be iterated as though it were a faster simulation with a new small time cap.

One writable head supplies the block-visit structure. Additional read-only heads are tracked in the short controller, but additional writable tapes change the dependency pattern. The manuscript does not claim the same two-fifths bound for general multitape machines.

The accessor must work at every coordinate within distance TTT relevant to the capped invocation, including coordinates inspected during proposed local computations. Providing only the symbols visited by the actual unknown run would be a weaker and insufficient interface.

The final tape is not materialized. A user needing every final cell has a different output requirement and may face an output-size cost absent from the stated decision simulation.

The paper explains why adjusting its three scales alone does not lower the exponent further. That observation concerns this construction, not a lower bound on all methods. Better space exponents, useful time–space tradeoffs, and extensions to more writable heads remain distinct questions.

8. Sources and further reading

Williams gives the modern square-root-space result and the one-tape question. Cook–Mertz and Goldreich explain the shared-storage interpolation background. The earlier tape-simulation papers locate the historical tradeoff problem. The source manuscript below specifies the symbol-access interface, weighted dependency evaluator, and two-fifths calculation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Simulating One-Tape Time in Two-Fifths-Power Space (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Noiseless Gaussian regression: the sample price of finite memory and precision
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 140 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 1/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

An unknown unit vector s∈Rds\in\mathbb R^ds∈Rd generates exact linear observations. Each observation gives a fresh Gaussian vector xxx and the noiseless value y=⟨x,s⟩y=\langle x,s\rangley=⟨x,s⟩. With unrestricted storage of real numbers, ddd independent equations determine sss almost surely.

What changes if a learner reads the observations once and can retain only finitely many bits between them?

Exact observations contain arbitrarily fine real information, but a finite state cannot preserve an arbitrary collection of real equations. To obtain a more accurate estimate, the learner may need additional fresh observations even though no measurement noise is present.

This family contains six manuscripts developing a common precision lower bound through different geometric and information-theoretic methods. The broad fixed-memory statement is that, for every fixed A>0A>0A>0, retaining at most Ad2Ad^2Ad2 bits forces a sample horizon of order at least dlog⁡(1/ε)d\log(1/\varepsilon)dlog(1/ε) to achieve angular error ε\varepsilonε. Other manuscripts give subquadratic-memory consequences, explicit constants, and analytic comparisons that support this conclusion.

2. Background and essential definitions

The signal lies on the unit sphere

Sd−1={s∈Rd:∥s∥=1}.S^{d-1}=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s\|=1\}.Sd−1={s∈Rd:∥s∥=1}.

At time ttt, the learner receives

Xt∼N(0,Id),Yt=⟨Xt,S⟩,X_t\sim N(0,I_d),\qquad Y_t=\langle X_t,S\rangle,Xt​∼N(0,Id​),Yt​=⟨Xt​,S⟩,

with independent Gaussian rows and exact labels. The signal is fixed before sampling, or drawn independently from a stated prior. The main average-case prior is uniform on the sphere.

An MMM-bit learner has at most 2M2^M2M persistent states at each index. It may perform unrestricted computation on the current observation and use fresh randomness, but only its next finite state survives. It cannot choose the Gaussian rows or reread discarded observations.

A data-independent shared seed may select the rules, which can depend on dimension, accuracy, and sample index. The seed and initial state are jointly independent of the signal and rows. This permits very general algorithms without granting hidden data-dependent advice.

The learner stops by a prescribed deterministic horizon TTT. Its unit-vector output S^\widehat SS depends only on the terminal state, stopping index, and fresh randomness. In particular, the final raw observation is not available to an uncharged output computation after it has been discarded.

Angular error is

arccos⁡⟨S^,S⟩.\arccos\langle\widehat S,S\rangle.arccos⟨S,S⟩.

Success at accuracy ε\varepsilonε means that this angle is at most ε\varepsilonε. The main statements cover 0<ε≤1/100<\varepsilon\le1/100<ε≤1/10, uniformly across this range at sufficiently large dimension.

Mutual information measures how much observing a random variable reduces uncertainty about another. A finite state has limited entropy, but this elementary fact alone does not produce the sharp sample bound: exact observations and highly concentrated conditional signal distributions require geometric analysis.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Work on memory-constrained learning established that stored information can be a statistical resource independent of computation time. Steinhardt and Duchi studied minimax rates in sparse noisy regression. Steinhardt, Valiant, and Wager connected memory with communication and statistical queries.

For discrete learning, Raz proved a quadratic-memory versus exponential-sample separation for parity. Finite-width branching programs became an important way to model a learner’s retained state. Exact real observations create different technical issues from finite-alphabet samples, so those results do not directly settle the present regression model.

The closest precision comparison is Sharan, Sidford, and Valiant. Their Gaussian-regression theorem includes a small positive additive noise, memory at most d2/4d^2/4d2/4 bits, and Euclidean accuracy d−rd^{-r}d−r in a specified range. It gives a sample lower bound of order dlog⁡rd\log rdlogr.

The new family claims a stronger precision dependence and exact labels. A lower bound for noisy observations alone cannot establish one for noiseless observations: the latter provide more information. Conversely, a noiseless learner can add synthetic noise, so an exact-observation lower bound can transfer to appropriately matched noisy models.

Dagan, Kur, and Shamir studied related linear-prediction space barriers, including approximate null vectors and empirical residuals on a random-order equation system. Those objectives and joint data distributions differ from recovery of one fixed signal under independent fresh Gaussian rows.

The geometric tools have older roots in projection theory, inverse-distance energies, and affine-volume formulas. The manuscripts combine these ideas with finite-message selection, conditional information, and the need to control increasingly localized signal distributions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The common regression conclusion

M1 states that, for every fixed finite A>0A>0A>0, there are cA>0,dAc_A>0,d_AcA​>0,dA​ such that memory M≤Ad2M\le Ad^2M≤Ad2, dimension d≥dAd\ge d_Ad≥dA​, and uniform-sphere average success at least 2/32/32/3 imply

T≥cAdlog⁡(1/ε).T\ge c_A d\log(1/\varepsilon).T≥cA​dlog(1/ε).

No relation between accuracy and memory is assumed. The constant may depend on AAA; this is not a uniform statement when AAA grows with dimension. For M(d)=o(d2)M(d)=o(d^2)M(d)=o(d2), the lower-bound constant can be absolute, with the dimension threshold depending on the memory sequence.

A guarantee of success for every fixed signal implies the average guarantee and therefore the same bound. This does not mean every individual signal is difficult for every learner.

What the six manuscripts contribute

ManuscriptPrincipal contribution and stated scope
M1Backward propagation of future-success concentration; the bound for every fixed quadratic-memory coefficient AAA.
M2Conditional-information inequalities from several posterior replicas and an analyst-only independent projection; a subquadratic-memory streaming consequence.
M3Localization and information-growth arguments that account for the cost of revealing cells, scales, or other auxiliary information; separate cube-chart and spherical-prior formulations.
M4Exact projection moments, positive domination by spherical-cap measures, and fixed-offset inverse-distance estimates; several regression proofs and an explicit memory tradeoff.
M5Comparison of actual observation rows with fresh independent rows after a finite message has been selected; a subquadratic-memory consequence already at average success 3/53/53/5.
M6Residual-subsphere analysis with the explicit subquadratic-memory bound T≥2−16dlog⁡2(1/ε)T\ge2^{-16}d\log_2(1/\varepsilon)T≥2−16dlog2​(1/ε) at success 2/32/32/3.

M4’s integrated-projection argument also states

T≥c dlog⁡(1/ε)1+M/d2T\ge\frac{c\,d\log(1/\varepsilon)}{1+M/d^2}T≥1+M/d2cdlog(1/ε)​

for arbitrary nonnegative integer MMM, at an absolute sufficiently large dimension and under its stated success convention.

M3’s cube-based routes begin with the image of uniform cube volume on a spherical patch, not uniform spherical area. Their full-range learner applications use an every-signal guarantee; its spherical routes use uniform-prior average success. The different priors and success thresholds should remain attached to their respective statements.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 1/5. This family supplies a focused precision–memory law for a tightly specified streaming-regression model. Its direct application concerns exact isotropic Gaussian measurements, a finite persistent state, one-pass access, and a controlled terminal-output rule.

Within that setting, the conclusion is informative. It explains why the availability of exact equations does not eliminate a precision-dependent sample cost once the learner must compress each observation into finite memory. For ε=d−r\varepsilon=d^{-r}ε=d−r, the scale becomes drlog⁡ddr\log ddrlogd, making the dependence on requested precision explicit.

The six manuscripts provide several routes to the same central phenomenon and develop useful geometric estimates. Their number does not multiply the scope of the application. The relative score reflects that concentration of subject matter; it is not a judgment about proof difficulty or correctness.

The analytic tools may support broader applications, but the digest attributes only the consequences stated in the sources. General noisy regression, chosen measurements, multiple passes, and arbitrary covariate distributions are separate settings.

6. The main idea

Count the information needed to localize a direction

An angular ball of radius ε\varepsilonε occupies a very small fraction of a high-dimensional sphere, on the scale of εd−1\varepsilon^{d-1}εd−1. Accurately locating a random direction therefore requires information proportional to dlog⁡(1/ε)d\log(1/\varepsilon)dlog(1/ε).

The challenge is to show that a learner with limited memory cannot retain all the useful information in each block of exact equations. Conditioning on exact labels places the signal on lower-dimensional fibers, so the conditional distribution can be singular relative to the original sphere. Treating it as an ordinary bounded density would miss this issue.

Propagate future success backward

M1 fixes a possible state and asks for the probability of eventual success as a function of the signal, using fresh future observations. This continuation function is defined even at states that the actual learner might never reach for that signal.

At termination, successful signals lie near the possible output direction. The argument bounds the mass of success inside every ball and propagates that bound backward through blocks containing order ddd measurements. Each block can enlarge the concentration parameter by only a controlled factor when M/d2M/d^2M/d2 is bounded.

Exact Gaussian projection estimates control the effect of a block. High moments introduce several possible signals sharing labels; inverse affine volumes measure how concentrated those collisions can be. Local ball bounds control the singular factors. Choosing among many next states adds a cost softened by the high moment order, producing the relevant quadratic-memory scale.

Keep the cost of auxiliary information visible

M2 draws multiple signals independently from the posterior given the same observations. Each replica has the correct signal–message relationship, but the replicas remain correlated through their shared data. An independent projection, revealed only to the analyst, retains some of that correlation.

The argument bounds the loss of correlation after projection, rather than discarding all the dependence. This yields a conditional-information estimate with the message entropy divided by a quantity proportional to dimension, plus controlled geometric terms.

M3 addresses a related difficulty: earlier messages can concentrate the posterior in a small region. It reveals a cell or scale to restore a useful spread condition, then charges for the information in that revelation. Nested-cell entropy and confinement gains balance one another. Some routes track the full history; others use a corrected information potential for the current state. These auxiliary revelations belong to the analysis and do not give the learner extra memory.

M5 handles selection bias in the observation rows. After conditioning on a state chosen from data, the actual rows are no longer interchangeable with fresh independent rows. Its comparison quantifies the information difference and charges the bias, using exact projection-density estimates and finite fiber measures.

Use caps or residual spheres to control geometry

M4 develops three related analytic descriptions. Integrated projection moments bound density concentration across label space. Positive sums of cap measures dominate selected signal distributions. Fixed-offset estimates control densities at particular affine labels through inverse-distance potentials. Each route retains its own stopping and accuracy costs.

M6 conditions a block on its observed projection. The unresolved signal lies on a random residual subsphere. High moments account for choosing among continuation states, while comparisons of directions in a common random subspace control their dependence. The construction loses only a small amount of test dimension per block, and explicit beta-distribution calculations retain the stated numerical constant.

Across these approaches, roughly log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε) blocks of order ddd observations are needed to reach constant success. The common conclusion comes from controlling both local geometry and the information retained across blocks.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Memory is measured in bits, not exact real registers. Storing ddd equations at unlimited precision would evade the finite-state model and allow direct recovery. A real-valued iterative projection method also supplies no finite-bit upper bound merely by using only a few vector registers.

The rows are independent isotropic Gaussians fixed by the observation law. Active measurement selection, rereading past samples, additional passes, or data-dependent initialization changes the model. The terminal output cannot recover discarded raw observations through an uncharged final step.

The horizon is deterministic even though stopping may occur earlier. The sources explicitly account for the information carried by the stopping index. Replacing this with an arbitrary expected-sample convention would require another argument.

The family gives lower bounds and related analytic estimates; it does not by itself establish a matching finite-bit algorithm throughout every memory and precision regime. Optimal tradeoffs beyond quadratic memory and extensions to other distributions remain separate questions. The six proof routes are reported as stated without independent verification.

8. Sources and further reading

Raz provides the finite-memory learning background, and Sharan–Sidford–Valiant gives the closest earlier precision tradeoff with noisy Gaussian labels. The six manuscripts below develop the exact-observation geometric and information-theoretic arguments. Their distinct priors, success thresholds, and memory ranges are retained in the comparison above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Memory and precision in noiseless Gaussian regression (2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Posterior replicas and conditional information in Gaussian regression (2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Localization costs and information growth for exact Gaussian observations (2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Projection moments, positive cap domination, and Riesz estimates on the sphere (2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Replacing Gaussian observations in memory-constrained inference (2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Subsphere methods for memory–sample lower bounds in noiseless Gaussian regression (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Subset Sum: a smaller time exponent and a separate low-memory algorithm
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 138 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Given positive integers a1,…,ana_1,\ldots,a_na1​,…,an​ and a target ttt, does some subset add exactly to ttt? The statement fits in one sentence, but Subset Sum is a central NP-complete problem and a benchmark for exact exponential-time algorithms.

Trying all subsets takes roughly 2n2^n2n work. The classical meet-in-the-middle method splits the numbers in half, lists the subset sums of each half, and searches for complementary values. It brings the main exponential scale down to 2n/22^{n/2}2n/2.

Two questions motivate this family. Can a classical randomized algorithm improve the exponent below one half on every input? And how little memory can an algorithm use while retaining the half-exponential time scale?

The two manuscripts answer these separately. M1 claims worst-case O(20.49n)O(2^{0.49n})O(20.49n) time for polynomial-bit inputs. M2 claims ordinary O(2n/5)O(2^{n/5})O(2n/5) writable-word space with time polynomial times 2n/22^{n/2}2n/2. The family does not claim one algorithm simultaneously achieving both advertised bounds.

2. Background and essential definitions

A solution is an index set I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}I⊆{1,…,n} satisfying

∑i∈Iai=t.\sum_{i\in I}a_i=t.i∈I∑​ai​=t.

Repeated input values are allowed, and the empty subset is permitted. Indices distinguish equal-valued items. Both manuscripts treat positive input integers and a nonnegative target.

Let bbb be the maximum bit length of an input integer or the target. Their exponential guarantees apply under each fixed polynomial-bit convention b≤ncb\le n^cb≤nc, for a fixed positive integer ccc. The program does not receive ccc; constants and the threshold beyond which the resource bound applies may depend on it.

This is different from pseudopolynomial complexity. An algorithm polynomial in the numerical target ttt can be extremely fast for small targets but exponential in the bit length of a large target. A polynomial bound on bbb still permits enormous numerical values.

The stated machine is a word RAM with words of order n+bn+bn+b bits. Arithmetic, comparisons, shifts, memory accesses, and fresh random words have specified unit costs on those words. Larger operations must be decomposed and charged. The input is read-only; retained randomness and all writable data count toward memory where a space bound is claimed.

A bounded-error algorithm may give a wrong answer with probability at most 1/31/31/3 on each fixed input. A one-sided-error algorithm in this family never incorrectly answers YES, but may fail to find a solution that exists. Neither term means the inputs themselves are random.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Horowitz and Sahni’s meet-in-the-middle algorithm established the half-exponential time scale. Schroeppel and Shamir retained that scale while reducing space to roughly 2n/42^{n/4}2n/4: four smaller lists can generate the two large sum streams without storing them in full.

Recent worst-case improvements moved different parts of this frontier. Chen, Jin, Randolph, and Servedio obtained a polynomial-factor time saving below 2n/22^{n/2}2n/2 in specified RAM models. Dividing by a polynomial does not change the exponential rate from 1/21/21/2, so it does not already yield 20.49n2^{0.49n}20.49n.

Nederlof and Węgrzycki reduced the space exponent below one quarter, using representations and weighted disjointness. Belova, Chukhin, Kulikov, and Mihajlin improved it further to approximately 0.246 under their stated input-magnitude assumptions; see Improved Space Bounds for Subset Sum.

Representation methods originated in algorithms for random hard-knapsack instances, including work of Howgrave-Graham–Joux and Becker–Coron–Joux. They give a solution many decompositions, then filter the decompositions by modular conditions. Results for random inputs do not immediately imply a worst-case guarantee, because an adversarial instance may have very different collisions among partial sums.

A useful worst-case distinction is whether an input block has many or few distinct subset sums. Few distinct sums can be compressed and enumerated cheaply; many distinct sums can support plentiful filtered representations. Both new manuscripts exploit versions of that distinction while providing explicit resource caps.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A time exponent below one half

M1 states that one uniform classical randomized decision algorithm is correct with probability at least 2/32/32/3 on every input. For each fixed ccc, all sufficiently large inputs with b≤ncb\le n^cb≤nc take at most

Cc 20.49nC_c\,2^{0.49n}Cc​20.49n

word operations on every execution, including executions that answer incorrectly. All preprocessing, tables, input accesses, and random sampling are charged.

The intermediate analysis gives 20.489995npoly⁡(n+b+2)2^{0.489995n}\operatorname{poly}(n+b+2)20.489995npoly(n+b+2). The small strict slack below 0.49 absorbs that polynomial factor separately for each fixed polynomial-bit class. No separate low-space bound is attached to this theorem.

Less memory at the half-exponential time scale

M2 states that a uniform randomized algorithm never gives a false YES and succeeds on every YES instance with probability at least 2/32/32/3. Under the same type of polynomial-bit convention, every run uses at most

Acnkc2n/2A_c n^{k_c}2^{n/2}Ac​nkc​2n/2

operations and

Ac(n+b+2)1520.199nA_c(n+b+2)^{15}2^{0.199n}Ac​(n+b+2)1520.199n

writable words. Consequently, for every fixed ρ>0.199\rho>0.199ρ>0.199, its ordinary space is Oc,ρ(2ρn)O_{c,\rho}(2^{\rho n})Oc,ρ​(2ρn); in particular, it is Oc(2n/5)O_c(2^{n/5})Oc​(2n/5).

At the endpoint 0.199, the polynomial factor remains. The cleaner exponent one fifth has enough slack to absorb it. Each word has O(n+b)O(n+b)O(n+b) bits, so words should not be silently read as bits.

Both algorithms are finite uniform programs, with no input-size advice, externally supplied tables, random oracle, or free storage of previously used randomness. Their error probabilities concern arbitrary fixed instances, not a distributional promise.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. A fixed improvement below the meet-in-the-middle exponent would be a major advance for a foundational exact-search problem. Exponential-rate savings eventually dominate polynomial-factor savings, even when the numerical change from 0.5 to 0.49 looks small.

The separate memory result addresses a different practical and theoretical bottleneck. Exponentially many stored sums can make an algorithm infeasible before its operation count becomes the limiting factor. Reducing the space exponent while maintaining the classical time scale enlarges the range of possible time–space tradeoffs.

These are still exponential-time algorithms, so the claims do not resolve P\mathrm PP versus NP\mathrm{NP}NP. The word-RAM assumptions, polynomial-bit input regime, and asymptotic constants also matter before translating the bounds into concrete performance estimates.

The rating reflects worst-case improvements in two central resource measures. It does not combine the manuscripts into an unsupported simultaneous time-and-space guarantee or imply an immediate cryptanalytic impact for every structured instance family.

6. The main idea

Detect an isolated solution through a corrected checksum

M1 first adds small random tie-breaking weights. An isolation argument ensures that, with high constant probability, one of polynomially many transformed targets has exactly one solution whenever the original instance is solvable.

Choose a random prime modulus and assign a complex phase to each subset. The exact-solution checksum can be written as

∑exact solutionsχ(I)=∑modular solutionsχ(I)−∑modular aliasesχ(I).\sum_{\text{exact solutions}}\chi(I)=\sum_{\text{modular solutions}}\chi(I)-\sum_{\text{modular aliases}}\chi(I).exact solutions∑​χ(I)=modular solutions∑​χ(I)−modular aliases∑​χ(I).

An alias has the correct sum modulo the prime but the wrong integer sum. On a negative instance the left side is zero; at an isolated positive target it is one phase of absolute value one.

The modular sum is expressed by Fourier inversion, but the modulus is too large to scan all frequencies. M1 splits frequency indices into high and low digits and filters two corresponding lists using random phase information. Some groups are summed directly; others are sampled with an inverse-coverage correction so that frequencies appearing in several matches are not overcounted.

The required estimate has small absolute error. A relative estimate of a potentially huge modular sum would not suffice when two large quantities must cancel to leave zero or a unit-size answer.

A separate representation procedure lists the aliases. The construction avoids enumerating pairs satisfying the exact integer equation, so random-prime collision estimates apply to nonzero discrepancies. Combining alias subtraction with the checksum distinguishes the isolated case from the empty one. Finite-precision calculations and capped loops are included in the stated all-execution bound.

Compress collisions or exploit many representations

M2 runs two trials rather than trying to determine in advance which kind of instance it has. One chooses several disjoint blocks and compresses repeated subset sums. Sorted streams combine these lists without storing full Cartesian products, and modular buckets are processed one at a time.

The other trial gives a solution many decompositions across shared coordinate blocks. Records retain both an exact weight and a mask identifying selected shared indices. Equal weights with different masks cannot be merged indiscriminately, because they may have different compatibility with another record.

Nested modular filters reduce the candidate lists. An additional prime splits them into smaller buckets, while disjointness tests ensure that a combined representation does not use an item twice. Random separating sets reduce compatible-mask searches to exact two-sum checks.

Memory caps require careful handling of overflow. Some oversized buckets are skipped; others are subdivided by fixing successive mask bits and regenerated. Restrictions are imposed before joining the leaf lists, allowing repeated work to be charged to refinement depth. This controls raw tuple generation, not merely the number of distinct stored records.

The success analysis fixes a useful representation before exposing later randomness. The resource analysis bounds overflow and operation failures without conditioning on that rare successful representation. Independent repetitions then raise success to the stated constant while respecting the caps on every run.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 is a decision algorithm with bounded error; M2 has the stronger one-sided-error convention but a different time bound. Neither main statement here is a deterministic algorithm, and the digest does not add a witness-output guarantee that the statements do not advertise.

The polynomial-bit convention is essential for absorbing polynomial factors into the displayed exponent slack. If bbb grows faster, the same clean asymptotic expressions need not follow. Unit-cost operations also apply only to the specified word size.

The low-space theorem counts every writable register, stack, seed, and retained random value. Reusing random bits without storing them is not free. The time theorem similarly includes preparation rather than assuming precomputed input-dependent tables.

Sharper exponents, deterministic worst-case improvements, and algorithms combining the two resource savings remain natural questions. Practical crossover and behavior on cryptographic distributions require separate analysis. The checksum, filtering, and memory-accounting arguments are reported as manuscript claims rather than independently verified.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked time-improvement and space-improvement papers show the immediate earlier frontier. The source manuscripts’ bibliographies give the classical Horowitz–Sahni and Schroeppel–Shamir algorithms and the representation-method origins. M1 below supplies the 0.49 time claim; M2 supplies the one-sided low-memory claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Subset Sum in Time $O(2^{0.49n})$ (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Low-Space Algorithm for Worst-Case Subset Sum (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Exact real feasibility through a fixed number of counting layers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 141 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Can a system of polynomial equations and inequalities be satisfied by real numbers? A small example is whether there exist real x,yx,yx,y with x2+y2=1x^2+y^2=1x2+y2=1 and x>2x>2x>2. More substantial examples ask whether a graph can be drawn with prescribed geometric relations, or whether continuous parameters can satisfy exact design constraints. Numerical approximation is not always enough: a solution may exist only on a boundary, and an arbitrarily small residual need not mean that an exact solution exists.

Now add a second layer: can we choose parameters so that a polynomial condition holds for every value of some other variables? For instance, choosing aaa so that y2+a>0y^2+a>0y2+a>0 for every real yyy is an existential–universal question. Its answer depends on choosing a>0a>0a>0, including the distinction between strict positivity and zero.

Family 141 contains one manuscript, M1, claiming that this much more general two-block decision problem belongs to a fixed level of the counting hierarchy. This is a classification of exact computational difficulty. It does not provide an ordinary polynomial-time numerical solver. Its significance is that continuous quantification, with no bound on the number of variables, can allegedly be handled using a fixed number of layers of discrete counting power.

2. Background and essential definitions

Sentences, circuits, and input length

The input has the form

∃x∈Rr  ∀y∈Rs:Φ(x,y).\exists x\in\mathbb R^r\;\forall y\in\mathbb R^s:\Phi(x,y).∃x∈Rr∀y∈Rs:Φ(x,y).

Here xxx and yyy are tuples of explicitly listed real variables. The condition Φ\PhiΦ is a finite Boolean formula: equations and strict inequalities are joined using AND, OR, and NOT. Its basic tests are p=0p=0p=0 and p>0p>0p>0, where ppp is an integer polynomial. Other comparisons can be expressed with these tests and Boolean operations.

Each polynomial is represented by an arithmetic circuit: a finite acyclic computation using signed binary integer constants and addition, subtraction, and multiplication. A computed value can be reused. There are no division or exponentiation gates, although repeated squaring can represent enormous powers compactly. For example, kkk squarings turn xxx into x2kx^{2^k}x2k.

The input length NNN counts all encoded bits, including constants, variables, and circuit wiring. Expanding the polynomials is potentially exponential in this length. A complexity bound must respect the short circuit description, rather than charge only for an already expanded expression.

The existential theory of the reals, or ETR, is the version with no universal variables. The class ∃R\exists\mathbb R∃R consists of decision problems reducible to ETR by polynomial-time transformations of finite inputs. This class concerns ordinary discrete algorithms, even though their questions involve real witnesses.

What counting power means

The class P\mathrm PP contains problems decidable in polynomial time. The class PP\mathrm{PP}PP permits a polynomial-time randomized computation whose acceptance probability is greater than 1/21/21/2 exactly on yes-instances.
